What the lottery actually is

The SMN is Mexico’s compulsory military service. Under the Ley del Servicio Militar, the ‘service of arms’ is obligatory and of public order for Mexicans by birth or naturalization, according to press quotations. The law was originally published in 1940, with its latest reform on May 18, 2022.

The process runs in five steps: alistamiento (registration), sorteo (lottery), reclutamiento (recruitment), adiestramiento (training), and liberación (getting your cartilla freed). The lottery assigns men to ‘encuadrado’ status — meaning they must attend training — or to ‘disponibilidad’ (standby).

For 2026, the class is ‘Clase 2008’ — men born in 2008 who turn 18 this year. SEDENA officially informed that the lottery for this class will happen in November 2026. Those assigned encuadrado attend 13 Saturday sessions starting in 2027.

The 18-to-39 age range, explained

The 18-to-39 figure circulating online is real, but it doesn’t mean what the viral posts suggest. It describes ‘remisos’ — men who did not complete their SMN paperwork when they should have. These men are still under obligation to regularize their situation.

A remiso must regularize their status to obtain their cartilla. They remain under obligation until December 31 of the year they turn 40, which is why the range can span 18 to 39.

So the 18-to-39 window is about catching up on missed paperwork, not about a new draft sweeping in everyone up to middle age. The primary conscription class is still men turning 18 in 2026.

What’s compulsory, and for whom

For Mexican men, the SMN is an ‘obligación ineludible’ (unavoidable obligation), according to SEDENA communications as reported. If you’re a man who turns 18 in 2026, registration is not optional — it’s a legal duty.

If drawn encuadrado in the lottery, attendance at the 13 Saturday sessions is mandatory. Failing to present could lead to legal consequences, with up to one year of prison by court order referenced under the law.

For women, the rules are different. Participation in the SMN is strictly voluntary, and they are not subject to encuadramiento. This has been the case since 2000.

What’s actually new for 2026

The basic structure of the SMN hasn’t changed. There’s no new SEDENA notice and nothing in the official gazette for August 2026. The claim doing the rounds is the routine annual cycle being reported as news.

The 2026 convocatoria, which dates to January, opens the municipal registration window from 2 January to 15 October 2026. The Ley del Servicio Militar sets preliminaries for the second half of the year a man turns 18.

This is the same annual process. The November draw assigns a white or blue ball for ‘encuadrado’ — meaning you serve — and a black ball for ‘disponibilidad’. Cartilla liberation is in December 2026.

Why this matters for you

If you’re a Mexican man who never completed your SMN paperwork, the clock is ticking. The remiso window is real, and the November 2026 lottery for Clase 2008 is the one that applies to you most directly if you’re in that class. But even if you’re older, you still need to regularize to get your cartilla before turning 40.

For expats and investors, the practical takeaway is simpler: there’s no mass mobilization coming. The SMN is a long-standing administrative process, and the 18-to-39 scare is a misreading of the remiso rule. Your neighbor with a desk job isn’t about to be drafted.

If you have employees or family members facing this, the real deadline is paper-based: register, get your cartilla, and you’re done. The lottery is a formality for most.

Nothing in the sources suggests a shift that would affect labor markets, investment, or day-to-day life beyond the usual paperwork. The only people who need to act are those who’ve fallen behind on their SMN obligations — and they should treat this as a reminder to catch up.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is everyone aged 18 to 39 being drafted into the Mexican Army? No. The 18-to-39 range refers to ’remisos’ — men who missed registering for the SMN when they were due and must regularize their status to get their cartilla. The main conscription class for 2026 is men born in 2008, turning 18 this year. Claims about a mass draft of everyone up to 39 go beyond what the law and SEDENA state. When is the 2026 military service lottery? For Clase 2008, SEDENA officially informed that the lottery will be held in November 2026. The exact day hasn’t been published. Is military service compulsory for women in Mexico? No. Women’s participation in the SMN is strictly voluntary, and they are not subject to encuadramiento. This has been the case since 2000. What happens if I miss the registration deadline? You become a ’remiso’ — a man who didn’t complete SMN paperwork when due. You must regularize your status to obtain your cartilla, and you remain under obligation until December 31 of the year you turn 40. Legal consequences, including up to one year of prison by court order, are referenced under the law, though sources don’t clarify if this is newly enforced.

World.title: A Week On, Colombia’s Quake Toll Is Still Moving
World.content:
Colombia · Disaster

Key Facts The toll As of the national disaster agency’s 16 August evening cut, 287 people are dead. Also, 4,147 are injured, 194 are still missing, and 355 were rescued.

As of the national disaster agency’s 16 August evening cut, 287 people are dead. Also, 4,147 are injured, 194 are still missing, and 355 were rescued. The damage The disaster destroyed 26,392 homes and damaged 127,608 more. In total, 197 buildings collapsed across 472 municipalities in 15 departments.

The disaster destroyed 26,392 homes and damaged 127,608 more. In total, 197 buildings collapsed across 472 municipalities in 15 departments. The reach The event affected 185,996 people and 120,671 families. It also hit 3,207 schools, 304 health centres, and 410 roads.

The event affected 185,996 people and 120,671 families. It also hit 3,207 schools, 304 health centres, and 410 roads. Numbers move both ways The count was 294 on 15 August and 287 on 16 August. Falling tolls are normal in the first fortnight, because duplicates get removed as names are confirmed.

The count was 294 on 15 August and 287 on 16 August. Falling tolls are normal in the first fortnight, because duplicates get removed as names are confirmed. A private cheque David Vélez, the Colombian co-founder and chief executive of Nubank, is giving COP$100,000 million, which is about US$32 million, towards reconstruction.

David Vélez, the Colombian co-founder and chief executive of Nubank, is giving COP$100,000 million, which is about US$32 million, towards reconstruction. The politics A censure motion against Housing Minister Jaime Andrés Beltrán was announced on 17 August. This happened because of photographs of him on the beach in Santa Marta during the emergency.

Seven days after a magnitude 7.4 quake hit Chocó, the official count is still being revised in both directions — and the politics has arrived.

If you have been trying to follow Colombia’s earthquake from abroad, the hardest part is that the numbers keep changing. A week after the magnitude 7.4 quake struck on 10 August, centred five kilometres south of San José del Palmar in Chocó, the official toll has gone up and then back down. Here is where it actually stood at the last full count, and what has happened around it since.

President Abelardo De la Espriella announced the Nubank founder’s donation. A censure motion against the housing minister followed. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

Where the count stands

The national disaster agency, UNGRD, gives updates from time to time, not live numbers. Its last full count, at 18:30 on 16 August, showed 287 dead and 4,147 injured.

Another 194 people are still missing. Also, 355 have been pulled out alive.

Watch these two numbers because the gap between them shows where the toll will change next. The damage is huge for a country this size.

26,392 homes were destroyed. 127,608 were damaged, and 197 buildings fell.

Damage hit 472 municipalities across 15 departments. Public buildings also suffered: 3,207 schools, 304 health centres, and 410 roads were affected.

On 15 August, the official figure was 294. On 16 August, it was 287.

A falling toll can look scary if you have not seen it before, so here is why. In the first days after a disaster, the same person may be counted more than once.

For example, one count may come from a town, another from a hospital, and another from a rescue team. As names get confirmed, duplicate counts are removed.

For anyone watching from far away, write down the time and date for every number you see. A figure without a date is not very useful this week.

This is the mistake most news reports make. On 12 August, the governor of Chocó, Nubia Carolina Córdoba-Curi, said the search and rescue phase was over in her area.

She said they were no longer looking for people under the rubble.

Why the death toll went down

The search is over in Chocó, not nationally

That rule applies only to Chocó. The national emergency is still active, because 194 people remain missing.

So reports that Colombia has stopped searching are only partly correct. Chocó has moved to rebuilding, but other areas have not.

Money, tolls and a minister at the beach

David Vélez, founder and leader of Nubank, is giving COP$100,000 million — about US$32 million — for reconstruction. He confirmed this himself after President Abelardo de la Espriella announced it.

The road agency ANI, led by president Ricardo Ayerbe, has removed tolls, but less widely than news suggests. The waiver covers trucks with heavy machines, emergency gear, and aid supplies, on specific roads only.

Those roads are Buga–Buenaventura, Malla Vial del Valle, Armenia–Pereira–Manizales, Tercer Carril Bogotá–Girardot, and Girardot–Ibagué–Cajamarca. Fines for overloaded trucks are paused, so aid vehicles are not penalised.

Private car drivers still pay.

Politics has entered too. On 17 August, a censure motion was announced against Housing Minister Jaime Andrés Beltrán, due to photos of him at a beach in Santa Marta during the emergency.

It is announced, but not yet voted on.

What this means if you live in or invest in the region

Housing will shape the coming two years. With 26,392 homes destroyed and 127,608 damaged, this becomes a rebuilding and money story long after rescue work ends.

The roads on ANI’s list are the same ones used for cargo between Buenaventura, Colombia’s main Pacific port, and the inland areas. Businesses moving goods through that port should check ANI notices, not general headlines.

The Vélez donation matters for another reason. US$32 million from one private person is a big part of the early rebuilding costs.

This amount sets a new level for other big Colombian companies to compare with.

The censure motion shows how fast disaster aid turns into politics in this country. If you have projects waiting for housing-ministry decisions, this is a delay risk you should plan for.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many people died in Colombia’s earthquake? The national disaster agency UNGRD recorded 287 deaths in its cut at 18:30 on 16 August 2026, with 4,147 injured and 194 people still missing. The figure moves between cuts, so always check the date attached to it. Why did the death toll go down? It was 294 on 15 August and 287 on 16 August. Early counts often double-record the same victim through different channels, and duplicates are removed as identities are confirmed. Has the search for survivors ended? In Chocó, yes — the governor declared the search and rescue phase over on 12 August. Nationally it remains open, with 194 people still unaccounted for. Are Colombia’s toll roads free after the earthquake? Only for specific vehicles. A record wave of labour lawsuits

Argentina’s formal job market faces a wave of legal fights. The UART, the group that represents workplace-risk insurers, expects 137,800 new labour lawsuits in 2026.

This comes from press reports on 14 August 2026. It is a record, and it is higher than the 72,525 new cases filed in the first seven months of the year.

The same reports say there were 135,400 labour-law notices over the last 12 months. That is a heavy load for a system already stressed by economic uncertainty.

For comparison, the peso trades at about 1,487.75 per US dollar (as of 14 August 2026). So, the cost of legal battles adds pressure on employers who already face high expenses.

The rise is not the same everywhere. That is a regional hotspot within a national trend.

To put it in context, Argentina has 23 times more labour lawsuits than Chile, according to the same reports. Even after labour reform, the number of cases keeps growing.

Why formal jobs are vanishing

The background is a smaller formal workforce. Between November 2023 and April 2026, more than 235,000 private registered salaried jobs disappeared, a 3.7% drop.

Public employment fell by about 73,000 in the same period, leaving a net loss near 180,000 jobs.

Only 76 out of every 100 private registered salaried workers stay in the same job after a year. That is the weakest retention rate in ten years.

It means more turnover, more instability, and more reasons for workers to go to court when they lose their jobs.

This trend is not just about news headlines. It shows a slow process: businesses cutting back, workers moving to informal jobs, and the state struggling to keep pace.

The broader picture is stark.7% of the national workforce is in a situation of ‘labour vulnerability,’ meaning precarious employment or insufficient income, based on first-quarter 2026 data.

That aligns with the poverty data: poverty rose to 30% of the population in the first quarter of 2026, and indigence to 6.5%, according to another report.

Informality is now nearly half the workforce

Informal employment reached 44.2% of workers in the first quarter of 2026, according to INDEC, the national statistics agency. That’s the highest level in the recent series, up 2.2 percentage points from a year earlier.

This dual reality—more lawsuits among the formal, while more workers drop into the informal—suggests the system is pulling in two directions. Formal jobs become more expensive to maintain, so employers cut them, pushing workers into informal roles.

Informal workers have no registered contract, no social security contributions, and no legal protection if things go wrong. Nearly half of Argentine workers are in this situation, which means they have less income stability and less access to benefits, even as the formal sector struggles.

For investors, this fragility matters: a weaker formal workforce means lower tax revenue, less consumer stability, and a more volatile business environment.

Why the legal wave is a warning sign

The UART projection is an industry forecast, not an official government count. But the numbers are consistent with the 72,525 cases already filed in the first seven months of 2026, so the trend is credible.

A record wave of lawsuits raises the risk of higher costs for employers, which can feed into prices or job cuts. The rise in informality means more people outside the social safety net, which can hit consumption and public finances.

But there is another side. Courts are rejecting some claims.

In Resistencia, a judge dismissed a worker’s lawsuit. He ordered the worker to pay the employer’s legal costs.

He called the claim ‘manifestly unfounded.’

This shows some lawsuits may be speculative. But the large number still puts pressure on the system.

For people living in or investing in Argentina, this matters. A record wave of lawsuits could raise costs for employers.

That may lead to higher prices or fewer jobs.

More informal work means more people lack protection. This can hurt spending and government finances.

If you own Argentine stocks or bonds, watch the labour market. Formal jobs are shrinking.

The courts are getting busier. This is a sign of stress, not stability.

The data comes from UART projections via press reports. It is not official government statistics.

Treat it as an industry view.

But the direction matches the wider picture of economic strain.

The peso’s slide, now at 1,487.75 per dollar, makes things harder. It affects litigation costs and the real value of wages.

Watch the next few months. If the caseload keeps rising, expect more pressure on employers.

More workers may fall into the informal economy.

What this means for you

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the UART and why does its projection matter? UART is the Unión de Aseguradoras de Riesgos del Trabajo, the trade body for workplace-risk insurers in Argentina. They track labour lawsuits because they’re responsible for insuring against workplace accidents and disputes. Their projection of 137,800 lawsuits for 2026 is based on industry data, reported by press, and signals rising formal-sector friction. How does the 44.2% informality rate affect the average worker? Informal work means no registered contract, no social security contributions, and no legal protection if things go wrong. Nearly half of Argentine workers are in this situation, which means they have less income stability and less access to benefits, even as the formal sector struggles. Is the 137,800 lawsuits figure an official government statistic? No. It’s a projection from UART, based on industry data, and reported by the press. It’s not a government or regulator figure. The number is consistent with the 72,525 cases filed from January to July 2026, but treat it as an industry forecast, not an official count. What does the 76-out-of-100 retention rate tell us? It means that for every 100 private registered salaried workers, only 76 are still in the same job after 12 months. That’s the weakest rate in a decade, showing that job stability is eroding. High turnover can lead to more lawsuits and more informality, as workers lose formal posts and move to informal ones.

World.title: Peru’s Mining Boom: Investment Up 42.7%, Not 74%
World.content:
Peru · Mining

Key Facts Investment rise — Peru’s mining investment grew 42.7% year-on-year to US$3.304 billion in H1 2026, per MINEM and Andina.

— Peru’s mining investment grew 42.7% year-on-year to US$3.304 billion in H1 2026, per MINEM and Andina. The 74% myth — A widely shared figure of +74% is actually Fresnillo’s revenue increase (up 74.7% to US$3.38 billion), a Mexico-only company, not a Peru sector total.

— A widely shared figure of +74% is actually Fresnillo’s revenue increase (up 74.7% to US$3.38 billion), a Mexico-only company, not a Peru sector total. Top spenders — Leading investors include Southern Peru (US$432.7 million, up 101.1%), Shougang Hierro Peru (US$314.4 million, up 135.4%), Las Bambas (US$275.5 million, up 50.5%), Antamina (US$271.6 million, up 31.2%), Buenaventura (US$174.2 million, up 2.4%), and Cerro Verde (US$169.3 million, up 3.8%).

Company profits — MMG (which runs Las Bambas in Peru) reported profit after tax of US$1,366.0 million, up 89%—not 141%, which is the rise in cash.

— MMG (which runs Las Bambas in Peru) reported profit after tax of US$1,366.0 million, up 89%—not 141%, which is the rise in cash. Quellaveco shines — Anglo American’s Quellaveco mine brought in US$2.161 billion in revenue, up from US$1.524 billion a year earlier.

— Anglo American’s Quellaveco mine brought in US$2.161 billion in revenue, up from US$1.524 billion a year earlier. Copper giant — Southern Copper’s first-half net sales were US$8.54 billion, up 38.4% (US$8,540.4m against US$6,172.9m).

— Southern Copper’s first-half net sales were US$8.54 billion, up 38.4% (US$8,540.4m against US$6,172.9m). Weak spot — Exploration spending rose only 1.3%, to US$336.4 million, even as investment boomed.

The real story: Peru’s mining investment hit US$3.3 billion in H1 2026, up 42.7% year-on-year. That 74% figure? It’s a Mexican miner’s revenue.

If you’ve seen headlines about Peru’s mining sector surging 74%, you might be forgiven for thinking the country is swimming in cash. But the actual official figure is different: mining investment rose 42.7% to US$3.304 billion in the first half of 2026, according to Peru’s Ministry of Energy and Mines (MINEM) via state news agency Andina. The 74% bump belongs to Fresnillo, a Mexico-only miner—not Peru. Let’s clear up the confusion so you know what’s really happening on the ground.

An open-pit operation in the Peruvian Andes. Mining investment reached US$3.304 billion in the first half of 2026. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

The real numbers from MINEM

Peru’s Ministry of Energy and Mines (MINEM) reported that mining investment totaled US$3.304 billion in the first half of 2026, a 42.7% jump from the same period last year when it was US$2.3152 billion. That’s the official, sector-wide figure, and it’s solid growth—just not the 74% some headlines suggest.

The investment leaders, according to MINEM, are Southern Peru, Shougang Hierro Peru, Las Bambas, Antamina, Buenaventura, and Cerro Verde. Southern Peru alone invested US$432.7 million, up 101.1% from a year earlier.

But there’s a weak spot: exploration spending rose only 1.3%, to US$336.4 million. Investment is booming; the search for the next deposit is not. For context, that US$3.304 billion is roughly 11.1 billion soles at the current exchange rate of 3.3647 soles per US dollar. It’s a healthy number, showing that miners are putting money into the ground—and that confidence is a big deal for a country that’s the world’s second-largest copper producer.

Where the 74% figure really comes from

The 74% figure that’s been floating around is real, but it’s not about Peru as a whole. It comes from Fresnillo, a Mexico-based mining company, which reported a 74.7% rise in first-half 2026 revenue, reaching US$3.38 billion, and net profit of US$1.46 billion, up 213%. Fresnillo has no Peru operations at all—its mines are at Saucito, Herradura, Juanicipio, Fresnillo, Cienega and San Julian. So it’s not a reflection of Peru’s mining sector.

So when you see claims about Peru’s mining profits soaring 74%, double-check the source. The official Peruvian metric is the 42.7% investment increase, and that’s the one to trust for sector health. Why does this matter? Because investment is a forward-looking indicator—it shows companies are confident enough to spend on new projects and expansion. Profits can be volatile, but investment signals long-term commitment.

The confusion likely stems from a mix of company-level results and sector-wide data being shared without clear labels. For instance, MMG’s profit surged, but that’s a single company, not the whole sector. Fresnillo’s revenue jump is impressive, but it’s a different country entirely.

Company-level wins that tell the real story

Peru-linked miners had a strong first half, even if the 74% headline is wrong. MMG, which operates the Las Bambas copper mine in Peru, reported profit after tax of US$1,366.0 million, up 89%, with profit attributable to equity holders of US$897.2 million. The 141% rise some cite is actually the increase in cash, not earnings. Las Bambas was central to that result, and MMG called it its strongest financial performance in more than a decade.

Anglo American’s Quellaveco mine in Peru generated US$2.161 billion in revenue, up from US$1.524 billion in H1 2025. That’s a 41.8% increase, driven by higher copper prices and production—even though output was slightly lower. Southern Copper, which runs major mines in Peru, posted first-half net sales of US$8.54 billion, up 38.4%; the second quarter alone was US$4,289.0 million.

Buenaventura, a Peruvian miner, saw net income attributable of US$514.0 million on H1 revenue of US$1,153.6 million, both materially higher than the same period in 2025. Nexa Resources’ Peru subsidiary, Nexa Resources Peru S.A.A., reported US$669 million in revenue, up 45%—not the group. The Nexa group’s first-half revenue was US$1,796 million, up 34%.

Why this matters for you

If you’re invested in Latin America, these numbers matter because they show where capital is flowing. Peru is the world’s second-largest copper producer, and rising investment means more supply coming online—which could affect global copper prices and your portfolio. For instance, MMG’s record profit and Southern Copper’s revenue surge are signals that copper demand remains strong.

For expats living in Peru, a mining boom often translates into more jobs, stronger local economies in mining regions, and a firmer sol. The currency has been stable, with the exchange rate around 3.36 soles per US dollar. Mining investment also supports infrastructure and local businesses, from equipment suppliers to service providers.

But don’t get caught up in the hype. The 74% figure is a classic example of a number being taken out of context. Stick to the official MINEM data, and you’ll have a clearer picture of what’s actually happening. And if you’re watching specific stocks, remember that company-level results can vary widely—so look at each miner’s own numbers, not just the sector headline. Also, note that Peru’s energy and mines minister is Guillermo Shinno Huamani, sworn in in late July 2026 under President Keiko Fujimori—his office is the source for the official investment data.

Frequently Asked Questions

Peru’s Ministry of Energy and Mines (MINEM) reported mining investment of US$3.304 billion in the first half of 2026, up 42.7% year-on-year. Where does the 74% figure come from? The 74% figure is actually Fresnillo’s revenue growth—up 74.7% to US$3.38 billion. Fresnillo is a Mexico-only miner, not a Peru-specific metric. Which companies led mining investment in Peru? According to MINEM, the top investors include Southern Peru (US$432.7 million, up 101.1%), Shougang Hierro Peru (US$314.4 million, up 135.4%), Las Bambas (US$275.5 million, up 50.5%), Antamina (US$271.6 million, up 31.2%), Buenaventura (US$174.2 million, up 2.4%), and Cerro Verde (US$169.3 million, up 3.8%). How did Peru-linked miners perform in H1 2026? MMG’s Las Bambas contributed to a US$1,366.0 million profit after tax, up 89%. Anglo American’s Quellaveco saw US$2.161 billion in revenue. Southern Copper reported first-half net sales of US$8.54 billion, up 38.4%.

Key Facts Banking pause FEMSA put its plan for a banking license for OXXO on hold, but it’s not canceled. The CEO said on the second-quarter call that the company will look for funding sources, and that could include getting a banking license.

The CEO said on the second-quarter call that the company will look for funding sources, and that could include getting a banking license. The Mexican retail giant is betting on its payments app instead of a bank license, and the numbers explain why.

If you live in Mexico, you’ve probably bought a snack or paid a bill at an OXXO. Now FEMSA, the company behind those stores, has paused its plan to turn OXXO into a full bank. Instead, it’s pushing hard on Spin, its payments app, which processed 119.1 million transactions per month in the second quarter of 2026.

An OXXO store in Mexico City. FEMSA had 24,708 OXXO stores in Mexico at the end of June. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

Why FEMSA changed course

FEMSA has not given up on banking. It has just paused that plan.

On 31 March 2026, CEO Jose Antonio Fernandez Garza-Lagueera told investors the banking-licence request is on hold.

The priority is to make OXXO stores more efficient and profitable. This is part of a plan called FEMSA Forward.

On the second-quarter call on 28 July 2026, he said FEMSA will need to find funding. That could include getting a banking licence.

Look at the numbers to understand this change. Spin had 119.1 million transactions per month in Q2 2026.

That is up 61.5% from the same time last year. Active users reached 11.5 million, up 22.1%.

This is strong engagement to build on. And it happens without the heavy rules of a bank charter.

Spin by OXXO is not a bank. It never was.

It is an IFPE, which means Institucion de Fondos de Pago Electronico. Mexico’s CNBV allowed this on 7 October 2022.

In simple words, Spin can hold and move money for customers. But it cannot lend deposits like a bank does.

That difference is the main point of this story.

FEMSA is testing a small credit pilot programme. CFO Martin Arias spoke about off-balance-sheet structures as the credit book grows.

Off-balance-sheet means the debts are not shown fully on FEMSA’s main financial reports. If this business matures, FEMSA could use that funding option.

Then it might look at a banking licence again later.

So this is a ‘maybe later’, not a ‘yes now’. For now, the plan is to use the Spin system to keep customers inside the OXXO world.

That includes payments, credit, and other services.

Credit is a big part of this new phase. After years of growing users and transactions, Spin now wants to make money.

Credit is one key way to do that. The small pilot is the first step.

If it works, FEMSA could expand it without needing a bank licence right away.

There is clear proof that the credit business is growing. QED Investors has bought a strategic equity stake in FEMSA’s lending unit.

FEMSA still keeps control of that unit.

If you follow Mexican retail or fintech, this shows where growth is. FEMSA is choosing a digital-first path instead of a traditional bank model.

It is betting that millions of store visits can turn into app use.

The credit experiment

What this means for investors and expats

For anyone living in Mexico, it means Spin could become a bigger part of daily life — paying for goods, maybe taking small loans. The US dollar was trading at 17.0188 pesos, so the stakes are clear: a successful fintech play could add significant value in dollar terms.

And the market has taken notice.4% and up from 42 cents a year earlier. That earnings beat, driven partly by OXXO Mexico and Coca-Cola FEMSA, suggests the strategy is already paying off.

The pause on the banking license also reduces regulatory risk in the near term, which can be a plus for shareholders watching how FEMSA allocates capital. With the stock trading at $118.12 as of August 14, 2026, up 1.39% on the day, investors seem to be taking the news in stride.

The bigger fintech picture

FEMSA isn’t alone in chasing digital payments in Latin America. The region has seen a wave of app-based financial services, from Brazil’s Nubank to Argentina’s MercadoLibre, and Spin is FEMSA’s answer to that trend.

The key difference: OXXO’s physical footprint. With 24,708 stores in Mexico as of 30 June 2026, FEMSA has a distribution channel that pure digital players lack — a real advantage for cash-based customers making the leap to apps.

By keeping the banking license on the back burner, FEMSA can move faster and lighter, testing products like credit without the heavy compliance costs of a full bank. That flexibility is a competitive edge in a region where fintech is still evolving.

Why this matters for Latin America

This story isn’t just about one company. It’s a window into how big retailers across Latin America are choosing digital apps over traditional banking structures to reach millions of underbanked people.

For you, whether you’re a local or an expat, that means more options for everyday payments and credit, often with lower fees and faster approval times than traditional banks. And if FEMSA’s credit pilot succeeds, you could see similar moves from other retailers in the region.

FEMSA believes that small shops and big size will beat strict rules.

If Spin keeps growing this fast, you may never need a bank branch.

Just use a corner store and a smartphone.

India’s state miner expects to start pulling lithium from its five Catamarca blocks within four to five years, but that timeline is an expectation, not a done deal.

If you’re tracking Latin America’s lithium race, here’s a new player to watch: India’s state-owned miner KABIL expects to start extracting lithium in Argentina within the next four to five years. But before you bank on that date, know this — it’s an expectation from a parliamentary panel chaired by Anurag Thakur report, not a binding project schedule, and there are still feasibility studies and approvals ahead. The clearest confirmed piece of this story is the January 2024 agreement KABIL signed with Argentina’s state-owned CAMYEN for exploration and development of five lithium blocks in Catamarca province — an investment of ₹2 billion, which is about US$21 million.

Lithium evaporation ponds at Hombre Muerto in Catamarca — the province where KABIL holds its five exploration blocks. The plant pictured is not KABIL’s. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What KABIL has actually signed

In January 2024, KABIL signed an agreement with CAMYEN SE. CAMYEN SE is the mining company owned by the Catamarca provincial government.

The deal covers exploration and development of five lithium-brine blocks in Catamarca. This province in northwest Argentina is known for its salt flats and lithium production.

It was India’s first lithium exploration and development agreement anywhere in the world. It marked India’s entry into Latin America’s lithium triangle.

The five blocks include four called Cortadera and one numbered Cateo-2022-01810132. Together, they cover about 15,703 hectares.

The investment for this exploration pact is ₹2 billion, or about US$21 million. This money covers studying and developing the blocks, not building a full mine.

KABIL has reported no operating revenue for the last three years because it is still in the exploration stage. This shows the financial challenge of these overseas projects.

Catamarca has offered KABIL seven additional lithium brine blocks under the same arrangement. Greenfield means untouched land, so these are brand-new developments, not expansions.

KABIL is currently evaluating these seven blocks, according to the sources. But the commercial terms for them are not stated, so no numbers are known yet.

If KABIL accepts them, it would nearly triple its footprint in Catamarca. But evaluation means nothing is final.

Argentina’s lithium triangle includes more than Catamarca. KABIL is also in talks for two lithium projects in Jujuy, a neighboring province.

In Salta, Reuters says KABIL is working on a preliminary agreement with the Ministry of Production and Mining. That deal is not final yet.

These talks are active but lack public detail on stake sizes or investment amounts. They are less important than the 2024 CAMYEN agreement.

Reuters reports KABIL expects to start lithium extraction in Argentina in four to five years, after feasibility work. This comes from a parliamentary panel report, not a company schedule.

The same panel says first production may slip to December 2030. That is one year later than the earlier target of September 2029.

Before that, KABIL must finish feasibility studies and get later approvals. It may also need to renegotiate terms as the market changes.

In mining, timelines often slip, especially when they are expectations, not commitments. The panel also noted financial limits and execution gaps in India’s overseas mineral push, so nothing is certain yet.

The seven-block expansion in Catamarca

Beyond Catamarca: Jujuy and Salta

Why the 4-5 year timeline is soft

Why this matters for Latin America

For anyone living in or invested in Latin America, this is a signal of shifting demand. India is the world’s third-largest oil importer and a growing consumer of batteries for electric vehicles and electronics, and it’s looking to Latin America to secure lithium outside China’s supply chain. Argentina, Chile, and Bolivia form the so-called ‘lithium triangle’ that holds more than half of the world’s known lithium resources, and Argentina’s Catamarca, Jujuy, and Salta provinces are at the heart of it.

If KABIL moves from exploration to production, it would add a new buyer of Argentine lithium, potentially boosting provincial royalties and foreign investment in a country that needs both. But the project’s timeline is soft, and the financial stress of KABIL — no revenue for three years — could slow things further. For now, the five blocks are signed, the seven more are on the table, and the four-to-five-year date is a hope, not a promise.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is KABIL’s confirmed lithium deal in Argentina? In January 2024, KABIL signed an agreement with Argentina’s state-owned CAMYEN for exploration and development of five lithium blocks in Catamarca province, with an investment of ₹2 billion (about US$21 million). When will KABIL start producing lithium in Argentina? KABIL expects to start extracting lithium within four to five years, according to a parliamentary panel report cited by Reuters. But this is an expectation, not a binding schedule — feasibility studies and approvals are still pending. The panel says first production has slipped to December 2030. Is KABIL expanding beyond its five Catamarca blocks? Yes. Catamarca has offered KABIL seven additional greenfield lithium brine blocks, which KABIL is evaluating. Commercial terms for those blocks are not yet public. What other Argentine provinces is KABIL involved in? KABIL is in discussions for two lithium projects in Jujuy. In Salta, it is in the process of signing a preliminary agreement, but that is not yet a signed deal.

World.title: Noboa in China: Energy, Shrimp and Debt Talks
World.content:
Ecuador · Diplomacy

Key Facts State visit: Noboa is in China from 16 to 23 August, confirmed by China’s foreign ministry. After that, he goes to Singapore and Vietnam until 28 August under Executive Decree 469.

Noboa is in China from 16 to 23 August, confirmed by China’s foreign ministry. After that, he goes to Singapore and Vietnam until 28 August under Executive Decree 469. Trade volume: Bilateral trade reached $17.33 billion in 2025, which is up 24% from the year before. Ecuador had a surplus of $1.77 billion in this trade.

Bilateral trade reached $17.33 billion in 2025, which is up 24% from the year before. Ecuador had a surplus of $1.77 billion in this trade. Debt ask: Quito wants better terms on its Chinese debt, which was about $2.2 billion as of August 2025. That debt is down from $9.6 billion in 2016, but no renegotiation is confirmed.

Quito wants better terms on its Chinese debt, which was about $2.2 billion as of August 2025. That debt is down from $9.6 billion in 2016, but no renegotiation is confirmed. Shrimp wrinkle: China stopped imports from 14 Ecuadorian shrimp companies in October 2025. The reason was sodium metabisulfite residues and white spot virus, and Noboa wants those restrictions lifted.

China stopped imports from 14 Ecuadorian shrimp companies in October 2025. The reason was sodium metabisulfite residues and white spot virus, and Noboa wants those restrictions lifted. Hydropower deal: A possible PowerChina contract at Coca Codo Sinclair is reported at up to about $1.5 billion over 25 years. This is for operation and maintenance, but it is reported, not signed.

A possible PowerChina contract at Coca Codo Sinclair is reported at up to about $1.5 billion over 25 years. This is for operation and maintenance, but it is reported, not signed. No new package yet: No agreement, memorandum, or dollar figure has been announced from the August meetings. The Belt and Road framework and free trade agreement existed before this trip.

Ecuador’s president heads to Beijing with a wish list: mining cash, relief for 14 suspended shrimp exporters, and softer terms on roughly $2.2 billion in Chinese debt.

If you have money in Latin American commodities or trade, this is a trip worth watching. Ecuador’s President Daniel Noboa is in China from 16 to 23 August on a state visit at Xi Jinping’s invitation, carrying an agenda that covers energy and mining investment, a lifeline for 14 shrimp exporters, and easier repayment terms on Chinese debt. The trip is the first leg of a broader Asia tour that runs until 28 August and includes Singapore and Vietnam, where Noboa is also scheduled to meet both countries’ prime ministers.

Noboa and Xi Jinping at an earlier meeting. The August state visit runs 16 to 23 August. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What Noboa wants from Beijing

Noboa’s agenda is a shopping list of Latin America’s classic asks: investment, trade access, and debt relief. He is scheduled to meet Xi Jinping, Premier Li Qiang, and NPC Standing Committee Chairman Zhao Leji — all confirmed in their posts. The meetings are the core of the state visit, and the stated purpose is to deepen bilateral ties and attract investment.

Ecuador wants Chinese money in energy and mining, to strengthen exports, and to sort out the shrimp suspension that hit 14 companies. There is also the matter of the Coca Codo Sinclair hydroelectric plant, where the government wants PowerChina to handle operation and maintenance. The shrimp issue is especially urgent for a sector that employs tens of thousands of people, and any delay in lifting the suspensions hits export revenues.

The numbers behind the trip

Trade is the headline. Bilateral trade hit $17.33 billion in 2025, up 24% year on year, with Ecuadorian exports to China at $9.55 billion and a $1.77 billion surplus. That surplus gives Quito some leverage in talks, though China’s sheer market size means the leverage cuts both ways.

On debt, Ecuador’s total to China is about $2.2 billion as of August 2025, down from $9.6 billion in 2016. Better terms on that would free up fiscal room for a government juggling security spending and a tough economic outlook. Debt is on the pending list, but no renegotiation has been confirmed.

On the shrimp front, China suspended imports from 14 Ecuadorian companies in October 2025 over sodium metabisulfite residues and white spot virus. Getting those lifted matters for a sector that is a major employer and export earner. Ecuador’s shrimp exports to China were worth billions of dollars annually, and the suspension has already disrupted supply chains.

The Coca Codo Sinclair angle

Coca Codo Sinclair is a 1,500 megawatt hydroelectric plant, built by Sinohydro, and transferred to Ecuadorian control in April 2026. It’s a key piece of Ecuador’s energy grid, and its operation and maintenance are on the table. The possible PowerChina deal is reported at up to about $1.5 billion over 25 years — that’s reported, not signed.

The plant, built with Chinese financing, has faced operational issues in recent years. A new contract would ensure its continued operation while transferring technical expertise. The plant’s output is critical for Ecuador’s electricity supply, and any disruption would have ripple effects across the economy.

Why it matters for Latin America

This isn’t just about Ecuador. China is the top trading partner for several Latin American countries, and the terms of its deals in Ecuador — whether on debt, mining, or infrastructure — set precedents that ripple across the region. If Ecuador gets softer debt terms, other indebted nations like Argentina, Bolivia, or Venezuela will be watching closely.

For investors, the outcome of the shrimp talks is a bellwether for how China handles trade disputes with smaller partners. For mining, any new Chinese investment in Ecuador’s copper or gold projects could shift the regional balance of extraction rights and export routes.

Ecuador joined the Belt and Road in 2018, and Xi and Noboa signed a cooperation plan in June 2025. The free trade agreement has been in force since May 2024. Ecuador’s experience — combining trade, debt, and infrastructure — is a microcosm of the complex relationship.

What is not yet agreed

The reporting is strong on the planned agenda and the existing trade framework, but as of 17 August no agreement, memorandum, or dollar figure has been announced from these meetings. The outcome of the Xi meeting has not been reported. The Belt and Road cooperation document and the free trade agreement were signed and in force before this trip, so they are not new from these meetings.

Treat the trip as a negotiation, not a done deal. If you are an investor, watch for concrete numbers on mining concessions or debt restructuring terms in the days after the visit. The absence of a signed package so far suggests the talks are still fluid, and any announcements will likely come in the form of joint statements or press releases from Quito or Beijing.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does Noboa’s China visit matter for investors? Because Ecuador is a major exporter of shrimp, oil, and minerals, and China is its top trading partner. Any deal on mining investment or debt relief could move the country’s risk premium and the outlook for its exports. What is the status of the shrimp export suspensions? China suspended imports from 14 Ecuadorian shrimp companies in October 2025 over sodium metabisulfite residues and white spot virus. Noboa wants those restrictions lifted, but no agreement has been reported from the August meetings yet. How much debt does Ecuador owe to Chinese banks? Ecuador’s debt to China is about $2.2 billion as of August 2025, down from $9.6 billion in 2016. Quito is seeking better repayment terms, but no renegotiation is confirmed. What is the Belt and Road document mentioned in the reporting? It is a cooperation framework under China’s Belt and Road Initiative. Ecuador joined in 2018, and Xi and Noboa signed a cooperation plan in June 2025. It is not new from the August meetings.

World.title: Bolivia Doubles Diesel Price for Big Users, Keeps Subsidy for Drivers
World.content:
Bolivia · Energy

Key Facts New price Large users now pay Bs 18 (about US$1.55) per litre of diesel, up from Bs 9.80 (about US$0.85). This change comes from Decree Supreme 5676, issued on 16 August 2026.

Large users now pay Bs 18 (about US$1.55) per litre of diesel, up from Bs 9.80 (about US$0.85). This change comes from Decree Supreme 5676, issued on 16 August 2026. Who’s affected The price rise hits GRACOS, which are buyers using over 20,000 litres monthly, as well as direct clients using 5,000 to 19,999 litres, and direct users using 120 to 5,000 litres. These groups buy through YPFB, and the categories come from official briefings, not the decree itself.

The price rise hits GRACOS, which are buyers using over 20,000 litres monthly, as well as direct clients using 5,000 to 19,999 litres, and direct users using 120 to 5,000 litres. These groups buy through YPFB, and the categories come from official briefings, not the decree itself. Who’s spared Transport operators, private drivers, families, small businesses, and the general public still pay the old subsidized price of Bs 9.80 (about US$0.85). Their costs stay the same.

Transport operators, private drivers, families, small businesses, and the general public still pay the old subsidized price of Bs 9.80 (about US$0.85). Their costs stay the same. Daily updates The Bs 18 (about US$1.55) is just a starting or “referential” price, and it will change every day based on world market prices. The regulator ANH lists the daily referential price on its website for everyone to see.

The Bs 18 (about US$1.55) is just a starting or “referential” price, and it will change every day based on world market prices. The regulator ANH lists the daily referential price on its website for everyone to see. Exchange rate Bs 18 equals about US$1.55, and Bs 9.80 equals about US$0.85, using Bolivia’s official rate of 11.58 bolivianos per dollar. The boliviano is now floated, and the street exchange rate has matched the official one.

Bs 18 equals about US$1.55, and Bs 9.80 equals about US$0.85, using Bolivia’s official rate of 11.58 bolivianos per dollar. The boliviano is now floated, and the street exchange rate has matched the official one. Fiscal goal Officials say this step reduces YPFB’s financial burden and cuts the cost of imports. The decree aims to manage fiscal costs and keep a steady fuel supply for the domestic market.

Large consumers will pay Bs 18 (about US$1.55) a litre from August, while ordinary drivers and families keep the subsidized Bs 9.80 (about US$0.85). Here’s who is affected and why it matters.

If you run a big fleet or industrial operation in Bolivia, your diesel bill is about to double. Under Decree Supreme 5676, issued on 16 August 2026 and announced the next day, large consumers will pay Bs 18 per litre (about US$1.55) instead of the regulated Bs 9.80 (about US$0.85). The decree, signed by President Rodrigo Paz in the early hours of Monday, targets the biggest users while shielding ordinary drivers from the increase. The government calls Bs 18 (about US$1.55) a “referential initial price” that will be updated daily based on international prices, so the final cost could move with global markets. For now, the move is designed to ease the fiscal pressure on YPFB, Bolivia’s state oil company, and to curb contraband—the government’s public justification—though the decree itself cites fiscal cost and continuous supply. Here’s what you need to know about who pays, who doesn’t, and what it means for the economy.

Bolivian miners on an earlier march. Mining is one of the high-volume sectors that buys diesel through YPFB’s direct-purchase categories. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

Who pays the new diesel price

The new diesel price is Bs 18 (about US$1.55) per liter. It only applies to certain large buyers.

The government splits these buyers into three groups. The groups depend on how much fuel they use each month.

GRACOS use 20,000 liters or more monthly for their own needs. Clientes directos use between 5,000 and 19,999 liters.

Usuarios directos use between 120 and 5,000 liters. These categories come from official briefings, not from the law text.

All these groups buy through YPFB, Bolivia’s state oil company. Buyers must be registered in YPFB’s direct-purchase categories.

These categories are usuario directo, cliente directo, and GRACO. They need a certificate or approval from the regulator.

Hydrocarbons Minister Marcelo Blanco Quintanilla explained the three-tier system on Monday. He has held the job since 23 April 2026.

The law’s goals are to reduce fiscal cost and keep supply steady for the domestic market. The government says it also helps stop contraband, but that word is not in the law.

Ordinary drivers, families, small businesses, and the public still pay the regulated price of Bs 9.80 (about US$0.85) per liter. This price was set by Decreto Supremo 5516 in January 2026.

Your regular fill-up is not affected. The subsidized gasoline price stays at Bs 6.96 per liter (about US$0.60).

The higher price only applies to buyers registered in YPFB’s direct-purchase categories. These need a certificate or approval from the regulator.

Anyone using a normal pump pays Bs 9.80 (about US$0.85) per liter, no matter how much they buy monthly. So everyday travel costs stay the same.

Government officials say the measure should not raise food prices. Users below the limit keep the subsidized price.

Transport operators are also exempt from the increase. This helps keep food and goods moving without higher market prices.

If you are a small business owner with a couple of vans, you are safe. The new price does not touch you.

The law’s goals are the fiscal cost and steady supply for the domestic market. Bolivia imports a large part of its diesel.

Higher global prices have been putting pressure on state finances. The government says the move also fights contraband, though the law does not mention it.

What stays the same for most Bolivians

Why the government is doing this

The Bs 18 (about US$1.55) figure is a first, temporary price for reference. A government rule that sets how the price is calculated must come within five working days.

The regulator ANH posts the reference price every day on its website. It uses world prices plus transport costs and taxes.

This change does not end the big subsidy. It hits the largest users, like mining or transport companies that use many liters of diesel each month.

Smaller consumers still pay the old, lower price. The goal is to cut the government’s spending gap while keeping social peace.

If you run a business that uses thousands of liters of diesel monthly, expect higher fuel costs from now on. The price changes daily, so you should watch it closely—your fuel bill may rise or fall with world markets.

For expats and investors, the key point is that most people keep the subsidy. The chance of street protests over fuel is lower than if the government cut it for everyone.

Still, watch civic groups and unions. They have already asked to meet with YPFB to talk about the new rule.

The daily repricing shows Bolivia is moving slowly toward market-based fuel prices. Look to see if the subsidy grows or shrinks in the next months.

If the government’s money situation improves, it may raise the price for more users. If protests grow, it may pull back the change.

For anyone living or investing in Latin America, this is a test of how subsidized fuel systems handle world price shocks. Bolivia is choosing to end subsidies step by step, not all at once—a plan other countries with similar money problems may copy.

The region has seen fuel hikes cause protests before, from Ecuador to Peru. Bolivia keeps transport and small business on the subsidized price, which may reduce violent demonstrations while still easing fiscal strain.

That balance is a model other governments are watching closely. Former President Evo Morales attacked the decree on 17 August, saying it ‘llevará a la hambruna al pueblo, pone en riesgo la cosecha y la siembra’—that it will bring hunger to the people and put the harvest and planting at risk.

If the daily price plan works in Bolivia, expect similar ideas elsewhere in Latin America to cut fuel subsidy costs without upsetting voters.

What it means for you

Why this matters beyond Bolivia’s borders

Frequently Asked Questions

Does the diesel price increase affect regular drivers? No. Private motorists, families, and small businesses keep paying the subsidized Bs 9.80 (about US$0.85) per litre. Anyone filling up at an ordinary pump pays Bs 9.80 (about US$0.85) no matter how much they buy in a month. The higher price applies only to buyers registered in YPFB’s direct-purchase categories. Who exactly pays Bs 18 (about US$1.55) per litre? Large consumers (GRACOS), direct clients, and direct users buying through YPFB. GRACOS use 20,000+ litres monthly; direct clients use 5,000-19,999; direct users use 120-5,000. These tiers come from official briefings, and buyers must have a certificate or authorization from the regulator. Why is the price being doubled? To reduce the fiscal burden on YPFB and ensure continuous supply to the domestic market, as the decree states. The government also publicly justifies it as a curb on contraband. The Bs 18 (about US$1.55) is an initial, temporary referential price, with a ministerial resolution on pricing methodology due within five working days. Will the basic food basket be affected? Government officials say no, because users below the threshold—including transport operators—remain on the subsidized price. The measure targets only high-volume industrial users registered in YPFB’s direct-purchase categories.
