World.title: Middle East updates: Kushner meets Netanyahu in Jerusalem
World.content:
08/17/2026 August 17, 2026 Iran condemns drone attack on Iraqi Kurdistan premier's office

Iran's government has called a drone attack on the Iraqi Kurdistan prime minister's office "suspicious," while Baghdad has pledged to investigate the incident.

Prime Minister Masrour Barzani in the semi-autonomous region had reported the attack earlier on Monday, saying that his personal office had been "targeted by Iranian drone attacks earlier today."

The office of Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi later said that he had ordered an investigation into the incident.

Zaidi "directed the formation of an investigative committee tasked with identifying the sources and launching points of the attack," the statement said.

Meanwhile, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei condemned the drone attack, "describing it as a highly suspicious development that requires vigilance and careful attention," according to a statement carried by Iranian state news agency IRNA.

No organization or group immediately claimed responsibility for the apparent attack. Nobody was reported injured in the incidents.

Iran and Iran-backed armed groups often accuse the semi-autonomous government in the Kurdistan region of harboring and abetting Iranian Kurdish groups that Tehran sees as a security threat. Iraqi Kurdish authorities meanwhile maintain they do not allow their territory to be used to attack neighboring countries and also accuse Iranian groups of attacks on their territory.

Kurdish fighters in Iraq and Syria were instrumental in the defeat of the Islamic State militia and the region has close ties to NATO militaries, including the US, in no small part as a result of this.

World.title: Ayuso, sobre el ático de Chamberí: “No voy a necesitar una residencia oficial a 10 meses de las elecciones”
World.content:
La presidenta de Madrid, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, ha vuelto a enfrentarse este lunes a preguntas que la incomodan sobre la polémica compra del ático en Chamberí por 6,3 millones destapada por EL PAÍS, en principio para instalar “una oficina temporal” mientras se acometen obras en la Real Casa de Correos. Ayuso ha señalado que, en estos ocho años en el poder, no ha necesitado ni ha pedido nunca una residencia oficial, un servicio con el que solo cuentan los presidentes de cinco de las 17 comunidades, en muchos casos en desuso. “Y no la voy a necesitar a 10 meses de unas elecciones”, ha añadido Ayuso.

“Se podrán dar todas las vueltas que se quiera, pero yo estoy en lo importante, que es estar aquí”, ha indicado durante una visita a media mañana, que no constaba en su agenda, a la bodega Las Moradas de San Martín en San Martín de Valdeiglesias, en su ronda por los municipios arrasados por el incendio de la Sierra Oeste del pasado mes de julio. Allí, ha anunciado ayudas de 500.000 euros para apoyar al sector vitivinícola afectado por este desastre medioambiental.

Al ser preguntada sobre la compra del piso de 485 metros cuadrados por parte de una empresa pública madrileña en el paseo del General Martínez Campos, la presidenta madrileña ha indicado que lleva ocho años al frente de la Comunidad sin vivienda institucional: “No he necesitado una residencia oficial ni la he pedido y no la voy a pedir a 10 meses de unas elecciones”. Ayuso ha criticado que son muchos los ministros que cuentan con residencia oficial y se ha quejado de la distinta “vara de medir” aplicada a su caso, que le produce “sonrojo”.

Cuestionada sobre si se siente respaldada por la dirección nacional del PP, Ayuso no ha dicho ni palabra y ha tirado de gestión para asegurar que, tras el éxito de la visita del Papa y la llegada de la Fórmula 1, sus esfuerzos se concentran en recuperar las zonas afectadas por el incendio y en “organizar” la capital para los grandes eventos pendientes a partir del otoño. Sobre si ha dado todas las explicaciones sobre la operación por parte de Planifica Madrid, dependiente de la Consejería de Presidencia, Ayuso ha eludido responder y ha dicho que “poco más se puede decir, a las mismas preguntas, las mismas respuestas”.

Poco después, la vicesecretaria de regeneración institucional del PP, Cuca Gamarra, ha afirmado que Ayuso ya ha dado todas las explicaciones necesarias “por activa, por pasiva y por perifrástica” sobre la compra. Sin embargo, por no aclarar, el Gobierno regional no ha aclarado ni el precio de una operación de la que no se ha informado oficialmente.

Planifica Madrid adquirió el ático el 14 de abril y la operación no consta ni en el portal de transparencia, ni en las cuentas anuales de la compañía. En un primer momento, fuentes de su Gobierno apuntaron que el piso, con cinco habitaciones, seis baños y vistas panorámicas al skyline madrileño, se usaría como oficina provisional para unas obras en Sol de las que no se había informado, aunque se especula con que, en realidad, la Comunidad de Madrid quería convertir el ático en la residencia oficial de la Presidencia.

Sin embargo, la normativa no permite instalar allí oficinas ni tampoco es adecuado para residencia oficial, por lo que apenas un día después de estallar el escándalo, lo pusieron a la venta por 400.000 euros más de lo que costó. Su novio, Alberto González Amador, también puso a la venta el ático que posee en el mismo vecindario, en el que convive con la presidenta. El abogado Javier Flores ha interpuesto una denuncia ante el Tribunal de Cuentas para que investigue una posible responsabilidad contable por menoscabo de fondos públicos y sostiene que no se puede justificar la compra en unas obras que ni siquiera existían en el momento de la adjudicación. De hecho, fueron adjudicadas el 7 de agosto sin concurso y por casi 60.000 euros al estudio de Alejandra Pombo, 11 días después.

Tras estas escuetas declaraciones sobre el ático, Ayuso ha vuelto a arremeter contra el Gobierno y ha criticado que, mientras Pedro Sánchez “sigue de vacaciones con sus chanclas en La Mareta”, Ceuta está “al borde del colapso” 16 días después de una “invasión tolerada” por el Gobierno de España, con “la seguridad comprometida”, un “nuevo riesgo de epidemias”, así como “agresiones y violaciones diarias [hay seis denuncias por agresión sexual registradas, según fuentes policiales]”.

“Y mientras, seguimos sin saber cuánto le están costando las vacaciones al presidente ni qué políticos y amigos están utilizando instalaciones públicas, no un día ni dos, sino un mes entero, mientras España arde, está sufriendo una invasión y tiene problemas enormes”, ha proseguido en su ataque.

A su juicio, Sánchez es el político “con menor credibilidad de toda Europa”, pero “tiene las vacaciones más largas y las mayores crisis, mientras está al borde del banquillo, desnortado y, eso sí, de vacaciones”. A su juicio, el “desastre legislativo y de gobernabilidad es absoluto” y el Gobierno, “con 170 normas paralizadas en el Congreso”, tiene a España “totalmente abandonada y paralizada”.

World.title: Por Mónaco sin datos en el móvil ni wifi, la mejor manera de recorrer el Principado
World.content:
Del Casino de Montecarlo a la catedral, pasando por Le Rocher y el Palacio Principesco, esta pequeña ciudad-estado hay que pasearla sin distracciones

En mis artículos para El Viajero no suelo usar la primera persona. Sin embargo, en esta ocasión procede hacerlo, no tanto como aviso para navegantes, sino para que se entienda mejor lo narrado.

A lo largo de los últimos años he visitado en más de una ocasión el Principado de Mónaco, al que es muy fácil llegar con el tren que bordea la Costa Azul, hallándose, por ejemplo, a menos de media hora de Niza. Mi primera vez en la patria de Raniero y Grace Kelly vino precedida de un vendaval de optimismo. Recordaba consejos de profesores del pasado, bien felices de narrar al alumnado cómo esta ciudad-estado consta de unos dos kilómetros cuadrados de superficie total, lo que hace suponer un fácil dominio de ese espacio, poblado por poco más de 38.000 habitantes, de los cuales 9.600 son de nacionalidad monegasca.

Más información Viaje por la Polonia judía

Bien es sabido que las apariencias engañan. Mónaco, independizado de Génova desde 1297, no forma parte de la Unión Europea pese a sus contactos más que frecuentes con Francia e Italia. Este factor, a priori, no supone ningún problema, o al menos antes no preocupaba a ningún visitante por el hábito de ir, a lo sumo, con un mapa para orientarse por sus calles. Pero los tiempos han cambiado y ahora mismo para muchos turistas resulta imprescindible disponer de internet para caminar con garantías. En mi caso confieso que suelo usar los mapas digitales como brújula base, para, a continuación, prescindir del móvil y así poder mirar bien aquello que piso sin condenarme a la pantalla.

El problema es que en Mónaco no puedes ir tan suelto —el roaming gratuito de la UE no se aplica de forma automática por ley—, al menos si es tu primera vez en el Principado, donde un exceso de confianza puede costarte una gran frustración, como fue mi caso tras bajar del tren, sentirme satisfecho por alcanzar el Casino de Montecarlo, que es el nombre de uno de los cuatro barrios del centro de Mónaco pese a confundirse por todo el conjunto, y luego soltarme hasta, literalmente, perderme en una serie de avenidas sin ninguna referencia visual válida para rehacer el camino y recuperar la cordura del itinerario.

Lo más grotesco de esa experiencia fue que pude entender con rotundidad mi fracaso al subir una cuesta e informarme un cartel de estar en Beausoleil, pueblo francés que junto a Montecarlo forma una sola aglomeración urbana. A partir de ese punto respiré hondo gracias a las vistas, perfectas para situarme y pasear sin necesidad de datos ni de conexión wifi al comprender la morfología de la ciudad.

Exterior del casino de Montecarlo. David Gee (Alamy / Cordon Press)

La clave de todo estriba, sobre todo para caminar sin riesgo a extraviarse, en salir de la estación por el sitio justo, que siempre es la Rue Grimaldi, e ir hasta la Avenue d’Ostende, desde la que cualquier ruta es fácil, si bien recomiendo ascenderla e ir hacia el Casino de Montecarlo porque siempre es el mejor punto de partida al ser un icono alejado del resto que sirve como Kilómetro cero hacia los demás.

Mónaco legalizó el juego en 1854 y necesitaba un edificio de postín para atraer a buscadores de fortuna que quisieran combinar la osadía con el prestigio de ganar dinero en un marco de veras incomparable, como lo fue el casino desde 1878, cuando Charles Garnier, autor de la Ópera de París, le confirió su actual aspecto. Este templo mundial de la apuesta, inmortalizado por Stefan Zweig en la novela 24 horas en la vida de una mujer (1924), ha proporcionado ingentes dividendos a la familia Grimaldi, si bien en nuestro siglo su facturación no es decisiva para las finanzas del Principado.

Desde el casino, con una plaza dispuesta para transitar entre el lujo y la egolatría contemporánea del selfi, lo mejor es volver a la Avenue d’Ostende, parándonos en cualquiera de sus pequeños miradores para aprehender mejor por dónde nos movemos sin marearnos por la enorme densidad de edificios entre imposibles rascacielos y hoteles de la Belle Époque afeados por estos excesos constructivos. Al final la vista se habitúa a los mismos porque cada sitio tiene su propia belleza, aunque aquí siempre es más hermoso mirar a la izquierda para admirar el Puerto de Hércules del barrio de La Condamine, que rodearemos para llegar al otro espectáculo que la vista nos ofrece en esta panorámica: Le Rocher, o la roca en las alturas donde se concentran los distintos poderes monegascos.

Vista de Le Rocher, donde se concentran los distintos poderes monegascos. Westend61 (getty images)

La encrucijada hacia esta meta se ubica, valga la redundancia, en el cruce de la Avenue d’Ostende con su paralela dedicada a John Fitzgerald Kennedy, que da paso al Quai dedicado a Alberto I, con comienzo y final capitalizado por dos estatuas que honran a leyendas del automovilismo. La primera es de William Grover, mientras la segunda, ya en las estribaciones de las escaleras hacia Le Rocher, es un homenaje al campeonísimo argentino de la especialidad Juan Manuel Fangio, quien cosechó dos victorias en el Gran Premio más famoso del circo de la F1.

Monumento en recuerdo del piloto argentino de Juan Manuel Fangio, en Mónaco. Paul Quayle (Alamy / Cordon Press)

Desde esta estatua, una de las más fotografiadas de nuestro recorrido, disponemos de un pequeño abanico de opciones para escalar hacia la roca, aunque mi consejo es ir por las avenidas du Port y de la Porte Neuve para no repetir nuestros pasos y no aburrirnos cuando regresemos de esta expedición, que tiene como cumbre el Palacio Principesco en su homónima plaza, donde cada día, a las 11.55 en punto, se produce el muy vitoreado cambio de guardia de los Carabineros del Príncipe.

El Palacio Principesco, ubicado en la plaza homónima.

La primera piedra de la residencia real se puso a finales del siglo XIII, remodelándose hasta finales de la decimonovena centuria, cuando aún se rodeaba de una rica vegetación en los alrededores, poco a poco rebajada sin desaparecer del todo pese al crecimiento de estos aledaños, que en nuestra época mezclan lo esencial de cualquier centro urbano con un apabullante número de tiendas dedicadas a vender baratijas y souvenirs. Lo mejor, como sospecharán, es parar poquito en esos negocios y, aquí sí, caracolear por las callecitas sin temor a descarriarse porque todo queda cerca, de los miradores a la catedral, construida en 1875 y firmada por el arquitecto Charles Lenormand, con una blanquísima fachada que oculta un rico interior dividido en tres naves, a rebosar de obras de arte, muchas de ellas provenientes del anterior templo, demolido como preludio a su completa renovación de estilo neorromántico.

La catedral de Nuestra Señora Inmaculada, conocida también como catedral de Mónaco. Barry Winiker (getty images)

De la catedral —lugar de entierro del príncipe Rainiero III y la princesa Grace— al último hito de este pequeñísimo país median menos de 300 metros. Se trata del Museo Oceanográfico, impulsado por el príncipe Alberto I, cuya fama de gran navegante se simboliza por este legado, abierto al público en marzo de 1910 y dirigido a partir de 1957 (y durante más de 30 años), en coincidencia con el auge turístico, por el comandante Jacques-Yves Cousteau, fundamental para armar el aparato pedagógico de la institución, muy en consonancia con el transmitido en sus documentales televisivos que tanta popularidad le dieron durante la segunda mitad del siglo pasado.

Mónaco no encierra muchas dificultades para el visitante y puede saborearse al detalle en pocas horas con la virtud añadida de conseguir que muchos se sientan menos dependientes de la tecnología por esa carambola de no poder usar los datos del móvil como en la Unión Europea. Ahora que terminamos les confesaré que claro, seguro encuentran alguna red wifi disponible brindada por las autoridades, pero créanme, si prescinden de teclear su contraseña ganarán tiempo y el privilegio de poder andar con el cuerpo bien erguido y los ojos fijos en el horizonte, algo que, por desgracia, cada vez es menos habitual en cualquier latitud del planeta.

World.title: Marc Vicente (InPost Iberia): “El estrés no significa tener mucho trabajo, sino poco control”
World.content:
El lugar en el mundo del directivo catalán está en Andalucía: “Es donde se mejor se vive en España”

El estajanovismo de Marc Vicente (Igualada, Barcelona, 44 años) es solo comparable a su obsesión por la planificación, hasta el punto en que su calendario define lo que ha de hacer con intervalos de 20 minutos. Dirige InPost Iberia, una compañía logística con sede en Polonia que en España tiene unos 800 empleados.

Pregunta. ¿Qué estudió?

Respuesta. Turismo. Tuve la suerte de que lo hice en ese momento de la burbuja puntocom y la revolución del comercio electrónico. Me ofrecieron un puesto de becario en una agencia de viajes que resultó ser Lasminute.com, una de las primeras que se digitalizó.

P. ¿Ha visto mucho mundo?

R. Estuve seis años en Londres, luego en EEUU, República Checa, Alemania, en periodos intermitentes en Japón, Francia… lo que empezó como una pequeña aventura se transformó en un estilo de vida nómada. He cambiado de país, de media, cada tres años, al principio solo y ahora con dos niños y mi esposa. Hace un año y cuatro meses volvimos a Barcelona, cada vez cuesta más cambiar por los niños (tiene un niño de 11 y una niña de 7). El mayor, cuando tenía ocho años ya había vivido en 4 países.

P. ¿Cómo vivió el Brexit como expatriado?

R. Nos mudamos por segunda vez a Reino Unido después del Brexit, en la fase de implementación de medidas. Mi puesto requería visado, tuve que sacar la skilled workers visa, un proceso de mucho papeleo con un examen de inglés complicado que se hace en un centro de Madrid. Una vez allí, noté que la libra no es lo que era, y percibí una sociedad polarizada. Una Londres donde la gente está resignada y entristecida y zonas menos urbanas que tenían una idea determinada del Brexit y que ahora se sienten decepcionados y un poco engañados.

P. ¿Cuánto tiempo libre tiene?

R. Prácticamente, a nivel mental trabajo todo el tiempo. Debo hacer unas 12-13 horas al día entre semana, dos o tres los fines de semana. El 90% de mi tiempo es profesional, lo hago como elección, porque lo disfruto. Del 10% restante, el 9% lo dedico a la familia y los amigos, y un 1% a veces consigo dedicarlo a mí mismo. Lucho para conseguir un poco más de tiempo para mí.

P. En España vamos a por la jornada de 35 horas, está usted muy lejos...

R. Si, pero tengo que reconocer que no siento que esté trabajando, hago lo que me gusta.

P. ¿No se arrepentirá en el futuro de trabajar tanto?

R. Probablemente me arrepentiré en ciertas cosas, pero no me arrepentiré de haber dedicado mi energía a lo que me apasiona y a intentar generar un buen ejemplo para mis hijos. Para conseguir las cosas que he conseguido, a mí solo me ha funcionado trabajar duro. Si algo quiero que ellos conozcan es la disciplina del esfuerzo, que es necesaria para conseguir cualquier cosa que quieras en la vida.

P. ¿Qué aficiones tiene?

R. Soy un gran amante de la música, toco la guitarra asiduamente. Me permite aislarme mentalmente. Toco de todo, desde Metálica a un buen blues. Me gusta la lectura y escucho podcast.

P. ¿Qué tipo de contenidos suele escuchar?

R. Canales sobre economía, temas de crecimiento, aprendizaje, liderazgo… hay varios canales que me encantan sobre historias de compañías, entrevistas con líderes que admiro. Para desconectar escucho historias de true crime cuando paseo con la perra.

P. ¿Viaja por placer?

R. Solemos veranear en el sur. Aunque soy catalán en el fondo soy andaluz, me encanta Andalucía. Tengo la certeza de que algún día acabaré en Andalucía. Esté donde esté en el mundo Andalucía siempre es el sitio donde voy y creo que, de lo que yo conozco, es donde se mejor se vive en España.

P. ¿Cómo lleva el estrés?

R. Bien, tengo una muy buena relación con él. No sufro de estés con demasiada frecuencia. Para mí no aflora por tener mucho trabajo, sino por poco control. Lo domino dedicando mucho tiempo a la planificación, mucho más de lo que la gente se imagina. Soy enfermizo hasta puntos absurdos, tengo un calendario donde planifico casi cada 20 minutos lo que hago cada día. Y eso, que obviamente no siempre cumplo, me permite tener control sobre el estrés.

(En este punto enseña el calendario, donde anota desde cuándo se levanta a cuánto tiempo dedica a tomar un café).

P. Dígame un defecto.

R. Tengo que elegir entre todos los que conozco… tengo poca paciencia. Es algo que voy mejorando con los años, pero me genera inquietud. Suelo tender a querer controlarlo todo con bastante nivel de detalle, tanto mi tiempo como lo que sucede a mi alrededor.

P. ¿Si piensa en el futuro qué le preocupa?

R. El futuro me preocupa en relación a mis hijos. Me preocupa el entorno sociocultural y político al que nos enfrentamos a nivel internacional. Qué oportunidades van a tener y qué mundo les va a tocar vivir en el futuro. Desde la IA, las guerras, la polarización política, los disparates que se suceden aquí y allá, la educación... me preocupa qué entorno se van a encontrar para poder ser felices.

World.title: Schools return as new Dutch and maths targets become law
World.content:
Schools in the north of the Netherlands are the first to go back after the summer holidays, and they return to a new set of legally binding targets for what pupils have to learn in Dutch and maths.

The updated core curriculum objectives (kerndoelen) were written into law this month for the first time, NOS reported on Monday. They set out the knowledge and skills pupils are expected to acquire in primary school and the first years of secondary education.

The previous objectives dated from 2006 and were criticised as out of date, vague, and non-committal. There are now fewer of them for Dutch, but what pupils should be able to do is described more concretely. Literature has a clearly defined role, and language development is to be built into other subjects as well.

Junior education minister Judith Tielen said the change was needed because of a serious decline in basic language and maths skills.

Falling standards

The Netherlands was previously seen internationally as one of the leaders in reading, but standards have dropped sharply in recent years.

Tielen wrote to MPs recently that no other European country has seen learning performance fall as far, and school inspectors have found year after year that many children cannot read, write, or do basic maths at the expected level.

Earlier attempts to turn this around – a masterplan on basic skills launched in 2022 and the national programme set up to make up for learning lost during the coronavirus closures – have not had the intended effect, Tielen said. She is working on a new approach prioritising language.

The objectives for the remaining subjects, including two new ones – digital literacy and citizenship – are due to be made law next summer. Schools have until 2031 to incorporate all of them into their teaching.

Ilja Cornelisz, an education researcher at the Vrije Universiteit in Amsterdam, said ambitious objectives do matter because basic skills are under pressure, but that more is needed to improve schooling.

The real task, he said, is giving teachers the professional room, the reliable knowledge, and the support to deliver the goals in their own classrooms, while leaving schools free to decide how they get there.

World.title: Two minors held after second Zaandam explosion in five days
World.content:
Police have arrested two minors on suspicion of involvement in an explosion that blew the back wall off a Zaandam flat in the early hours of Monday.

The blast at the Hof van Zaenden was reported at about 1.40am and was followed by a fire, which the fire service put out quickly. Residents of the block were evacuated because of fears it might collapse, regional broadcaster NH reported.

Nobody was in the flat where the device went off and no one was hurt by the blast, police said.

Officers found the two suspects in a car close to the block shortly after the explosion. Police have not given their ages, saying only that both are under 18.

Debris from the wall was scattered on both sides of the building, and windows and frames in neighbouring flats were damaged. Forensic officers worked with the defence ministry’s bomb disposal unit to secure evidence at the scene.

It is the second explosion in Zaandam in five days. A blast damaged a window at a house on Saenredamstraat late on Thursday, and police are still appealing for witnesses.

World.title: The IamExpat Fair is back in Eindhoven: what’s new this year?
World.content:
The IamExpat Fair returns to Eindhoven on Saturday October 3 for its second outing in the city, with a bigger careers section, two international centres and a new supervised kids area.

The fair, which takes place in the Klokgebouw in Strijp-S, provides advice and services of all kinds for the international community, including special offers only available for attendees. You can register for free online.

“We are bringing back the large career section, expanding the number of expat centres at the fair, and growing the Family & Kids section,” says event manager Claire Leunissen.

Careers and partners

The careers section includes Brainport and recruitment agency Undutchables, and is aimed particularly at the partners of people who have moved to the region for work.

“The international community of Eindhoven can’t be underestimated,” says Claire. “This small but mighty international community also means that we are able to help the partners and families of expats looking to settle into Dutch life as well, through career opportunities, community groups, fitness schools and Dutch classes.”

Families and newcomers

New this year is a kids area, supervised by childcare provider Korein, where families can play while parents work their way round the stands.

Two international centres will be on hand for questions about registration and residency: Holland Expat Center South, based in Eindhoven, and Expat Centre Maastricht Region. Orion Immigration Law returns with a stand double the size of last year’s.

Language schools include Language Institute Regina Coeli in Vught, Una Paloma Blanca, Bart de Pau and Taalkracht, while the health and leisure exhibitors range from bike subscription service Swapfiets to Happy Bodies and Shakti.

Every stage covered

Workshops and presentations by experts run for most of the day, covering renting, buying a house and securing a mortgage, tax, careers and schooling.

“The fair is an incredible one-stop shop for every part of life in the Netherlands,” says Claire. “International students or young professionals might be looking for Dutch language classes or job related information, but a decade later, they can come to the fair and learn more about preparing for retirement, buying their first home, or choosing the right daycare for their kids.”

“We are excited to bring the IamExpat Fair back to the Klokgebouw, a historic building that embodies the history of technology, innovation and immigration of Eindhoven,” says Claire.

The IamExpat Fair Eindhoven takes place in the Klokgebouw, Strijp-S on Saturday October 3 from 10am to 5pm. Entrance is free with online registration.

World.title: Dutch destinations: Move on up to Midden-Groningen
World.content:
The area of countryside known as Midden-Groningen describes itself as the “playground” of the city of the same name. The region is home to country estates, windmills, little museums and plenty of outdoor places to explore by bike, foot and by boat.

Dotted around the countryside you will also see some of the traces of the regional gas industry, which has now been shut down because of the damage caused by earthquakes.

Five things to do in Midden-Groningen

Visit a country house

The Groningen country house, or borg, Fraeylemaborg in Slochteren was lived in by its wealthy owners well into the 20th century, but parts of the complex date back to the 13th. The entire building is now open to the public, from the attic to the kitchens and offers a fascinating glimpse into the lives of wealthy Groningers.

The grounds are also open to explore and regular re-enactments are staged in the grounds. When we visited a medieval battle, complete with tents, villagers and cannon, was being re-created much to the delight of the many children in the audience. The café with its sunny terrace is a good stop for lunch.

Take in a museum

There are plenty of small, regional museums in the region. In Hoogezand you will find the national bus museum, which attracts bus fans from all over the globe, and a historic wharf that has been virtually untouched since 1922.

In Sappemeer is the fire brigade museum and your offspring will be able to help put out a fire on certain days in the summer. Zuidbroek is home to a railway museum, in the old station, with a treasure hunt, train simulator for budding drivers and a collection of model trains.

Check out a windmill

The region is home to several windmills, some of which were used to pump out water when the land was being drained. De Wachter, on the edge of Zuidlaren, is a working oilseed mill with a small museum and great views if you can brave the ladders to reach the top.

It still produces linseed and corn oil, and four types of spices, all of which you can buy in the shop. Open on Saturday and Wednesday afternoon.

Wander in nature

The Drentsche Aa national park, on the edge of Zuidlaren, takes its name from the river Aa which meanders through the countryside from Drenthe into Groningen province. Home to plenty of wildlife and megalithic tombs known as hunebedden, it is one of the oldest landscapes in the country. You can follow various cycling and walking routes and the visitors centre has a welcoming café for lunch or high tea.

See the Veenkoloniën by boat

Pick up a canoe or an electric motorboat at Peddel en zo in Kiel-Windeweer and follow one of several routes along canals and rivers, from one hour to a full day. You will pass through ribbon villages and the remains of old peat workings, with plenty of opportunities to stop for lunch or a swim.

Where to eat

There is plenty of choice throughout the region. De Amshoff in Kiel-Windeweer comes highly recommended for dinner but was fully booked when we were there. It also offers overnight stays. Van Heijningen Bosch in Veendam is housed in a listed country house and serves lunch and evening fine dining.

The Grand Café in Zuidlaren offers traditional Dutch café fare – steaks, spare ribs – as well as cheese fondue and a hearty Dutch stew. Be aware, many places are closed Monday, Tuesday and even Wednesday, so check first.

Where to stay

We stayed in a little wooden cabin in the small-scale complex known as Romala’s Home in Kiel-Windeweer, where they also have a fascinating (enormous) shop full of bric-a-brac.

Het Torentje van Trips is a B&B in a converted water mill which sleeps up to eight in the east of the region. Zuidlaren has a couple of fairly ordinary hotels while Pieks in Noordlaren gets rave reviews online. There are also plenty of campsites if you are looking for something a little less refined.

How to get there

There are some bus and train services, but a car is probably the best, and easiest, way to get around. Rent a bike if you like cycling.

Anything else?

If you are looking for a longer stay, there is plenty more to explore in north eastern Groningen, including the fortified village of Bourtange and lots more borgs (manor houses).

World.title: Warning after Dutch blood donor infected with West Nile virus
World.content:
A case of West Nile virus has been detected in a Dutch blood donor in the first infection of its kind for six years.

The donor, who lives in Utrecht province, is though to have contracted the virus in the Netherlands, as they have not been abroad recently, the public health agency RIVM said.

The virus was confirmed after the patient reported mild symptoms of West Nile fever. Blood bank Sanquin subsequently carried out laboratory tests on a number of samples.

Some 80% of people who contract the virus have no symptoms, but around 1% develop neurological problems, mainly people over 50 with weakened immune systems. In rare cases it can be fatal.

The disease mainly occurs in birds, but can be transmitted to other species, including humans, by mosquitoes. There are no known cases of transmission between humans.

Horse and bird infected

The RIVM said the virus had also been detected in a horse and a bird in different locations in the Netherlands, indicating that mosquitoes that carry the virus are active in the country.

The agency advised people to wear clothes with long sleeves, apply mosquito repellent and use screens or mosquito nets to keep the insects out. It added that the risk of contracting West Nile virus in the Netherlands was small.

World.title: Limburg brewery’s Pils scoops top global award for second time
World.content:

Limburg brewery Alfa has won one of the top prizes at the World Beer Awards for the second time.

The family firm, based in Thull, was awarded the title of World’s Best Classic Pilsener for Edel Pils, which previously won the honour in 2021.

It was one of four Dutch beers to win a Gold award at the annual festival in the English city of Norwich, along with Grolsch’s Cal and Herfstbok and the Gouverneur Superieur Pilsener made by another Limburg brewery, Lindeboom.

Edel Pils was also named as the best Dutch national beer by the international jury.

Alfa has been brewing beer in Thull for 156 years, using traditional family recipes and its own water source.

World.title: Dutch companies to receive €1bn in Trump tariff compensation
World.content:
Dutch companies are set to recoup a €1 billion windfall from the Trump administration after the United States Supreme Court ruled most of his “liberation day” tariffs announced last April were illegal.

Philips, one of the first companies to claim a refund following the ruling in February, received €186 mln, which accounted for around 4% of its turnover for the second quarter of 2026.

The figures were included in the health tech giant’s latest quarterly results, which showed a 4% increase in sales compared to the same period in 2025.

The Supreme Court ordered the US government to compensate companies when it upheld a lower court’s decision that the Trump administration had wrongly used emergency powers to justify the tariffs.

Exactly how much has been paid out is unknown because the government has not published details, but experts have calculated that the top 10 Dutch exporters stand to receive more than €1 bn altogether.

Philips, which makes 40% of its turnover in North America, was one of the first Dutch companies to claim a refund. Other major exporters include Heineken, which is expected to receive between €150 mln and €350 mln, and Ahold Delaize, owner of Albert Heijn, which will get an estimated €100 mln to €300 million.

Altogether more than a quarter of a million companies have claimed refunds worth a total of $129 bn (€111 bn) from the US customs administration, in addition to the $166 bn (€143 bn) which will have to be repaid to American firms.

“We are surprised by how quickly and efficiently this has happened,” Casper Roerade of Dutch entrepreneurs’ association EvoFenedex told AD.nl.

World.title: Far-right FVD-linked school opens in Almere with state funding
World.content:
A primary school linked to the far-right Forum for Democracy (FVD) has opened with state funding in Almere, teaching pupils that “the old Europe was better than the new,” and doing away with the “dogma of equality”.

The “Renaissance School” started with one class of 18 four and five-year-olds. Its founders say the curriculum follows the view of humanity found in classical antiquity, the middle ages and the early modern period.

The school’s site says it approaches scientific views such as climate change as “falsifiable theories” and that boys and girls may be taught differently in recognition of biological differences, NRC reported.

School head Douwe Filz told De Telegraaf that classes are mixed and there are no separate subjects for boys or girls, although material may be presented in different ways.

Pupils are taught Latin and English alongside Dutch, and the school works with printed books, has no wifi and makes limited use of computers.

FVD has presented its Renaissance schools as an answer to what it calls left-wing indoctrination in the classroom, a theme it has pursued since setting up a reporting hotline for pupils in 2019. Ralf Dekker, who led the project for the party, told NOS in 2022 there would be “no woke thinking in the teaching material”.

The school is run by Stichting Tocqueville, formally separate from FVD, although several of its board members and staff are active in the party. Party chairman Thierry Baudet has described it as part of an FVD pillar alongside the party itself.

Questions in parliament

VVD MP Arend Kisteman and D66 MP Ilana Rooderkerk have written parliamentary questions about the school, which will be answered when parliament reconvenes after August 31.

“It is too easy to set up a small school in the Netherlands,” Kisteman told De Telegraaf. “That worsens the teacher shortage and the taxpayer picks up the bill.”

Rooderkerk told the paper she wanted inspectors to step in before four-year-olds were indoctrinated with FVD’s ideas. Judith Tielen, the VVD junior education minister, is drawing up options for tightening the rules and said inspectors would carry out a full quality inspection within the school’s first year.

The Dutch constitution has allowed publicly funded faith and worldview schools since 1917. Most of those founded since a 2020 law relaxed the rules are faith schools, the biggest share of them are Islamic.

Market research tactics

Schools seeking state funding normally have to collect 100 signed declarations from parents, which FVD failed to do.

Instead, the school’s backers used market research to show that the population of the area will increase, boosting the need for a new school.

An earlier attempt to open the Renaissance School in Almere, which was fully funded by parents and private sources, failed and closed in 2024.

Initial findings indicate that the cause of the accident was the driver of the coach falling asleep. Political leaders in both Poland and Hungary have offered condolences to the families of the victims, while the Polish foreign ministry has set up a special helpline for those affected. Later on Sunday morning, Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar confirmed that 12 people had died and at least 10 were seriously injured. According to information from the Hungarian emergency services, 57 passengers and two drivers had been on the bus. “The driver probably fell asleep at the wheel”, resulting in the vehicle veering off the road and into a ditch, said police in a statement quoted by Polsat News. Polsat reports that the group is from around Strzyżów, a town in southeastern Poland. The owner of the local company that had been transporting them told Business Insider Polska that the coach “was driven by two experienced drivers”. Twelve people lost their lives and at least ten were seriously injured overnight when a bus carrying Polish tourists overturned and went off the road into a ditch on the M3 motorway. My sincere condolences to the families of the victims. I am grateful to all those who took part… — Magyar Péter (Ne féljetek) (@magyarpeterMP) August 16, 2026 Polish media outlets reported that the group in the bus were pilgrims on their way back to Poland from Medjugorje, which is a popular destination for Catholic pilgrimages due to a series of reported visions of the Virgin Mary that have occurred there. Polish foreign ministry spokesman Maciej Wewiór later confirmed to broadcaster TVN that “everything indicates they were returning from Medjugorje”. The authorities in Podkarpackie, the province of Poland where the group was from, also reported that they were pilgrims returning from Bosnia and Herzegovina. The accident on Sunday morning took place just after the end of celebrations of the Assumption of Mary on Saturday, which had included the unveiling in Poland of Europe’s tallest statue of Mary. Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki, issued a statement on Sunday morning expressing his “deep sorrow…in the face of this unimaginable tragedy” and offering “prayer and profound compassion for the families and loved ones of the victims”. Prime Minister Donald Tusk likewise expressed his “deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of the victims” and thanked the Hungarian emergency services for undertaking the rescue operation. Andrii Sybiha, the foreign minister of Ukraine, which borders both Poland and Hungary, also offered his “heartfelt condolences” and said that “Ukraine stands in solidarity with the friendly Polish people and shares their grief”. The Polish embassy in Budapest has set up a special helpline for family members and loved ones of those involved in the crash. World.title: Europe’s biggest Virgin Mary statue – taller than Rio’s Christ the Redeemer – unveiled in Polish village
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The tallest statue of the Virgin Mary in Europe has been officially opened in the small village of Konotopie in central Poland. Towering over the rural landscape at 55.6 metres high, the monument, whose construction was funded by a wealthy local couple, is taller than the famous Christ the Redeemer statue in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. The new landmark, which is also the tallest religious statue of any kind in Europe, was unveiled on 15 August, when Catholics celebrate the assumption of Mary into heaven. The consecration ceremony was led by Krzysztof Wętkowski, bishop of the diocese of Włocławek in which Konotopie, which has a population of only around 130 people, is located. The local community hopes that the statue will become a major site of pilgrimage. Among those to attend the ceremony was former Polish president and Nobel Peace Prize winner Lech Wałęsa. “We sinners ask Our Lady of Mercy to take care of the whole nation,” wrote the 82-year-old in a post on social media, sharing photos of himself at the statue. Construction of the concrete statue took 18 months and reportedly cost around 100 million zloty (€23.2 million). Those costs were covered by the couple behind the project, Roman and Grażyna Karkosik. After making his fortune investing in undervalued companies during Poland’s post-communist transition in the 1990s, Roman Karkosik had by the early 21st century become one of Poland’s richest people, though his fortune has since diminished somewhat, according to estimates. The couple – who keep an extremely low profile, rarely giving interviews and never speaking publicly about the project to build the statue of Mary – live in a restored 18th-century palace around 2 kilometres away, from where they can see the new monument. Konotopie’s statue of Mary has now overtaken one in Miribel, France, as Europe’s tallest. But it is still some distance behind the tallest in the world, the 98-metre Mother of All Asia–Tower of Peace in Batangas City, Philippines. Until recently, Poland also had the tallest statue of Jesus in the world, the 33-metre-high Jesus Christ the King of the Universe monument, erected in the town of Świebodzin in 2010. However, in 2024, it was overtaken by a 61-metre-tall statue of Jesus in Indonesia. The design for the statue of Mary in Konotopie was originally conceived in the form of a two-metre-high model by sculptor Adam Jakub Matejkowski, who told the Polish edition of Forbes magazine that the Karkosiks had specifically requested that the statue be larger than Świebodzin’s Christ. Chief engineer Bartłomiej Niesłuchowski told broadcaster TVN that it took months to find a company willing and able to undertake such a project. Because no suppliers in Poland could produce the material needed for the unique mould into which the concrete would be poured, it had to be manufactured in Italy. The monument will be free for the public to access, including its observation deck, located 15 metres up on the pedestal upon which Mary stands. The site is expected to become a place of pilgrimage, with local authorities preparing for an influx of people. “We’re already seeing growing interest in investment plots, including restaurants,” Renata Gołębiewska, mayor of the nearby town of Kikoł, told the Rzeczpospolita daily. “But it’s too early to assess the impact.” Poland is one of Europe’s most religious countries. Just over 70% of the population identify as Catholic, according to the most recent national census, while around 30% attend Sunday mass. However, religiosity has been falling rapidly in recent years, especially among young Poles. The Catholic church in Poland has also been hit by a series of scandals relating to historical child sex abuse as well as accusations that it interferes in politics. The proportion of Catholics who attend Sunday mass in Poland has stabilised at around 30% after falling from a peak of 57%, new church data show. World.title: Polish opposition expels 40 lawmakers who formed breakaway caucus led by ex-PM Morawiecki
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s largest opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), has expelled 40 of its lawmakers in response to them forming a breakaway parliamentary caucus led by PiS deputy leader and former prime minister Mateusz Morawiecki. The decision formalises a split that began last month, when Morawiecki and his supporters refused to resign from a political association they had formed and sign a pledge of loyalty to PiS. They represented a more moderate faction that had long been unhappy with the party’s move in a hard-right direction. Koleżeński Sąd Dyscyplinarny PiS podjął decyzję o wykluczeniu z partii 38 posłów i 2 senatorów wchodzących w skład klubu Rozwój Plus, w tym byłego premiera Mateusza Morawieckiego – przekazał rzecznik dyscyplinarny PiS Karol Karski. https://t.co/Qe6KuPVUVZ — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) August 13, 2026 On Thursday, PiS’s disciplinary spokesman, Karol Karski, announced that its disciplinary court had found that 38 MPs and two senators “seriously violated the PiS statute by leaving the PiS parliamentary caucus and joining a new caucus” founded by Morawiecki, called Development Plus (Rozwój Plus). Karski added that all 40, including Morawiecki, had been notified of the decision by email and been sent scans of the ruling. They have seven days to appeal. If no appeal is filed, they will officially cease to be PiS members, Karski said. A statement from the party’s disciplinary court, cited by news website Onet, also noted that Morawiecki had committed a further “serious violation” of the party’s statute by announcing last week that Development Plus would become a political party. Mateusz Morawiecki has confirmed that his Development Plus group, which is splitting from the national-conservative opposition PiS party, will soon form a party of its own. However, he categorically ruled out ever working with Prime Minister @donaldtusk https://t.co/J6mQaer4MA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 4, 2026 Among those to be expelled are several former government ministers, including Janusz Cieszyński, Paweł Jabłoński, Olga Semeniuk-Patkowska and Szymon Szynkowski vel Sęk. Some of the ousted lawmakers expressed their disappointment at PiS’s decision. “Someone who has done everything for PiS is being expelled simply because he wanted to broaden the party’s voter base,” Grzegorz Puda, another former minister, told the Fakt daily. Another, Łukasz Schreiber, told news website Onet that, in reality, the decision to expel them had been taken when party leader Jarosław Kaczyński said in July they had effectively resigned by refusing to sign the loyalty pledge. “Everything else was just a formality.” Morawiecki served as prime minister from 2017 until 2023, when PiS lost power to the current government, a more liberal coalition led by Donald Tusk. The party has plunged into crisis this year, with its support in polls falling to the lowest level in over 15 years. In response to a growing challenge from the far right, Kaczyński has shifted PiS itself rightwards. That frustrated more moderate figures around Morawiecki, who founded the Development Plus association in April this year as a way of promoting their ideas. However, that prompted criticism from some other members of the party, who saw it as a step towards creating a breakaway group. The split in PiS is a blow to the party and its leader, Jarosław Kaczyński. But the potential emergence of a new centre-right party led by Mateusz Morawiecki could actually help the opposition win a majority at next year's elections, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/xMP7e4rOFf — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 31, 2026 Matters came to a head in July, when Morawiecki and his supporters refused to quit their association and sign the pledge of loyalty demanded by Kaczyński. They then formed their own caucus, which immediately became the third largest in parliament and meant that PiS’s was no longer the biggest. Last week, Morawiecki confirmed that his group would soon form a new party of its own. He laid out a vision of a more moderate, centre-right party that would focus on economic development rather than “ideological disputes”. Its first policy proposal was to establish a special “salary” for parents, equivalent to the minimum wage, that they would be paid for the first three years of a child’s life, with the aim of boosting Poland’s birth rate, which is one of the lowest in the world. According to poll aggregator eWybory.eu, Development Plus already has average support of 5.6% in polls, despite not yet being a party. Support for PiS has fallen to 20.3%, down from 24.4% in July. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has introduced a new type of account that will allow individuals to invest up to 100,000 zloty (€23,200) without paying capital gains tax. The government says the scheme is designed to encourage Poles to build long-term savings and channel billions of zloty into the domestic financial market. Osobiste Konta Inwestycyjne to nowe narzędzie, które ułatwi inwestowanie i oszczędzanie na preferencyjnych warunkach podatkowych. Nowe przepisy wejdą w życie 1 stycznia 2027 r. Szczegóły w komunikacie ⤵️ https://t.co/Z6zEHKkQsY — Ministerstwo Finansów (@MF_GOV_PL) August 13, 2026 The new legislation, which was signed into law on Thursday by President Karol Nawrocki and will take effect on 1 January 2027, creates Personal Investment Accounts (OKI). All assets held in an OKI will be completely exempt from the usual 19% capital gains tax. Amounts up to 100,000 zloty, including up to 25,000 in savings assets such as bonds and deposits, will be completely tax free. Assets above 100,000 zloty will be subject to a new tax on their value. The government has said the tax will amount to 0.85% in 2027 and will be adjusted annually. Finance minister Andrzej Domański earlier described the introduction of OKI as “the biggest change in years for individual investors and the largest project aimed at building domestic capital to drive the development of the Polish economy”. While Nawrocki, who is aligned with the opposition, regularly clashes with the government and has vetoed a record number of laws, in this case he approved their idea, which he office said “could have a positive impact on both citizens and the state”. “Poles will gain a tool to promote family wealth building thanks to an attractive tax-free allowance and a guarantee of no account maintenance fees,” they added. Sejm przyjął ustawę o Osobistych Kontach Inwestycyjnych. Do 100 tys. zł bez podatku. To największa od lat zmiana dla indywidualnych inwestorów i największy projekt budowy krajowego kapitału napędzającego rozwój polskiej gospodarki. 🇵🇱 — Andrzej Domański (@Domanski_Andrz) July 3, 2026 The government estimates the scheme could result in about 74 billion zloty flowing to the Warsaw Stock Exchange by 2040. Kamil Gemra, an assistant professor at the Warsaw School of Economics, said he considered the projection realistic. “Society is getting wealthier; we have record amounts in our bank accounts. It would be enough for just a few per cent of that money to flow into the capital market for the figure cited by the finance ministry be achieved,” Gemra told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). The government also forecasts, however, that the tax exemption will reduce state budget revenues by nearly 9 billion zloty over 10 years, at a time when public finances are under increasing strain amid rapidly rising debt. Poland’s WIG20 stock market index has hit its highest ever level, surpassing a record that had stood for almost 19 years. The WIG20 has been Europe’s best-performing major blue-chip index so far this year, gaining almost 25% https://t.co/CBbv99v2Uk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 4, 2026 Poland already has three mechanisms that allow people to accumulate assets with tax advantages: Individual Retirement Accounts (IKE), Individual Pension Schemes (IKZE), and Employee Capital Plans (PPK). However, in all three cases, the capital gains tax exemption is conditional on withdrawing funds after reaching retirement age. Despite the Polish stock market’s strong performance in recent years, Poles’ direct participation remains modest. Shares make up only 2.9% of household assets, the equivalent of 3% of GDP. That is well below the EU average of 8.2%. By contrast, households’ cash holdings are equivalent to 11.5% of GDP, well ahead of the EU average of 4.5% and behind only Slovenia (11.7%) and Germany (11.6%). World.title: Polish PM confirms he wants his “right-hand man” to be made constitutional court judge
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Prime Minister Donald Tusk has confirmed that he will seek to have Maciej Berek, a government minister who stepped down this week and whom Tusk calls his “right-hand man”, appointed as a judge on Poland’s constitutional court. The move has generated considerable controversy given that Tusk’s ruling coalition has repeatedly pledged to “depoliticise” the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) after the previous national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government appointed its former politicians to the court. At a press conference on Thursday, however, Tusk defended the idea, describing Berek as an “apolitical and nonpartisan” figure who would help “fix the Constitutional Tribunal” after it was rendered illegitimate by PiS. Premier @donaldtusk potwierdził, że @MaciejBerek – do tej pory minister ds. nadzoru nad wdrażaniem polityki rządu – będzie kandydatem na sędziego Trybunału Konstytucyjnego. – To jeden z najwybitniejszych polskich prawników – uzasadnił szef rządu.https://t.co/RsKLhLjHhC — PolsatNews.pl (@PolsatNewsPL) August 13, 2026 Berek is a longstanding associate of Tusk. During Tusk’s first period as prime minister, from 2007 to 2014, Berek was head of the Government Legislation Centre (RCL) while also serving as secretary of the cabinet. After Tusk returned to power in 2023, heading a coalition of parties ranging from left to centre right, Berek was appointed as a minister without portfolio and then, in 2025, was made minister in charge of overseeing the implementation of government policy. He has, however, been an extremely low-key figure, rarely speaking in public. Berek is also not a member of parliament, and indeed not even a member of any political party. On Tuesday this week, Tusk unexpectedly announced before a cabinet meeting that Berek, whom he called his “right-hand man”, was leaving the government in order to “move on to other tasks”. The prime minister did not say what those tasks would be, but multiple media outlets reported that Berek would be presented as a candidate to become a judge on the Constitutional Tribunal. Since Tusk’s government came to power in December 2023, it has ignored all TK rulings because three of the tribunal’s judges were appointed illegitimately under the former PiS government. Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025 The new ruling coalition also criticised the fact that some TK judges were former PiS politicians. Two of them, for example, were appointed in 2019 shortly after stepping down as PiS MPs. Another, the current TK chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, previously served as a deputy justice minister in the PiS government (though he was never a member of the PiS party). When Tusk’s coalition came to power, it promised to restore the legitimacy of the TK, including by “depoliticising” it. In 2024, it approved legislation that would have banned anyone who had served as a politician in the last four years from becoming a TK judge. However, the measures were referred by the then-president, PiS ally Andrzej Duda, to the TK itself, which subsequently declared them unconstitutional, meaning they did not come into force. Poland’s constitutional court has rejected two government bills seeking to overhaul the court itself, with the aim of reversing the politicisation that took place under the former administration. It found that the measures "violate judicial independence" https://t.co/uBJr1bXFv4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 30, 2025 At a press conference on Thursday, Tusk confirmed the rumours that he would seek to make Berek a TK judge. He called Berek “one of the most distinguished Polish legal practitioners, who has made his apolitical and nonpartisan nature a hallmark”. Berek has a doctorate in law and, between his stints in government, worked as an assistant professor in the department of constitutional law at the University of Warsaw. “For him, compliance with the law and the constitution has always been paramount,” declared Tusk. “I don’t know anyone better equipped, better prepared, to help rectify the situation we face with the flawed Constitutional Tribunal.” 💬 Premier @donaldtusk w #Warszawa: Nie mamy żadnych innych interesów w tej sprawie. Zależy nam na naprawieniu Trybunału Konstytucyjnego, żeby nie był na smyczy prezydenta i PiS-u, tylko wykonywał swoją robotę. — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) August 13, 2026 The prime minister acknowledged that his government had tried to ban politicians from serving on the TK. But he said that Berek himself had recently told him that, “under the current political circumstances, we must do everything we can to remedy the situation” at the tribunal. “Since methods that are unconstitutional are being used from the other side, I must also demonstrate my determination and that we won’t give in to such methods,” added Tusk. Those remarks, in which Tusk also called Święczkowski’s leadership of the TK “embarrassing”, were a reference to the fact that the current PiS-aligned president, Karol Nawrocki, and Święczkowski have refused to accept four new TK judges chosen by parliament earlier this year. “We have no interests in this matter other than to repair the Constitutional Tribunal so that it is not a tool and is not under the thumb of the president or PiS, but rather that it performs its work as objectively as possible,” said Tusk. A newly sworn-in @TK_GOV_PL judge says he will not take his seat until four colleagues appointed by parliament are allowed to take theirs. He said their appointments had been blocked "unlawfully", in the latest twist in a long-running disputehttps://t.co/X30rm1Gfzs — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 29, 2026 However, there remain major potential stumbling blocks on Berek’s path to the TK, not least doubts over whether Tusk’s coalition partners will support his nomination in the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, which is responsible for nominating new TK judges. Anna Maria Żukowska, the head of The Left’s (Lewica) parliamentary caucus, declared on Tuesday that, if rumours of Berek’s nomination were true, “he won’t get votes from The Left because we promised our voters that politicians wouldn’t end up on the TK”. Given that the government has a majority of just nine in the 460-seat Sejm, it would only require a small number of MPs from Tusk’s coalition to oppose Berek’s nomination for him to lose the vote. On Thursday, Tusk said that he “understands” concerns from some coalition partners but that he would “try to convince those who have doubts”. Jeżeli to się wydarzy (a raczej nie), to do niedawna czynny polityk nie dostanie głosów klubu @__Lewica, gdyż obiecaliśmy naszym wyborcom, że politycy nie trafią do TK. Ale IMHO to bardzo krzywdząca dla @MaciejBerek plotka, on by się jako państwowiec w życiu na coś takiego nie… https://t.co/QWFFmdy4V3 — Anna-Maria Żukowska 💁🏻‍♀️ (@AM_Zukowska) August 11, 2026 The next vacancy on the TK’s 15-judge bench is due to open on 18 September, when the nine-year term of Justyn Piskorski, one of the PiS-era judges regarded as illegitimate by the current government, ends. After that, a further vacancy will open in January. However, even if Berek is approved by the Sejm, the law states that new TK judges must swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki has used this requirement to refuse to swear in four of the judges chosen by the Sejm this year. He has, however, sworn in three others. It remains unclear what the president would do in the case of Berek. Earlier this week, his chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, told Radio Zet that Nawrocki would “accept the oath if procedures are followed”. However, he added that he does “not know if [the Sejm] is able to carry out those procedures properly”. World.title: Poland reintroduces VAT cut and daily price caps to lower fuel costs for drivers
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s government has announced that, from Monday, it will reintroduce some of the measures that were used earlier this year to lower prices for consumers at petrol stations amid the energy crisis triggered by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The package, known in Polish as CPN and which will be in place from 17 August until at least 31 August, includes reducing VAT on fuels from 23% to 8% and introducing retail consumer price caps on fuels set daily by the energy minister. Announcing the measures on Thursday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said they should result in prices falling by around 1 zloty (€0.23) per litre. Currently, average retail prices are 7.29 zloty for 95-octane petrol and 8.09 zloty for diesel, according to Polish price monitoring service E-Petrol. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️ Polska będzie w absolutnej czołówce europejskiej, jeśli chodzi o najniższe ceny paliw. pic.twitter.com/ar3IZbzFHQ — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) August 13, 2026 Tusk acknowledged that CPN will entail “serious costs” for the state budget. When similar measures (which also, unlike now, included cuts in excise duty on fuels) were in place between the end of March and end of June, they cost the state an estimated 4.7 billion zloty. On Thursday, the prime minister renewed his criticism of opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki for last month refusing to sign into law a windfall tax on fuel companies’ excess profits this year. The government said that the tax, which would have raised an estimated 4 billion zloty, was intended to help cover the costs of fuel subsidies. The profits of many fuel companies have boomed during the crisis, with Polish state energy giant Orlen last week announcing record half-year results. Nawrocki’s chancellery, however, has argued that fuel companies would seek to pass the costs of tax increases onto consumers, thereby increasing prices. CPN was first introduced in March in response to soaring fuel prices in the wake of US and Israeli attacks on Iran and subsequent disruption to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies. CPN subsequently helped bring Polish fuel prices to among the lowest in the EU. Since the measures were withdrawn in June, prices at the pump in Poland have risen significantly, placing pressure on the government to again cushion the blow for consumers. E-Petrol reports that prices have recently started to fall, but remain well above the levels seen before the crisis. Economists at PKO, a major bank, wrote on Thursday that higher fuel prices in July, which stemmed from the expiry of CPN and an increase in global oil prices, were the main drivers of inflation accelerating from 2.5% in June to 3.0% last month. Polish state energy giant Orlen posted a record profit in the first half of 2026, as turmoil in the Middle East boosted earnings in the fuel sector. It also saw its highest-ever proportion of revenue from foreign markets https://t.co/uhGWJVQvf3 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 7, 2026 On Thursday, Tusk claimed that the reintroduced CPN would lead to Poland having among “the lowest prices in Europe”, helping “possibly millions of Polish drivers, on critical days, when they return from holidays”. But he also acknowledged that fuel would “still be expensive”. Nawrocki’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, however, criticised the government for what he claimed was a belated response to high prices. World.title: Polish household assets hit record 4 trillion zloty amid fastest growth in years
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poles are building up wealth at the fastest pace in years, with the combined value of household financial assets surpassing 4 trillion zloty (€930 billion) for the first time, according to new data from the Polish Development Fund (PFR), a state entity. The figure reached 4.1 trillion zloty at the end of the first quarter of this year, up 4.3% from the previous quarter, said PFR. That was the largest quarterly increase in just over six years. On an annual basis, assets rose 15.3%, the fastest pace in five years. After deducting liabilities, household net financial assets stood at 3.2 trillion zloty, also a record. Net assets were up 18.4% from a year earlier and 4.9% from the previous quarter. Ponad 4,1 bln zł – tyle wynoszą już aktywa finansowe polskich gospodarstw domowych. To historyczny rekord. W najnowszej analizie PFR pokazujemy, że w ciągu roku wzrosły o 15,3% – to jedna z najwyższych dynamik w historii. Skala i tempo wzrostu aktywów pokazują też, jak duży jest… pic.twitter.com/fSx1yOZtkn — Mikołaj Raczyński (@MikRaczynski) August 7, 2026 The biggest contribution to the quarterly increase came from what PFR classifies as “other equity holdings”, which include shares in limited liability companies, partnerships, cooperatives and mutual insurance societies. They rose by 61.5 billion zloty. Bank deposits recorded the second-largest increase (44.4 billion zloty). Despite the strong rise in equity holdings, bank deposits and cash remained the largest components of household financial assets, accounting for 26.3% and 11.1% respectively. Pension and disability funds accounted for 10.5% of household financial assets. Meanwhile, shares listed on stock exchanges and regulated over-the-counter markets made up 2.9% of household financial assets. Their value is equivalent to 3% of GDP, one of the lowest shares in the European Union, where the average is 8.2%. Although shares make up only a small share of household assets, the Polish stock market has performed strongly in recent years, with its blue-chip index reaching a record high last week and breaking its previous high set 19 years ago. By contrast, Polish households have a relatively high level of cash holdings. Cash was equivalent to 11.5% of Poland’s GDP in the first quarter, well ahead of the EU average of 4.5% and behind only Slovenia (11.7%) and Germany (11.6%). PFR’s data also show that household liabilities in Poland increased by 5.2% year-on-year to more than 891 billion zloty in the first quarter, well below the rate of asset growth. Long-term loans accounted for 92.2% of liabilities, while short-term loans accounted for 5.1%. Rising household wealth reflects three decades of strong economic growth in Poland, accompanied by a rapid rise in wages and living standards. Earlier this year, state research agency CBOS found that a record 39% of Poles say they are financially comfortable, up from just 3% in the early 1990s. Separate data from Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, show that only 2% of the population live in severe deprivation, the lowest level on record. Poland last year rose to its highest-ever level in a measure of household prosperity in European Union member states, overtaking four other countries. That growth has also fuelled a rapid increase in the number of ultra-wealthy people in Poland, whose number has almost doubled since 2019. However, the PFR data show only total combined household assets and liabilities, not how they are distributed across society. The number of ultra-wealthy individuals in Poland has more than doubled since 2021, a faster rate of growth than anywhere else in the world, according to a new study https://t.co/MNKgmjzn2U — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 11, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Romanian Community to Celebrate Culture and Traditions in Prague
World.content:
The Romanian community in Czechia will come together in Prague on September 6 for the 12th edition of the Romanian Celebration, an annual event highlighting Romanian culture, traditions and the community’s ties with Czech society.

The main event will take place at the Ethnographic Section of the National Museum of the Czech Republic in Kinský Park, Prague 5.

The program will bring together Romanian music, dance, food, literature and activities for children.



Organized by the Association of Romanians in the Czech Republic (ARRC), the event is part of a wider cultural project running from March 1 to November 30, 2026.

Visitors can expect traditional music and dance performances, educational activities for children, cultural exhibitions, book presentations and Romanian gastronomy.

The event is aimed at members of the Romanian community, Romanian-speaking families, children and young people, as well as Czech residents interested in Romanian culture.

According to ARRC, the project aims to preserve and promote Romanian cultural and linguistic identity among Romanians living in the Czech Republic while creating opportunities for greater interaction between the Romanian and Czech communities.

“Through this project, we aim to offer the Romanian community, Romanian speakers, and lovers of the Romanian language a space for meeting, dialogue, and celebration of our cultural values, while also contributing to the consolidation of intercultural relations between Romania and the Czech Republic,” the ARRC leadership said.
