Our guest today is Astamur Tania.

Astamur Tania: Good day.

Inal Khashig: Good day. Generally, what do you think about this whole situation that has arisen with these amendments to the constitutional law?

Astamur Tania: Here, the topic of the Abkhaz language is periodically raised in the form of certain information campaigns, usually during some pre-election period or in connection with certain events. It is also impossible to manage without information campaigns. It is necessary to sharpen public attention on this problem.

I hope that this information campaign will not have an independent significance of its own, but will transform into some programmatic actions. Because, probably, everyone understands—both supporters of one approach and supporters of the second approach—that in itself this decision means little. Because here it should still be about a state program.

This program is both educational and ideological, because much rests even on questions of self-awareness. Because it is clear that with the help of the Abkhaz language it is impossible to obtain the volume of information necessary to participate in any competition. So, there must be some other incentives. Just like that, in a natural way, unfortunately, it will not work.

These must be administrative measures and measures of an ideological nature. The Abkhaz language is inextricably linked with issues of identity. This is a big task on all fronts.

Now, regarding the presidential initiative specifically: to be honest, I consider it rational. Some argue that it involves an unequal approach, but I believe it is not aimed at discrimination.

On the contrary, its purpose is to address potential concerns so that advancing the Abkhaz language development program is not perceived as discriminatory by non-Abkhaz residents. After all, preserving interethnic harmony, maintaining consensus, and building a unified civic platform are fundamental for our society.

From this perspective, the approach is entirely sound. However, we must ensure this does not lead to endless postponements. The state must actively work on this by defining clear criteria in legislation to specify what constitutes fluency in the Abkhaz language.

This requirement should apply not only to the parliament but also to the executive branch. Implementing it within the judiciary will be more complex, as it requires extensive work to adapt the full body of legal terminology, which demands highly specialized legal expertise.

Inal Khashig: There are terminologies. All of that exists.

Astamur Tania: I know that preliminary work has been carried out—mostly at the level of compiling dictionaries of legal terms, as far as I am aware. However, implementation within the judiciary is far more difficult purely due to professional constraints.

That is why I believe the presidential initiative reflects today’s realities. It creates a space for compromise among political participants and allows us to develop proper criteria for assessing Abkhaz language proficiency.

If we fail to reach an agreement and leave everything as it is—which could easily happen if the president’s proposed law fails to pass—we will remain at a standstill. The entire process could degenerate into a formalistic routine, similar to what we witnessed during the presidential elections, and only spread further.

Therefore, as an initial step, I view this approach as very reasonable. Since there is no discrimination involved, I see no basis to claim it is unconstitutional.

Inal Khashig: I have my own perspective on this, though doubts constantly trouble me. The initiative grants a deferment to non-ethnic Abkhazians, but I am convinced that in five years, by 2032, we will find ourselves with the exact same results.

Astamur Tania: That certainly cannot be ruled out.

Inal Khashig: Indeed. But my concern is the formalistic approach toward the Abkhaz language itself. For instance, the language law was adopted in 2007 and was meant to take full effect in 2015, requiring the entire Abkhaz bureaucracy to be fluent in the state language.

Yet, even if a good half of them are fluent today, we should consider ourselves lucky—especially since no actual testing or measurements were ever conducted.

Astamur Tania: If at least a “bad half” had command of it.

Inal Khashig: Yes, yes. I am afraid that, strictly speaking, we will simply do this—formalize the commission itself, which we will bring to formal absurdity. Like, here is a good guy, he knows 10 words.

Astamur Tania: If we do not change our attitude toward our state, then in the Abkhaz language, and in security, and in the economy, we will have roughly the same result. You are right. This is a broader question than the Abkhaz language. It is just that now it is at the peak of relevance due to the debates in parliament and in society. In fact, this is a question of our attitude.

Various arguments are brought up that the quality of parliamentarism may drop from this. It seems to me that despite the absence of this norm, the quality of our parliamentarism was declining anyway. So the problem, after all, is not only in the Abkhaz language. This is a hackneyed phrase that we always get the government we deserve, that it is a reflection of our society. Therefore, this is a giant societal problem. But it must be dealt with.

First of all, the authorities, you see—to change the quality of authority, those in power must work on changing the quality of society as well. This goal must be set. Not simply to sit out one’s tenure in parliament or executive power. It is necessary to influence society, its enlightenment, its self-awareness, its creative potential. Therein lies the main task. Otherwise, you are right, it will drift on its own, like everything else.

Inal Khashig: It seems to me that the situation around the Abkhaz language is indeed much broader. It shows, probably, our attitude toward the law in general. This applies not only to the Abkhaz language.

We have passed very many all sorts of legislative acts, proper laws, but then we tried in every way to bypass them. An active advertising campaign is taking place on the internet: acquire Abkhaz real estate, and so forth. So many lances were broken over this law on apartments, and still they sell Abkhaz real estate to foreigners. It is possible, it can be acquired.

Astamur Tania: Yes, that is also—you know what the matter is? It is impossible to contain the onslaught; it can only be directed into some profitable channel. Of course, it is possible for some time to contain the natural course of events with prohibitions. But we must nevertheless forecast how we can direct these investments, where our weak zones are.

Simply sitting like a dog in the manger will not work. Therefore, we must understand how in this harsh reality—what is our place. Today one hole was plugged, in another place it tore open. We must have some clear program of action, at least for the short term.

This concerns the economy, security, foreign policy, everything. What I am saying is very banal, but unfortunately, we always have a reactive response to something, to already accomplished facts. Although it was not difficult to predict that the course of events was leading to this. And we live for today. If an individual person can live for today like that, the state should not live like that.

Inal Khashig: The state somehow manages to.

Astamur Tania: It should still plan its future, the society.

Inal Khashig: I would like to switch to another topic now. Periodically, we are reminded of the unresolved Georgian-Abkhaz conflict, which continuously remains at a dead end. Last time, we discussed how Georgian perceptions of Abkhazia and the Abkhaz people have changed, particularly through the influence of Pavel Ingorokva’s theory, which took a strong hold in Georgian thought.

Shortly after our conversation, I watched an interview with the Georgian historian Tsurtsumia on a Georgian YouTube channel. He noted that Ingorokva’s theory is actually marginal and lacks official state support.

Nevertheless, just the day before yesterday, I came across a vividly animated video. It was set in Sukhumi on the embankment, depicting peaceful civilians in a setting reminiscent of 1992, when a Russian military aircraft suddenly swoops in and begins bombing. The people are shown fleeing the embankment, trying to escape by ship or heading into the mountains.

Astamur Tania: Those are slightly different scenes, probably. Maybe it is one pie, but different slices.

Inal Khashig: Yes, but you see, this is proceeding very actively – why I understood this is not only Ingorokva’s theory about who the Abkhaz are and what their origin is, but in Georgian society the understanding of what the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict was is changing very actively. And what happened 33 years ago, 34 years ago. How the war started.

According to this cartoon… A cartoon is a certain part of upbringing. It also has its own audience. Directed at a certain audience. At children. It is important for me to understand why the Georgians converted this conflict into a conflict not between Georgians and Abkhaz, but a certain conflict between Russia and Georgia.

Astamur Tania: That is completely understandable, as acknowledging it would require admitting responsibility for starting the armed conflict. By the way, Shevardnadze did admit this responsibility—and while he claimed Kitovani was to blame, Kitovani was not the Defense Minister of Russia, but of Georgia. Everyone remembers, and archival footage still shows, how this war began and how the local Georgian population reacted.

Acknowledging this would require erasing entire sections of history. Instead, there is an effort to reshape the narrative of 1992 and merge it with the events of 2008, framing everything around legislation and the narrative of post-2008 occupation. Yet, a detailed examination—including the report by the International Fact-Finding Commission led by Heidi Tagliavini—confirmed that responsibility for initiating military action in both instances lay with the Georgian side.

Naturally, there is a desire to obscure this in the media space to advance narratives about occupation, aiming to shape international opinion to justify a forceful resolution or delegitimize the Abkhazian state.

We must react to this. The fact that animated videos are being produced on this topic shows an intent to pass this worldview down to the next generation. If we carry such a perspective into the future, achieving a peaceful settlement or joint progress will be extremely difficult. This is why it is essential to present the fullest possible picture, starting with the factual timeline.

Regarding Zura Tsurtsumia’s comments: first, it is positive that Georgian-Abkhaz relations are being examined at a solid academic level, attempting to move beyond today’s propaganda clichés toward a historical assessment of the conflict’s roots.

However, claiming that Ingorokva’s theory is marginal ignores reality in the Georgian media landscape, where it remains the most widespread view on the origins of the Abkhazian people. While prominent Georgian scholars considered it pseudoscientific—such as Javakhishvili, who noted that ancient Adyghe tribes inhabited Western Georgia prior to the Kartvelians and recognized the Apsilals and Abasgs as direct ancestors of modern Abkhaz—these classical works are largely ignored by mainstream media.

Instead, hate speech dominates the discourse among commentators—and we must acknowledge that hate speech exists on the Abkhaz side as well. Neither side benefits from this.

Objectively, neither we nor Georgia have any interest in a renewed armed conflict, which would yield disastrous consequences for both. Some in Georgian society may assume their larger population makes it an easy victory, but that is far from reality. We cannot afford to trigger such a dangerous cycle.

Both sides are equally served by abandoning hate speech and language that demeans human dignity and belittles culture, especially given that all human cultures, including Abkhazian and Georgian, are products of historical interaction and symbiosis.

Finally, addressing Tsurtsumia’s assertion—which is not unique to him—that the Abkhaz nation was deliberately engineered by Soviet authorities to counter Georgia: while Soviet policies influenced the development of both the Georgian and Abkhazian nations in the late 19th and 20th centuries, it is vital to recognize that the Abkhaz national identity was not an artificial creation.

In fact, during the 1930s and 1940s, deliberate repressive measures were used in an effort to suppress the formation of the Abkhaz nation.

Inal Khashig: That was when schools were closed.

Astamur Tania: Schools were closed, and the destruction of the intelligentsia—the bearers of this very idea—took place at that time. This inflicted a serious trauma.

But one must understand that this process is accomplished. It is an accomplished fact. And in dialogue with the Abkhaz, everyone must proceed from the premise that this is not simply an ethnos, but a formed nation. With its own ideas about borders, policy, with its own national mythology. This is not always equal to history. Here there is a completely different approach.

As I once spoke with an Abkhaz, he said in his heart: why did Gurandukht, the daughter of the Abkhaz king, marry Gurgen, the ruler of Tao-Klarjeti? Since then, the unification of the Abkhaz state with the Georgian one began. That is the feudal era. It is an accomplished fact. We can only look at it like that. It sounds like a parody.

The same applies to this issue. It is closer to us. These are already accomplished facts. We must take them into account. Proceed from the fact that this is a given. Second, there were in fact certain inaccuracies there.

I do not want to delve into that now. In itself, this attempt to approach the understanding of the origins of the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict with a cool head, using academic material—if this happens more or less regularly, in the same calm atmosphere, then it seems to me that both societies can win from this.

Inal Khashig: On the other hand, it seems to me, given that this seems to be a recent event—the war is relatively a historical event, only 30 years ago—nevertheless, judging by what I read in social networks, certain articles, certain speeches of politicians or experts…

Astamur Tania: Very much so.

Inal Khashig: I still see a lot of statements specifically adjusting to the political opportunism of the moment. If you remember, in the 80s, in the 90s after the war, what were we called? Abkhaz separatists. Now you practically do not hear this term.

Astamur Tania: By the way, they started calling us Abkhaz separatists back during the war, and before that—Gudauta separatists. Although during that period Abkhazia had not yet declared that it was ceasing any relations with Georgia and was not going to live with it within common borders.

In its time, on the initiative of Georgian figures, the process of all kinds of division began in Abkhazia. They separated the Georgian sector from the Abkhaz State University. Then they withdrew the football team. Then they withdrew the Georgian faction from the Supreme Council. They began to sit separately. That is, they apparently assumed that gradually they would somehow paralyze things. And here the question arises: who was the separatist?

And the same with this term. And, by the way, “Gudauta separatists”—later this very term migrated into the documents of the United Nations. And for some time after the end of the war, when our authorities were already located in Sukhumi, they continued to call us Gudauta separatists. I think for the Abzhua Abkhaz this is a bit offensive. Gudauta-Abzzua separatists would have been sound better.

Inal Khashig: But, nevertheless, this term somehow went out of circulation. And we have already been switched to the idea that Abkhazia is a territory occupied by Russia. And at the same time, as for the Abkhaz—let us leave aside those social networks where we generally came down from the mountains, according to the Georgian version—in official rhetoric nothing is said about us anymore.

Astamur Tania: “Came down from the mountains” is also quite amusing, because on most of the coast, based on climatic conditions and the unhealthiness of this climate, it was practically impossible to live permanently. Even if you open the press of, say, the late 19th and early 20th centuries, it is evident that the affluent portion of the residents of the city of Sukhumi left Sukhumi for the summer period. Precisely when there was the peak of this disease, people left for the foothills, because living here was a bit dangerous.

Inal Khashig: And the most prosperous ones lived there.

Astamur Tania: Generally, we have a perception as if in the Middle Ages communications in Abkhazia—this applies to everything, we are talking about Abkhazia—ran along the coast like that; there was the Ancient Roman railway running, next to it the Byzantine highway, but in reality all communications passed through the foothills and across the ridges. It was later, with the arrival of the Russian Empire, that this network of communications familiar to us began to develop. And psychologically we begin to tie our perception of the past to what had already taken shape in the 19th and 20th centuries. There was no railway at the beginning of the 20th century yet.

Inal Khashig: This highway that exists now.

Astamur Tania: For example, construction of the Black Sea railway continued in 1918 still. The Russian Empire no longer existed, but it was unclear what would happen. But they continued to build it in the Gagra region in 1918. And now it seems that it was always there.

Inal Khashig: But nevertheless, I tried to understand. Why do they depict Abkhaz who did not participate in this conflict, or played some secondary role in this Georgian-Abkhaz conflict? In the war that took place in 1992-1993.

Astamur Tania: A moment is omitted. What quantity of weapons was transferred to Georgia under the Tashkent Agreement on the eve of the conflict? The Russian authorities of that time were far from being, to put it mildly, pro-Abkhaz.

This is evident from everything. This is visible if one reads at least the transcript of September 3 of the meeting of Shevardnadze, Yeltsin, Ardzinba, representatives of the North Caucasus, representatives of our various parliamentary deputations. Not only should documents be studied, one should read the transcript.

But why did Georgia start armed conflicts? It received at its disposal several motor rifle and tank divisions of the Transcaucasus Military District. Therefore, in their joy, they thought that it would be possible to quickly finish this business.

Inal Khashig: But nevertheless, why am I saying all this—I read an interesting Georgian perspective on why this is happening, that Abkhaz are being excluded from this conflict, that through such an exclusion—and, say, when a certain image of the enemy is removed from the Abkhaz in this conflict, in this war, if the Abkhaz played a non-primary role, it means they are not enemies. There is a hypothetical possibility they retain that later at some point we will make peace with them.

Astamur Tania: That is very hypothetical. In my opinion, it is impossible to do that. Because how can one take a segment of a section of thinking and take something out of there… It seems to me this is very much a laboratory theory.

Inal Khashig: But this is laboratory on the one hand, and on the other hand the Abkhaz themselves have their own perception of the war.

Astamur Tania: To reiterate: those in Georgia who deal with the Georgian-Abkhaz settlement or seek to study this issue must start from the accomplished fact of the Abkhazian nation’s existence. A nation cannot be treated as a third-party observer—it is an active subject. We are an active subject in our relations with Georgia. Recognized or unrecognized, by our internal structure, we are a nation—with our own statehood and our own distinct perception of both the past and the future.

Our perspectives may not always align, but if we look at history honestly, our centuries-long—even thousand-year-old—relations with various Kartvelian peoples, primarily Megrelians, cannot simply be painted in black-and-white. History saw different periods, including feudal wars, which, it should be noted, occurred internally among those groups as well. There was continuous interaction, symbiosis, and movement back and forth. This is why we find Megrelian surnames in Abkhazia, Abkhaz surnames in Zugdidi, and why Gali in particular serves as a concentrated microcosm where everything is intertwined.

We, too, must draw important policy conclusions from this. But there must be a foundational understanding that if there is a real desire to settle our relations or develop a pragmatic approach—though I do not expect major breakthroughs given our disagreements—it starts with recognizing that a political nation has formed here. Its members are not solely ethnic Abkhazians, but all citizens of Abkhazia. We, too, must recognize this and move away from a narrow communal mindset.

Inal Khashig: But, by the way, it is present.

Astamur Tania: That is natural, because that is where it started. But we must nevertheless move in the direction of a civic nation.

Inal Khashig: Well yes, a political nation. This distinction is crucial because, unfortunately, many people’s perception of the Abkhazian situation and where we stand today was shaped back in Soviet times.

Astamur Tania: In fact, the post-Stalin Soviet period wasn’t all bad. Despite setbacks during that recovery process, it was unthinkable to express such vile ideas in writing back then.

Inal Khashig: My point is slightly different. In Soviet times, the Abkhaz struggle focused on ethnic rights—opening schools, theaters, literary journals, and universities—since few anticipated the collapse of the Soviet Union. The political nation back then was subsumed under the concept of the ‘Soviet people,’ right?

Astamur Tania: Well, ‘the Soviet people’ was an ideological construct, though autonomous frameworks did exist.

Inal Khashig: Yet today, some still take a fragmented approach, viewing society purely as separate ethnic groups—Abkhaz, Armenians, Russians, and so on—rather than…

Astamur Tania: You mean moving toward a unified civic nation?

Inal Khashig: Exactly. That is essential.

Astamur Tania: That requires active political education. Some processes occur naturally: living within the same state fosters shared views on security, peaceful development, and the necessity of an independent Abkhazia. However, we must establish clear criteria for this political nation to avoid repeating the mistakes made in Georgia during the Gamsakhurdia era. As a polyethnic society, we must embed protections that guarantee the survival of the Abkhaz people. Our fellow citizens understand this foundational principle.

That brings us back to language. Over time, our entire society must achieve sufficient command of the Abkhaz language for daily communication. Naturally, our society will remain bilingual due to demographic and geopolitical realities. This is why Russian is constitutionally designated alongside Abkhaz. But ‘alongside’ must not mean replacing Abkhaz. Striking this balance requires preserving the Abkhaz language while maintaining interethnic harmony. We should engage Abkhaz academic circles and draw on international experience—such as the major initiatives used to revive and preserve Welsh alongside English.

Ultimately, we need a sense of proportion in both domestic and foreign policy. Though emotions run high, avoiding extremes is vital. A population of our size can only survive through moderation and consensus.

Inal Khashig: Having come full circle, it seems clear that the survival and development of Abkhazia depend on building an inclusive civic nation that encompasses all ethnic groups residing here as citizens…

Astamur Tania: Including Georgians, of course.

Inal Khashig: …who would also command the state language.

Astamur Tania: Regarding the Gali district specifically, we must rethink our policy. We must acknowledge that regardless of how they identify ethnically, the residents there represent a native Megrelian-Georgian population, many with historical Abkhaz roots.

Inal Khashig: We can dedicate a separate conversation to that topic. But building a civic nation—governed by the rule of law and grounded in our constitutional language framework—is key to securing our future so that we aren’t constantly fearing our own disappearance.

Astamur Tania: Though I think we are destined to sound the alarm for many years to come!

Inal Khashig: Building a civic nation takes time and represents a broader movement toward a state governed by the rule of law.

Astamur Tania: To end on a reassuring note: perhaps artificial intelligence will solve all these problems for us!

Inal Khashig: I hope so! On that note, we will wrap up today’s broadcast. Today, Astamur Tania and I discussed the Abkhaz language, the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict, and why these complex questions persist. Goodbye. Until new meetings. Thank you.

Astamur Tania: Thank you.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: “When the state serves an oligarch, people leave” – from a march in Tbilisi. “Protests in Georgia” video blog
World.content:
For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. The results of the parliamentary elections held in autumn 2024 are still not recognised by part of Georgian society.

Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms.

For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti.

In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years.

To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

World.title: Judges vs ordinary pensioners in Azerbaijan: what the law and figures show
World.content:
Judges and pensions in Azerbaijan

The pension of Azerbaijani judge Jahangir Yusifov was increased from 4,700 manat (around $2,765) to 7,500 manat (around $4,412) after he took the matter to court. Thanks to special pension rules, judges’ pensions can be dozens of times higher than the country’s average pension.

For comparison: the minimum labour pension in Azerbaijan is 320 manat (around $188).

When Baku Court of Appeal judge Jahangir Yusifov retired in 2025 at the age of 65, the State Social Protection Fund awarded him a monthly pension of 4,700 manat. That amount was equivalent to around 58% of his average monthly salary while serving as a judge.

Yusifov demanded that his pension be increased to 8,200 manat (around $4,824), arguing that he had worked all his life under difficult conditions, possessed special professional qualifications, and had been subject to a high level of responsibility.

The Baku Administrative Court upheld most of his claim, increasing his pension to around 7,500 manat. His request for additional financial assistance equal to 10% of his pension was rejected.

This is not the first such case. Other retired judges have filed similar claims, including Azad Majidov, Anvar Seyidov, Ulvi Mayilov and others. The courts have upheld all of the claims filed.

These cases clearly demonstrate how the special social protection mechanism provided for judges under Azerbaijani law is applied in practice.

Judges’ pension provisions

Under Article 109 of the Law “On Courts and Judges,” judges’ pensions are calculated according to special rules and depend on their length of service as a judge.

For those who have served as a judge for at least five years, the pension may be set at 45% of their average salary.

For between 5 and 10 years of service, an additional 2% is added to the 45% for each additional year.

For between 10 and 15 years of service, the pension is set at 55% of the average salary, plus 5% for each additional year, but cannot exceed 80% of the average salary.

Pension calculations also take into account pension capital and other allowances предусмотренные by law.

These higher percentage rates and additional benefits based on length of service provide judges with special pension conditions compared with other groups of the population.

Is it possible to live on a pension?

A judge’s pension of 7,500 manat (around $4,412) is 23 times higher than the minimum pension and 12–13 times higher than the average pension.

For comparison, the official subsistence minimum for a pensioner, regardless of profession, is 245 manat (around $145).

The average pension is significantly higher than this threshold. Nevertheless, it can be difficult for a single pensioner to maintain a stable standard of living solely on an average pension. Older people often need additional sources of income, such as employment, family support or targeted social assistance.

According to official statistics, as of April 1, 2026, more than 105,000 old-age pension recipients were still working.

But state officials, prosecutors and judges are provided with a fundamentally different level of social protection. Many people in Azerbaijan view this approach as a “double standard” enshrined in law. And when it comes to lawsuits filed by judges seeking higher pensions, public discussions often include comments along the lines of: “Apparently, even that wasn’t enough for the judges.”

News in Azerbaijan

World.title: Heavy rain floods streets, basements and metro stations in Tbilisi – video
World.content:
Heavy rain in Tbilisi

Following heavy rainfall overnight on 14 August, the Georgian capital was once again flooded. Tbilisi City Hall issued a statement on the situation, saying the intense rainfall had “caused certain problems”.

According to the city authorities, central districts were the worst affected. Private homes and basements were flooded, while a retaining wall at one residential property collapsed. Streets across the city and areas around several metro stations were also inundated.

Throughout the night, residents posted videos from different parts of the capital showing flooded streets and squares. Residents of one street in the city centre also blocked the road, calling for help in dealing with the damage.

Videos published by city residents:

“The heavy rainfall in the capital caused problems in all ten districts. Gravel and stones were washed onto roads. Our staff are carrying out clean-up work around the clock. The rain was particularly heavy in the Vake, Mtatsminda and Krtsanisi districts.

“More than 500 personnel and 30 pieces of equipment have been mobilised across all affected areas and are involved in the clean-up operation. The work will continue until all the problems have been fully resolved,” said Giorgi Papava, head of Tbilisi’s main municipal services operator, Tbilservice Group.

World.title: LIV Golf ending season early after cancelling final event
World.content:
LIV Golf is ending its season one week earlier than planned, announcing on Monday it will not hold the team championship in Michigan next week and instead crown the team champion this week.

The 12 events this year — New Orleans was previously postponed — are the smallest schedule for LIV since it was launched with massive Saudi Arabian funding and eight tournaments in 2022.

Jon Rahm has already clinched the individual season title for the third straight year. LIV Golf Indianapolis, which starts on Thursday at The Club at Chatham Hills, will determine who finishes second and third among the players, and the top team.

Embattled LIV Golf tour asks to defer payment to Adelaide golf club The future of LIV Golf Adelaide has been further "shrouded in doubt", the SA opposition says, after LIV asked for an extension on a payment to Kooyonga Golf Club, which is scheduled to host the event next year.

The Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia, the financial muscle of the rival league from the start, decided in March this would be the final year of funding.

LIV Golf announced earlier this month it had an agreement with a lead investor that would sustain a new version of the league for 2027.

"By concluding the season now, we can put our full resources behind what comes next and maintain the operational rigor this transition demands," LIV CEO Scott O'Neil said in a statement.

"We are reimagining LIV Golf as a fundamentally new league owned by the players and anchored in a sustainable business model, with an evolved fan experience built for the markets where the game is growing fastest across the globe and the support of world-class partners."

The cancellation of LIV Golf Michigan was not surprising.

There have been reports in recent weeks the tournament had not even started preparing with grandstands and other amenities. LIV Golf said ticket holders would get refunds.

In another cost-cutting move LIV attributed to "unavoidable changes in the entertainment program", the league informed Thomas Rhett and Disco Lines their live performances would not take place at LIV Golf Indianapolis.

The final event, with a $US20 million ($28.1 million) purse that pays $US4 million to the winner, could be the last big pay-off for LIV and its 57 players.

LIV did not identify the lead investor or how much of a cash infusion was involved, or say whether it was an investment or a loan.

O'Neil has said the LIV 2.0 version for 2027 and onward would involve making players equity owners. He referred to it as a "second bite at the apple" being equity instead of cash.

But this likely is the end of $US20 million purses for individual outcomes, and there have already been cutbacks. Rahm earned $US6 million for winning the points title, down from $US18 million the previous two years.

"As we concentrate on finishing the season strong and building the next chapter of LIV Golf, we'll carry the energy and enthusiasm our fans have shown us into what comes next," O'Neil said.

The format for the 2027 season and the rosters also remain unclear.

Still to be determined is whether Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau — the two biggest names — and other players who joined the league for its exorbitant prize money will want to stay for LIV 2.0.

As for the final event, Joaquin Niemann, Lucas Herbert and Tyrrell Hatton are in the mix for third place, which pays a $US1 million bonus. DeChambeau is comfortably in second, which pays $US3 million.

Dustin Johnson's 4Aces team has a narrow lead over Australia-based Ripper, with Rahm's Legion XIII and Bryson DeChambeau's Crushers team all in the mix for the team title.

AP

World.title: Race to save cherry blossom avenue dedicated to Vietnam vets
World.content:
As veterans and their families commemorate 60 years since the deadliest day of the Vietnam War for Australian troops, one community is fighting to preserve a unique avenue of Japanese trees planted to honour the fallen.

A memorial walk in Bowral in the NSW Southern Highlands, believed to feature the country's only avenue of Japanese Tai-Haku "great white" cherry trees, is being rebuilt tree by tree, as veterans mark 60 years since the Battle of Long Tan.

The 307 trees are spread over a 5-kilometre walkway, creating an avenue of soldier-like trees in standard formation leading to the Bowral Vietnam War Memorial, and their boughs cascade with white flowers when in bloom.

However, many have developed phytophthora, or root rot, a fungal disease that prevents the trees' roots from absorbing water and nutrients, and they are slowly dying.

Some of the hundreds of trees planted along Cherry Tree Walk have survived 30 years, while others have been replaced. (ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss)

Veteran Tony Blake fondly recalls his involvement in the construction of the memorial 30 years ago.

Posted to the 7th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment, Mr Blake moved to Bowral when he returned and was welcomed by Wingecarribee Shire Council, which recognised his contribution to the war effort and elected him to the memorial committee.

"The quality [of the memorial] is stunning. I don't believe there are any in Australia like this, not to this quality anyway," he said.

Step by step

The idea of a memorial belonged to the late Effie Kerr OAM, a former member of the Highlands Garden Society Bowral.

"In 1996 they formed the Bowral Trust with Vietnam veterans and established the Vietnam War Memorial Trust with Effie and a couple of others, and I was on the committee," Mr Blake said.

Effie Kerr OAM with General Peter Cosgrove MC. (Supplied: Tony Blake)

Thought to be extinct in Japan by the 1920s, the flowering cherry (Prunus serrulata or Tai-Haku) was spotted by a British plant collector in England, who identified the Japanese tree from a painting of a white cherry.

Ms Kerr, who died in 2014, saw a parallel between the nearly lost tree and the Vietnam War veterans she believed Australia had forgotten, Mr Blake said.

Choosing the tree was also a symbolic connection to the part of the world in which they served.

"She wanted something different to honour the fallen, and that was the Eastern link," Mr Blake said.

Battle of Long Tan 60 years on

Lowering the Australian flag for the last time at Nui Dat on November 7, 1971. (Supplied: Australian War Memorial)

The Vietnam War (1962–72) was Australia's longest military commitment until Afghanistan, with the Battle of Long Tan becoming one of its most significant encounters.

"The Battle of Long Tan eventually became synonymous as a focal point for commemoration for Australia's service in Vietnam in general," said Craig Tibbitts, senior historian at the military history section of the Australian War Memorial in Canberra.

Craig Tibbitts says the Battle of Long Tan is a focus of commemorations of Australia's involvement in the Vietnam War. (Supplied: Australian War Memorial)

When the Delta Company 6th Battalion of the Royal Australian Regiment was sent to fight the enemy who had attacked the task force base at Nui Dat during the night, 18 Australian soldiers were killed and 24 wounded.

"That's why they picked the 18th of August to become known as Long Tan Day, more broadly as Vietnam Veterans Day for Australians," Mr Tibbitts said.

Tony Blake at the Vietnam War Memorial in Bowral, which lists Australians who fought and died in the war. (ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss)

For some, ceremonial occasions such as the one held in Bowral on the 60th anniversary of the Battle of Long Tan can be triggering.

"There have been a lot of men diagnosed with PTSD [post-traumatic stress disorder], and a lot in more recent years too," Mr Tibbitts said.

"Soldiers had to endure the gruelling physical demands of being out on patrol, sometimes for weeks, and the exacting toll that took on you physically and psychologically.

" But it was a real test of the Australians' resolve and enhanced their fighting reputation, demonstrating they were a force to be reckoned with. "

Overcoming adversity

For decades, the cherry blossom trees stood tall at the Bowral Vietnam War Memorial, but six years ago, veterans approached the Wingecarribee Shire Council for help.

Some of the trees had developed root rot, for which there is no practical cure.

"They [veterans] were pleading with us saying, 'We need to do something. [We] can't keep letting the trees die and not replace them,'" said Charlene O'Connor, the council's senior arborist and leader of the tree management team.

"There are 120 species of root rot in Australia, but what we have here is specific to these cherry trees because you can see there's other trees growing perfectly fine," she said.

Loading...

To resurrect Cherry Tree Walk, Ms O'Connor engaged a nursery in Millbrook, Victoria, which specialises in grafting trees, essentially cloning the original trees.

"We sent them original branches, and they grafted them onto rootstock, and they've been doing that for six years now," Ms O'Connor said.

"We're replacing the exact canopy and the flowers are exactly the same."

The trees are being grafted to replicate the canopy. (ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss)

Ms O'Connor said she enjoyed working on the project and appreciated everything the veterans had done.

"It's something they value that we should all value as well," she said.

"I like the trees, [their] purpose and its meaning. It's very sentimental."

World.title: Live: Taylor issues ultimatum to PM over NDIS and widows' tax
World.content:
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor says the Coalition will only back Labor's NDIS overhaul once the government scraps its so-called "widow tax".

The tax emerged as an issue after May's budget because it means someone who inherits an investment property from their spouse after they die could face a less generous tax treatment and lose existing negative gearing access.

The chief critic of the legislative flaw, independent senator David Pocock, said it would disproportionately hurt women.

Labor has promised to "fix" the issue and is consulting on changes, but Taylor wants it dealt with immediately and has issued an ultimatum, in a letter to the prime minister.

World.title: Pygmy blue whale beaches and dies off NT coast in historic first sighting
World.content:
A pygmy blue whale has beached itself and died on the coast of Groote Eylandt in the Northern Territory in what researchers believe is a first of its kind.

Traditional owners on the island spotted the 6-metre-long whale beached about 500m offshore in the Gulf of Carpentaria on Friday morning.

They called the sighting in to the Anindilyakwa Land and Sea Rangers, where land and sea manager Kirsten Eden jumped in a car and headed to the beach.

Anindilyakwa ranger Kirsten Eden says the rare sighting of the whale was "gobsmacking". (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

"Lo and behold, it was a whale," she said.

" I've never, ever seen anything like this before, quite a remarkable thing to witness, and the sheer size of that whale is just gobsmacking. "

She said the animal died the following night and was positively identified by researchers as a pygmy blue whale through photographs and tissue samples.

'A pretty exceptional finding'

Charles Darwin University (CDU) marine life researcher Rachel Groom said while it was too early to tell why the whale became beached, it was an extremely rare occurrence.

Researchers say the "extraordinary animal" was likely "well off course" based on satellite tracking data. (Supplied: Anindilyakwa Land & Sea Rangers)

"I actually thought it's probably a humpback, but then I saw the photos and like, oh my god, that's actually a blue whale," she said.

" I was incredibly excited but also sad because there was no way that animal was going to survive. "

She said two pygmy blue whales had beached in the NT before: the first in 1981 and again in 2003.

That meant 22 years had passed between the first two beachings and another 23 years between the 2003 incident and last week's.

Carol Palmer says it is likely the first time a pygmy blue whale has ever been seen in the Gulf of Carpentaria. (ABC News: Jane Bardon)

"Maybe it's coincidence but could also relate to climatic events as well," she said.

"This is a pretty exceptional finding. It's an extraordinary animal, and it's well off course from what we know from satellite tracking records."

Fellow CDU researcher Carol Palmer said based on everything she could confirm, it was likely the first time a pygmy blue whale had ever been recorded in the Gulf of Carpentaria.

"Over a number of years, they've satellite tagged six pygmy blue whales off [Western Australia], and they go to Timor-Leste and up to Indonesia, where they give birth," she said.

Pygmy blue whales are typically found in the Indian and Southern Pacific oceans. (Supplied: Anindilyakwa Land & Sea Rangers)

Dr Palmer said the samples taken could help confirm the whale's sex and potentially some other data through DNA analysis.

"It's quite long and tall but very skinny … it's all a bit of a worry really," she said.

"It makes me very sad."

Nature to take its course

Anindilyakwa rangers are now trying to work out how best to manage the whale's carcass, which is still sitting off the coast in a popular hunting location for traditional owners.

"Every traditional owner I've spoken to is absolutely gobsmacked and mortified," Ms Eden said.

Groote Eylandt is off the coast of Blue Mud Bay in Arnhem Land, south of Nhulunbuy, and home to the Indigenous Anindilyakwa people. (ABC News: Erin Parke)

"Unfortunately, [because of] the size of the whale and the location of it, we're unable to get any large vessels in there," she said.

" Groote has a lot of mammals in the water [so] that unfortunately, nature will take its course. "

Ms Eden said she had already seen tiger sharks begin feeding on the whale as its carcass continued to degrade naturally.

World.title: 'Very fortunate' no collision yet at Sydney Airport, former pilot says
World.content:
Sydney Airport could face "catastrophic" consequences if safety issues are not addressed, following three incidents in as many weeks, a former pilot and aviation safety investigator says.

The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) revealed last Thursday it was investigating a third mishap, this time involving a Qantas flight crossing the path of a departing Virgin Australia aircraft.

It said at 10am on August 9, Virgin flight VA555 to Perth had its clearance to take-off rescinded by air traffic control soon after it had been given.

It is understood Qantas flight QF728 began to cross the runway more than 1,200 metres away from the Virgin plane, after also receiving clearance.

Just three hours earlier, there was a near miss between a Jetstar plane and a Qatar Airways aircraft at the same airport.

A Jetstar cabin crew worker was injured when the A320 plane had to brake suddenly to avoid colliding with a Boeing 777 under tow.

Two weeks prior, on July 27, a Qantas Link flight and a Qantas plane were involved in a near-miss on the tarmac.

Geoff Klouth has 35 years of experience working with commercial airlines. (Supplied: Geoff Klouth)

Retired commercial airline pilot and former aviation safety inspector, Geoff Klouth, said if the safety issues were not rectified "quickly", a worse incident could occur.

"We've been very fortunate that there haven't been collisions, but it doesn't mean it won't happen in the future," he said.

"It's only luck preventing the aircraft coming together because the system is not working at present.

" I'll say that the chances from a risk management level ... are high that something will happen and the consequences of that could be catastrophic. "

ATSB chief commissioner Angus Mitchell said on Friday there were "multiple lines of defence" in an emergency situation like the trio of recent incidents.

"I will say in all three instances, there was a layer of defence that kicked in and prevented an escalation," he said.

"We find in a lot of our investigations it is very rarely a single point of failure. For it to progress through to an actual accident, multiple things need to go wrong."

'Matter of significant interest'

The trio of incidents began with a near miss in late July. (ABC News)

Mr Klouth's aviation career spanned 35 years, making his way from flying instructor to piloting Kendell, Ansett and Qantas commercial airlines in Australia and overseas.

While mostly based at Melbourne Airport, he frequently flew in and out of Sydney.

He also spent 18 months as a senior aviation safety investigator at the ATSB, followed by a long stint with Jetstar as a first officer, fleet safety investigator, training captain, and flight operations auditor from 2006 until he retired in 2023.

Mr Klouth said one of the reasons he retired was because the systems that used to support pilots were "diminishing in quality and standards".

He said this included a reduction in air traffic controllers employed by Airservices Australia, as well as procedures managed by airports and the regulatory Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA).

"You were expected to maintain a safe flight, but you weren't given the processes around it," Mr Klouth said.

Staffing issues are one reason Mr Klouth decided to retire. (Supplied: Geoff Klouth)

CASA did not answer questions sent by the ABC about safety systems, citing the current investigation.

However the regulatory authority said the third incident was a "matter of significant interest" to them and it was working with Airservices Australia.

"It is important that we allow time for the ATSB to investigate this and the other incidents fully and that we do not prejudice its investigation by speculating on their cause," it said in a statement.

The ABC also contacted Sydney Airport for comment about safety issues and risks of a possible collision, to which it responded safety was and always will be "the first priority".

"Australia has one of the safest aviation systems in the world, supported by rigorous oversight from safety regulators, airlines, airports, and air navigation service providers," a spokesperson said.

Mr Klouth said Airservices Australia "tried to diminish" the latest runway incident by suggesting there was "still plenty of room".

"The point is that the system should be there, the procedures should be in place, so that never happens," he said.

Airservices Australia says it is working with the ATSB. (Supplied: Geoff Klouth)

Airservices Australia did not respond to Mr Klouth's allegation about safety measures and staffing levels, instead pointing to previous statements.

The company previously said safety was its top priority.

On Friday, CEO Rob Sharp said initial reviews of the recent incidents had not uncovered systemic issues compromising passenger safety.

He said the government body responsible for managing air traffic did not believe the incident met the threshold for reporting because an "experienced controller" rescinded clearance to the Virgin pilot immediately, the aircraft was stationary, and it was 1,300 metres from the Qantas plane.

"We do take our reporting requirements very seriously," he said.

"But we will work closely with the ATSB because there are some data points that need to be resolved and clarified ... we look forward to any learnings that come from that particular incident."

'Structural challenge'

Mr Klouth said the Sydney Airport "crisis" was a "long time coming".

"I could see that [safety issues] already starting to happen due to staffing levels ... but what we're seeing is the end result of that," he said.

"If one controller is busy doing multiple tasks or they've been called in to come into work on multiple days off, fatigue can have an impact on your performance."

Air safety boss 'trying to understand' Sydney Airport incident reporting delay A third safety issue on the tarmac at Sydney Airport prompted the nation's air safety boss question why investigators were not notified for four days about another incident on Sunday.

Last week, Minister for Transport Catherine King released a statement after a meeting with the Airservices Australia boss to discuss the airport's challenges.

"It has been a big focus of ours to encourage more people to enter the profession, and 95 people are expected to be endorsed as air traffic controllers by the end of the year," Ms King said.

"Six controllers are currently training in Sydney Tower, with another 15 expected to commence before the end of 2027."

Ms King said the company commitment to improving roster practices for Sydney's air traffic controllers would begin early September, and that a new Sydney Tower simulator had been installed to increase training capacity.

Mr Sharp said there had been a 44 per cent decrease in delays at the airport over the past two years, and the organisation was focused on the "structural challenge" of the shortage of air traffic controllers.

World.title: FIFA executive who criticised Infantino's World Cup sale plan departs
World.content:
FIFA's chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, has left soccer's governing body, weeks after he publicly criticised president Gianni Infantino's plan to sell a stake in its tournament business, including the World Cup.

"FIFA can confirm that the working relationship between FIFA and Kevin Lamour as FIFA's chief operating officer has ended on 17 August 2026," a FIFA spokesperson said.

How Gianni Infantino's FIFA leadership imploded over two weeks The FIFA president has faced more than a fortnight of international turmoil, embroiled in a World Cup sell-off saga that sparked loss of confidence in his leadership.

"FIFA thanks Kevin for his two years of service and wishes him the best of luck for the future. No further comment will be made on the matter."

Lamour had publicly criticised the proposal last month, saying FIFA staff had been "deceived" over the plan and describing it as "the project of one person".

"Our mission … is to serve football. Not to serve the personal interests of a person who, unfortunately, believes he embodies FIFA when he is supposed to be at its service," Lamour said in a statement at the time.

Lamour's comments came hours after Carlos Cordeiro, a senior adviser to Infantino, resigned in protest at the proposal, calling it "a bad deal for football".

The internal dissent came as FIFA faced widespread opposition to its plan to create a $US20 billion ($28.1 billion) subsidiary to run its tournaments, including the World Cup, and sell up to a 20 per cent stake to external investors. FIFA subsequently abandoned the proposal following the backlash.

Reuters

World.title: Donkeys, camels and the 'Emu Man' call this 'ghost town' home
World.content:
On the long winding road out to one of the country's largest outback music festivals, a convoy of caravans containing thousands of people will pass through what may appear to be a virtual ghost town.

But what many may not realise is that the village of Silverton, roughly 25 kilometres north of Broken Hill, is in itself a tourist hotspot, complete with its own line-up of quirky characters.

From the self-professed "mayor, sheriff and town drunk" all rolled into one, to the curator of a museum dedicated to Mad Max 2, to a former police officer turned camel farm owner, all are ready to welcome visitors with open arms.

'Mayor', 'town drunk' and 'Emu Man'

Artist John Dynon goes by many names and self-appointed titles: "Mayor", "sheriff" and "town drunk".

He's also affectionately known as the "Emu Man" due to the number of them that feature in his artwork.

Mr Dynon's Silverton gallery sits opposite the pub, and has a corrugated iron facade covered in brightly coloured paint.

Silverton artist John Dynon, also known as The Emu Man, paints from a studio in Silverton. (ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen)

In the front yard, an old Volkswagen Beetle and countless bicycles are littered about, all of them similarly painted.

Inside, Mr Dynon stands by a table and paints outback landscapes and emus with seemingly human personalities: drinking beer, working in the mines, making camp fires — some are even kitted out in leather jumpsuits.

For the past 40 years, Mr Dynon has found inspiration for his paintings in Silverton and the surrounding outback.

Although he now lives in Broken Hill, he spends most of his time at his gallery in Silverton.

"I like the old town because it's a ghost town, and I love the surrounding area," he said.

"I love all the bush, the beautiful skies, the sunsets, the animals, everything."

The most lucrative week in the gallery's year is the Mundi Mundi Bash week, which sees Mr Dynon set up a pop-up shop at the festival.

While the artist says he enjoys the Bash, he admits disappointment in his favourite genre of music never making an appearance.

John Dynon finds a lot of inspiration for his paintings in Silverton. (ABC Broken Hill: Oliver Brown)

"There's no techno … they don't bring the techno people out," he said.

"But I still love all the music … it's good for the town, it's good for everybody."

The makings of a Mad Max museum

Only a short walk up the road from Mr Dynon's gallery is a metal shed painted with the colourful characters of Mad Max 2, which was filmed in and around Silverton in 1981.

Inside, visitors are greeted by a treasure trove of costumes, vehicles, props and memorabilia from the movie, along with the museum's cheerful owner, Adrian Bennett.

Adrian Bennett moved to Silverton all the way from the UK, driven by his passion for Mad Max 2. (ABC Broken Hill: Oliver Brown)

Mr Bennett, a die-hard fan of the movie, moved from the United Kingdom to Silverton with his wife Linda in 2009 and said he has not looked back.

"Sometimes dreams can come true; I just followed a passion, and this [museum] is the result of it," Mr Bennett said.

"It really has been a wonderful 16 years since we opened and seeing the place evolve … we just add where we can as we come across things."

Mr Bennett himself is a walking encyclopedia on Mad Max, having met and become friends with people involved with it over the years, and he is more than happy to share that knowledge.

Adrian Bennett always looks forward to the surge in tourism driven by the Mundi Mundi Bash. (ABC Broken Hill: Oliver Brown)

While they typically enjoy a steady stream of visitors, with the Mundi Mundi Bash again on the horizon, Mr Bennett and his team are excited to see Silverton come alive.

"It really helps us out, especially after the slow start we had to the tourist season this year," Mr Bennett said.

"You meet some wonderful people so it's a great thing to look forward to."

An accidental cameleer

While Silverton has a human population of around 27 people, its animal locals are also an integral part of the community.

Free-range donkeys regularly roam the dusty streets of Silverton. (ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen)

It's not uncommon to see the town's resident free-range donkeys wandering the streets, but many more can be found on the village's outskirts at the Silverton Camel Farm.

Sheep, goats, donkeys, emu, deer, alpacas, pigs, peacocks, geese, guinea fowl and, of course, camels, are just some of the residents living at Petah Devine's farm.

Having always been an animal lover, the former police officer was on the hunt for a block of land where she could keep a few animals back in 2017 when, through a dare, she took on camels.

"My workmates dared [me] because I was living in the outback, [so they said] … I should have pet camels," she said.

"I got my first two within a month of buying the farm."

Former police officer Petah Devine (right) says she started her camel farm business on a dare. (ABC Broken Hill: Kristina Rosengren)

Within a few short years, those camels became an integral part of her business, Silverton Outback Camel Farm.

During Bash week, Ms Devine has punters staying at the farm itself and operates camel tours and a petting zoo at the festival grounds.

But it's not just her business that benefits, with all of Silverton seeing an influx of tourism traffic during Bash week.

While the community is used to visitors, Ms Devine said tourism numbers have boomed this time of year since the first festival four years ago.

"It's certainly putting us on the map … we're about to see carloads, caravans, everything heading this way," she said.

Hospitality businesses welcome customer boost

Also eager to welcome the thousands of people coming for the Bash are part-time bakers, part-time outback station owners Steve and Naomi Schmidt.

Over the course of the festival, the couple typically bake around 2,000 pies.

Naomi and Steven Schmidt typically bake around 2,000 pies over the course of the festival every year. (ABC Broken Hill: OIiver Brown)

While Mr Schmidt has lived in Silverton almost all his life, Ms Schmidt has lived there for the past 40 years.

"I love meeting new people, and the people we employ have come from all over the world," Ms Schmidt said.

"It's a very diversified group of people that operate here … I don't think you'd find that mix anywhere else in the world."

Meanwhile, relatively new publicans Liz Murphy and Norm Matau are nervous but excited for their first Mundi Mundi Bash.

The couple took over the lease of the Silverton Hotel in March after chucking in their lives in the city.

Liz Murphy is a recent addition to Silverton, after moving to the town earlier this year to take over the pub with her partner. (ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen)

"We're up for the challenge, and we've got some fabulous staff here that have done Mundi Mundi before," Ms Murphy said.

"We've got a massive set up, I'm really looking forward to seeing how it all goes."

Accidental tourists excited to return

While all locals agree tourism is Silverton's biggest economic driver, and that the Mundi Mundi Bash is its biggest source of that, the village does still get regular visitors.

Peter Jones from Western Australia recently passed through town for the first time by total chance after his plan to travel the Darling River Run was diverted due to wet weather.

"It reminded me of an old western town … there's just so much to see and do if you investigate a little bit," Mr Jones said.

Accidental tourist Peter Jones said he, his wife and their dogs will definitely be back to visit. (ABC Broken Hill: Oliver Brown)

"You can tell [the atmosphere] is building, the influx of thousands of people for Mundi Mundi, and we're very jealous because we hadn't planned to be here.

" We're so glad we got diverted … we'll definitely be back because even around some of the surrounding areas of this place, there's so much to investigate. "

World.title: Bird flu crisis will get to the stage where 'all we can do is euthanase', vets warn
World.content:
The vet industry has warned it may be forced to euthanase hoards of wild birds they could be saving due to a lack of funding and appropriate facilities amid the H5 bird flu crisis.

The deadly virus has now been confirmed in every Australian state with only the Northern Territory and Australian Capital Territory yet to detect it.

To protect other animals including domestic pets, some vet practices have put a blanket ban on treating injured or sick wild birds, even if they have not displayed avian influenza symptoms.

Those who are still taking in wild birds, like Mish Simpson's wildlife vet clinic in Adelaide's Onkaparinga Hills, have already experienced a spike.

"Last year I think we had 140 birds through our clinic and I think in the last few weeks we've had 20 to 30 alone," she said.

Vets say treating injured wild birds, like Squeak the rainbow lorikeet, will bolster populations in the H5 bird flu firing line. (ABC News)

Ms Simpson said she was expecting to be inundated with "hundreds" of wild birds during the spring breeding season, as greater numbers will be "getting themselves in trouble" like being hit by cars or hurt in fires.

She said conserving bird life has never been more crucial, to bolster populations at risk of serious decline from the deadly virus.

"Birds that we see every day in high numbers may disappear … for more vulnerable species it could wipe out the entire population," Ms Simpson said.

Unnecessary euthanasia 'devastating'

To prepare, clinics like Ms Simpson's have created temporary, isolated surgeries and triage spaces, either at their own cost or by looking for donations.

Mish Simpson's vets treat wild birds in tents and a gazebo they self-funded, and a transportable building loaned for free. (ABC News)

However, without help to keep up with demand, they fear they will be left with no choice but to euthanase animals they could have saved.

"Unfortunately euthanasia may be the most logical outcome, even if it is an otherwise recoverable injury or if it's just a bird that needs short-term care," Ms Simpson said.

"At some stage this situation will get to the point where everyone's at capacity and all we can do is euthanase to make sure the birds aren't suffering.

"We want to hold off that stage for as long as possible because that's not going to be a fun time for anyone."

The Australian Veterinary Association (AVA) is asking the federal government to commit to funding $7.5 million over four years to support vets responding to the bird flu crisis, but that call has so far gone unanswered.

Mish Simpson is urging governments to provide financial support so vets can help bolster bird populations. (ABC News: Luke Pike)

In the grips of a profession-wide mental health crisis, Ms Simpson said euthanasing savable wild birds would be "incredibly devastating", but she said there "hasn't been any government support".

"The vet industry is in crisis … the government's aware of that and this is only going to push it over the edge," she said.

"Vets that are already burnt out and have compassion fatigue are probably going to very early on in this process leave if there's not enough support for them."

The federal Department of Agriculture did not provide a reason why it was not meeting the AVA's request for funding.

It said the commonwealth is leading a collaborative response to the bird flu outbreak, working to minimise the impact on wildlife, livestock and human health, including mental health.

Dr Jackie Reed says urgent funding is needed for PPE like gloves and scrubs, to protect humans and animals. (ABC News: Luke Pike)

Wildlife vet Dr Jackie Reed has been treating injured wild birds at Ms Simpson's clinic.

She said some vets had already been forced to euthanase wild birds that could have been saved.

"It's an awful situation to be in because you know you're not doing your best," Dr Reed said.

"We need these isolation facilities, we need the PPE, there's so much money that needs to be spent on proper protection for humans and also for our patients."

Bird flu tests the 'missing piece'

Ms Simpson is also calling on the South Australian government to provide vets with H5 bird flu testing kits.

Positive cases would be euthanased and reported, but negative results would allow vets to confidently clear high-risk species like seabirds for treatment, even those that are not showing bird flu symptoms.

"It's the missing piece", Ms Simpson said.

"We still want to be able to test them, to make sure we're not sending them on to carers or putting them in another area of our facility.

"If they show to be positive in the days to come they've potentially exposed other birds.

"It makes sense that our vets who are already assessing it in the appropriate PPE should just be able to test so that it saves work for everyone."

Vets want the South Australian government to provide them with H5 bird flu testing kits. (Supplied: Queensland Government)

In a statement, South Australia's Department of Primary Industries said due to national lab testing protocols, it had "no current plans" to roll out bird flu testing kits to wildlife vets.

"PIRSA understands concerns raised by veterinary staff and is continuing to work closely with the sector … with regular updates through webinars, meetings and written advice," a department spokesperson said.

Advocate Garry Putland is urging the federal government to heed the plea for help from vets.

Sophie's Legacy co-founder Garry Putland says high workloads are a key contributor to the mental health crisis in the vet profession. (Supplied)

Mr Putland and his wife run Sophie's Legacy, a charity to reduce suicide rates in the veterinary profession, in honour of their daughter Sophie Putland who died by suicide in 2021.

"We're really asking governments to acknowledge the significant work that is done by (vets)," he said.

"To make sure that they are not increasing the pressures which will result in the mental health crisis worsening.

"But actually funding the veterinary industry so that we're doing exactly the opposite, and that is setting the industry up to reduce the suicide rate."

World.title: ‘The money will come’: Why Pritchard brothers turned down PNG riches to stay in rugby
World.content:
Exclusive SportRugby UnionWallabies ‘The money will come’: Why Pritchard brothers turned down PNG riches to stay in rugby Jonathan Drennan August 18, 2026 — 7:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Before making the biggest decision of their young professional careers, Treyvon and Kadin Pritchard thought back to two important lessons taught to them by their parents, Daniel and Brenda: never leave a job half done, and always show loyalty to those who backed you from the start. The brothers ultimately turned down the lucrative offer tabled by the PNG Chiefs to join the NRL expansion franchise for its inaugural season in 2028, opting instead to remain at their respective rugby clubs, with Treyvon signing an extension with the Reds until 2029 and Kadin remaining at the Brumbies until 2030. Both brothers also have the opportunity to play sevens in the 2028 Olympics. Treyvon (L) and Kadin Pritchard are staying in Australian rugby. Rugby Australia “I think from a young age mum and dad have always instilled in us the value of finishing what you’ve started and never doing a half job,” Treyvon told this masthead. “Our parents taught us to finish what we’ve started. Loyalty does come into play, too. It’s a big part of our everyday lives and something that our parents have made us follow, and it’s led into our everyday life.



“Also, coming through from being a 15-year-old in the Reds environment to moving up and training with the older boys while I was still in school with a couple of my mates. “We all have come through at the same time and we have those connections, and I think a big thing with footy is being able to trust your teammates. If you already have something in place, there’s no real reason to kind of change that and switch it up. Treyvon is one of the most exciting talents in Australian rugby. World Rugby “So I think the friendships and the connections that I already have are also a big part of my reasoning to stay in Australian rugby.” The brothers spoke highly of their dealings with the Chiefs, but ultimately turned down the lucrative offer because they felt they have unfinished business in rugby together – and believe the money will follow them eventually.



“Obviously, it was exciting [to get the PNG offer] and yeah, we did meet with them, and I think that was probably both our first real kind interest from league. So we tested the waters and we were trying to see what it was all about,” Treyvon said. “But I think Rugby Australia had a lot to offer as well. Like I said before, loyalty played a big part in where we are now and that helped us to a decision on where we wanted to be for the next couple of years... “The money is going to come, it’s probably not the biggest worry at the moment. We need to focus on establishing ourselves in our respective teams.” Kadin said that beyond immediate financial rewards, rugby will offer the brothers a chance to travel the world while playing the game they love. “I love rugby union and the possibilities that it can bring with the worldwide game were a big thing for me to stay here,” Kadin said.



“To travel around the world, playing international teams – and even if it’s club level, you can go over somewhere like France. The possibilities of doing that sort of thing, you don’t get that in other sports.” The Ella brothers brought an almost telepathic understanding to the Wallabies back line in the 1980s and the Pritchards believe they can eventually replicate that synergy as a centre partnership for the Australian Test team. Kadin Pritchard dreams of forming a centre partnership with Treyvon at Test level for the Wallabies . Getty Images “It’s definitely a dream of ours to link up at some point,” Kadin said. “We’ve been separated for a reason: to build ourselves up in our own teams and build the groups around us. “By the time we get to the Wallabies, we’ll be set to go, because we’ve got that brother intuition ... we want to play together in the centres, with Trayvon at inside centre.



“It’s definitely been a thought in my mind becoming that 12 and 13, and you probably don’t see it too often having brothers in the centres with that connection. We’re just almost interlinked and we know how each other plays from doing it so often in the backyard.” Having spent endless hours playing together as kids, the two brothers came up against each other for the first time last season, when the Reds faced the Brumbies in Super Rugby. But Treyvon says it is when playing together on the same side that their close relationship brings an extra edge. “We probably don’t have to speak as much as other players would; we can communicate with our body language and trust is a big factor in the connection that we have over other players,” Treyvon said. At 22 years old, Kadin has always felt protective of Treyvon, who is three years younger than him. Treyvon affectionately calls Kadin the family’s “test dummy”, the older brother who had to forge the way into professional rugby before passing on the lessons learned along the way. Though separated by distance, the brothers still speak regularly and operate as a unit when it comes to making decisions on their rugby future.



The brothers have been brought up to support one another, wary that there will always be others outside the family who want to tear one or another of them down. “We know what each other can do and why should we hate on our family when you’ve got haters outside already,” Kadin said. “The tightness of our family, it’s just been brought through by our dad. Treyvon Pritchard suffered serious injuries in this hip drop tackle against Wales at the Junior World Championship, but is recovering well after surgery. Stan Sport “We’re our own biggest supporters, we’ve got to support each other and build each other up so there’s no hate coming from within, and we have a support group here. “There’s no way I’m going to hate on what my bro’s doing. I’m just going to hype him up to be the best player in the world. What’s the point of trying to pull him down when everybody else is trying to do that?”



Both brothers are currently recovering from injuries. Kadin is nursing a hamstring strain but hopes to return to play for the Brumbies in the Super Rugby AUS competition, while Treyvon is recovering from an operation after breaking his right leg ain a hip drop tackle while representing Australia Under 20s. Treyvon’s current recovery timeline is between 12 and 18 weeks. Related Article Australian rugby ‘Run us off our feet’: Wallabies’ surprising ploy to prepare for Japanese heat Both brothers are focused on establishing their positions with their respective Super Rugby clubs ahead of a new season, but Treyvon is aware there will always be future possibilities, whether in rugby or the NRL. “We’re definitely not closed off to playing overseas, and I think once we make a decision on that, I think we would probably look to play together, I don’t see why we wouldn’t,” Treyvon said. “I think living in a different country is hard enough, so I think being with the older bro would be awesome. “I’m [also] not closed off to the NRL. Obviously all the noise that’s been happening recently probably sparked a bit of interest for everyone, but it’s definitely an option down the track. I’m with the Reds for three years and with Aussie rugby for three years, so whatever happens after that happen.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.
