World.title: This is, hands down, the most confronting thing I’ve seen on screen all year
World.content:
Alex Gibney is no stranger to challenging material. But his film about the stabbing of Salman Rushdie takes some topping.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This year’s Melbourne International Film Festival has kicked off. Here we take a closer look at some of what’s on offer. See all stories .

As Salman Rushdie lay in hospital after being repeatedly stabbed on stage in August 2022, his wife Rachel Eliza Griffiths started filming. Asking if he was OK with that, he told her yes. “We need to document this.” Now, Alex Gibney has turned that raw, unflinching and often hard-to-watch footage into Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie, one of the most confronting, but ultimately hopeful, movies you’ll ever see. “On this film, I acted mostly as an editor,” says the prolific documentarian who won an Oscar (with Australian producer Eva Orner) for Taxi to the Dark Side in 2007 and has five Emmy wins to his name. “My agent told me Salman and Eliza were interested in talking to me, and I learned they had this footage that Eliza took, starting on day five of his recovery and going right up to when they returned to the scene of the crime. And the first question I asked them was, ‘Why don’t you do it? No one knows more about what happened than you do’. And they said, ‘Well, that’s the problem. We feel too close to it. We want somebody else to come in and see if they can figure out a way to reckon with it.’” Gibney pitched an approach informed by The Singing Detective, the 1986 BBC drama series written by Dennis Potter, in which Michael Gambon played a bed-bound writer in hospital whose medication produces a blurring of his imaginative world and his memories. Despite its complex (and much-praised) structure, the show could be boiled down, says Gibney, to a pretty simple idea: a guy who is sick gets better, but along the way he reimagines his life through hallucinations and his detective fiction.



Rushdie, who had not yet decided to write his own account of the incident (his book Knife: Meditation on an Attempted Murder was released in August 2024), liked the idea, and the film Gibney has made – with Griffiths credited as executive producer and principal cinematographer – serves both as an account of the attack and its aftermath and as a meditation on Rushdie’s life more broadly. Knife opens with a recreation of the attack, with Rushdie asking in voiceover, “Why didn’t I fight back?” It’s a shocking way to start, but it’s nothing compared to what follows. Staff and audience members come to Rushdie’s aid at the Chautauqua Institution on August 12, 2022. AP The Booker Prize winner was in a chair on the stage of the Chautauqua Institution in New York State, about to be interviewed, when a man armed with a knife rushed up the steps and lunged at him. The attacker, Hadi Matar, stabbed the novelist 15 times, landing blows in his neck, stomach, chest and thigh. One of them struck Rushdie, who was 76 at the time, in his right eye (he has lost all sight in it). Matar had been inspired by the fatwa issued by Iran in 1989 in response to Rushdie’s novel The Satanic Verses, which Ayatollah Khomeini and his fellow clerics had deemed blasphemous. (Iran’s position on the fatwa has since become somewhat ambiguous, but it has never officially been rescinded. Last month a trial on terrorism charges against Matar – who has already been convicted of attempted murder – began in Buffalo, New York.) The film also includes real footage of the attack, which was only released during Matar’s first trial in February 2025. It’s horrendous in its brutality, and Gibney admits he wasn’t sure that he should even include it. “I mean, for a documentarian, it would be very hard not to show the actual crime, but I did ponder that maybe we shouldn’t,” he says. What got him over the line was the footage Griffiths had shot of her and Rushdie returning to Chautauqua, “and within that context it seemed to make sense to show it”.



The most challenging scenes in the film, though, are probably the shots of Rushdie’s horribly disfigured eyeball, bulging from its socket, occluded, pointing wildly out of focus. “Trust me,” says Gibney, “in a theatre you can hear the whole audience go ‘aagh’. It’s very difficult to watch.” There was never any chance of not including that footage, though. “Both of them [Rushdie and Griffiths] felt very strongly that they wanted to show this is what terrorism looks like.” For all that Griffiths’ footage was the rock on which the film is built, Gibney knew he had to go beyond it to tell the story he had in mind. “Too much of that, and it’s only about his physical recovery, rather than a deeper kind of mental recovery,” he says. “And once you enter the mind, it’s a chaotic and unpredictable place, and you have to sort of go with the flow.” Rushdie’s wife, Rachel Eliza Griffiths, began filming from five days after the attack. They had been married less than a year when it happened. Getty In archival footage, interviews from across the decades and in his own scripted narration, Rushdie reflects on being an outsider in his own family in Mumbai, of feeling the lash of racism at the English boarding school (Rugby) to which he was sent by his father when he was 14, of the cold shoulder some in the literary establishment turned on him when Iran called for his murder, with the offer of a massive bounty (starting at $1 million, it eventually rose to $6 million). There’s a sense overall of a man wounded many times in his life, and of his attempt to stitch himself back together in spite of it all. Whatever you might think of Rushdie, it’s impossible not to be moved by his resilience, his unflinching commitment to free speech, and his refusal of hatred.

World.title: Trump threatens to bomb ally Oman as US-Iran war agreement expires
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaMiddle East at war Trump threatens to bomb ally Oman as US-Iran war agreement expires Michael Koziol August 18, 2026 — 5:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: US President Donald Trump threatened to bomb US ally Oman if it “gets in the way” of reopening the Strait of Hormuz, while casting doubt on the possibility of reaching a new deal with Iran after their 60-day interim agreement expired. Next week will mark six months since the US and Israel launched a joint attack on the Islamic Republic. Although the fighting has subsided, the US continues to impose a naval blockade against Iran, and a permanent deal to end the conflict and restore free shipping remains elusive. Donald Trump in the Oval Office on Monday. He said Iran was not willing to make the kind of deal he thought acceptable. AP Photo/Manuel Balce Ceneta In an interview with Fox News, Trump reportedly confirmed the existence of back-channel communications between the US and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, the hardline militants responsible for shooting drones and missiles at ships in the strait. Iran and Oman – an American partner on the Arabian Peninsula, which sits across the Gulf of Oman from Iran – have been engaged in talks about management of the crucial waterway, as stipulated by the Memorandum of Understanding signed by the US and Iran in June. That agreement expired on Monday (Washington time).



At a news conference, Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said talks with Oman continued. The process was taking longer, he said, as multiple countries were trying to influence the outcome. The parties have suggested an agreement was close for nearly two weeks. Trump told Fox News on Monday: “If Oman gets in the way, we’ll bomb the shit out of them.” Later, in the Oval Office, he struck a different tone: “I don’t think [Oman] behave very well, but we handle them.” Iranian children swim in the Strait of Hormuz as cargo ships are anchored in the distance. Getty Images It is not the first time Trump has made such a threat, as Oman has previously countenanced the idea of setting up a tolling system in the strait with Iran. He insisted November’s midterm elections were not a factor in his thinking, despite many Iran experts arguing that Tehran was trying to run down the clock on Trump’s patience and political capital. Brent crude oil was trading at above $US90 a barrel on Monday.



Trump on Monday repeated his desire to declare the Strait of Hormuz a US territory, having teased the idea at a rally in Long Island, New York, last week. But he offered no explanation as to how that would work, nor what – if anything – it would entail. “We control it with the blockade. I like the idea of declaring it a territory,” Trump told reporters. “[Iran] can be a nuisance, they can put a mine in the water. But the blockade has been very effective.” Trump in the Oval Office on Monday, where he met with lifeguard Ryder Williams, left. AP Photo/Manuel Balce Ceneta The president also cast doubt on whether an acceptable deal with Iran to end the war and reopen the strait was possible. He implied that Iran was in a parlous state, which may lead it to reconsider its position at a later date. “They want to make a deal, but they’re not going to make the kind of deal that I feel is necessary,” he said. “Iran is in big trouble. They have 300 per cent inflation. The country is a mess and their military is totally defeated.”



Meanwhile, the US is relocating the USS George Washington aircraft carrier from the Asia-Pacific to the Middle East to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln, which is heading home amid growing concerns about living conditions on-board after a record-breaking deployment. That decision means there are no American aircraft carriers left in the Pacific. Addressing the apparent Middle East stalemate on Monday, Iran analyst Danny Citrinowicz, a researcher at the Israel-based Institute for National Security Studies, said the regime would not capitulate. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian with the memorandum of understanding signed with US in June. Iranian Presidency Office via AP “In the choice between submission and escalation, Iran will choose escalation,” he wrote on X. “One can debate its scope, timing, and the tools it will employ, but the expectation that American pressure will bring Tehran to raise the white flag is incompatible with the way the Iranian regime perceives itself and its survival.” Last week, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent flagged unprecedented sanctions against Iran in an attempt to apply even more economic pressure on the weakened regime. He has not yet announced further measures.



Related Article Updated

Trump diplomacy Trump praises North Korean dictator Kim Jong-un, slashes military drills with Seoul Aaron David Miller, a Middle East analyst who was formerly a long-time State Department negotiator, said it could include secondary sanctions that cut off any country or bank doing business with Iran from the US financial system, or directly targeting Chinese purchases of Iranian oil. “That’s a severe sanction,” he said. “It would involve everybody, including Australia.” But Miller said he did not believe it would make much difference. “I don’t think any of these things will in a reasonable period of time change Iran’s calculation on the core issues.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Six simple exercises physios wish everyone would do for lifelong strength
World.content:
LifestyleHealth & wellnessFitness Six simple exercises physios wish everyone would do for lifelong strength Danielle Friedman August 18, 2026 — 5:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In many cases, aches and pains can be a reflection of your daily routines. Habits like sitting at a desk all day, looking down at your phone or even straining to pick your socks up off the floor can lead to a body that feels creaky, tight and sore. Making time to practise good movement habits can keep you feeling limber and strong. Physical therapists say they repeatedly recommend these six exercises to patients. Getty Images Physical therapists know this all too well. “People come in with the same problems over and over again,” said Theresa Marko, a physical therapist in New York City.



She often found herself recommending the same exercises as solutions, she said — exercises that, for example, “counteract, you know, going to see The Odyssey for three hours”. Related Article Wellbeing Joyspan could be the secret to ageing happily. Here’s what to know We asked physical therapists to share the exercises they wish everyone incorporated into their fitness routines. Here are six that came up again and again. Standing on one leg Good balance is important for both fitness and everyday life, but it deteriorates with age, unless you’re “really deliberate about practising it”, says Conor Nordengren, a physical therapist in Wellesley, Massachusetts.



One of the simplest ways to do this is by regularly standing on one leg, experts say. This simple exercise could “strengthen all the muscles in your foot, your ankle, your knee, your thigh”, Marko said. It also helps to build stability — not only in your legs, but also in your hips, pelvis and lower back. “I stand on one leg in the kitchen, waiting for coffee, waiting for the elevator,” she added. If standing on one leg is challenging for you, lightly rest your hand on a chair, a wall or a counter top until you feel stable enough to let go. If the exercise feels easy, close your eyes. Stand on each leg for at least 30 seconds every day. Hip hinges



The ability to properly bend forward, or hinge, at the hips is useful both for daily tasks, like picking things up off the floor, and for exercises like deadlifts and kettlebell swings. But many people struggle with hip hinges, says Dhara Shah, a physical therapist at Emory Healthcare. It’s common to round your back and lock your knees when you bend over, which puts pressure on your spine and can lead to pain or injury. Regularly practising hip hinges can also strengthen your glutes and hamstrings. To do a hip hinge, send your hips backward while bringing your chest forward. Keep your back straight, your shoulders pulled slightly back, your abdominal muscles pulled towards your belly button and your knees softly bent. Practise this movement daily, doing two sets of 15 hinges.



Sit-to-stands Related Article Wellbeing Does the body keep the score? Our brains and bodies are more linked than we knew The act of sitting down and then standing back up may seem simple, but with age, it can become increasingly difficult without proper strength and stability. Making time to practise “sit-to-stand” exercises will pay off by strengthening your quads, glutes, hamstrings, calves and core muscles, and improve your ability to do lunges and squats, the experts say. To do a sit-to-stand, lower yourself into a chair and stand back up in a slow, controlled way. If this feels challenging, practise it several times a day until it feels easier. If it already feels easy, lower your body even more slowly and just barely tap your butt to the seat before slowly standing up again. The lower the surface, the more challenging it will be. “That control piece makes it a little harder,” Shah said.



Do two sets of 20 repetitions several times a week. For more of a challenge, do it while holding weights or a kettlebell. If struggling initially, you can also try a dead-bug with an exercise ball for added stability. Getty Images Dead bugs with diaphragmatic breathing Many people feel the effects of sitting for long periods in their neck, shoulders or back, but the problem often begins in their innermost core muscles, says Carrie Pagliano, a physical therapist in Virginia. “With a lot of these issues, people are just missing fundamental strength,” she said. When your core is weak, your neck and shoulders often compensate to keep you upright. Physical therapists recommend doing the dead bug exercise while practising diaphragmatic breathing to build core strength at the deepest level.



To do a dead bug, lie on your back and raise your legs at a 90-degree angle, then raise your arms straight towards the ceiling. With your spine pressed into the floor, slowly straighten and lower your left leg while also lowering your right arm, until both are fully extended. Return to the starting position, then repeat with the opposite sides. While extending, slowly exhale through your mouth to contract your deep core. While returning to the starting position, inhale and feel your belly expand. Do two sets of eight exercises a few times a week. This breath work helps “stabilise your core from the inside out”, says Alicia Ferriere, a physical therapist in New Jersey. Together with the dead bugs, it can help support your spine and relieve aches in your neck and shoulders. Wall push-ups Push-ups allow you to practise lifting your body weight, which is essential for staying independent as you age and getting up if you fall, Nordengren says. They primarily strengthen the chest, shoulders, arms and core.



Related Article Fitness How three oncologists exercise – and why Unless you’ve regularly been doing push-ups from the ground, experts recommended doing them with your hands on a stable, raised surface such as a wall or a counter top. As you build strength, you can gradually lower the surface until you reach the ground. “I’ll very rarely have people do them from the floor right away,” Nordengren said, especially since “a lot of people struggle with the technique”. Start in a plank position, with your back flat and your feet pressed into the floor. Next, engage your core and slightly tuck your tailbone underneath you to prevent your back from arching. Bend your elbows into a 45-degree angle, while slowly lowering your chest, then push yourself back up. Imagine that you are pushing the floor away, Nordengren says, and be sure to reach your arms long at the top. Do two sets of 10 reps twice a week. Cat-cows



To counter the effects of sitting or standing for long periods of time, many physical therapists recommended the cat-cow stretch, in which you alternate between arching and curving your back while on all fours. Take a few deep breaths in each position to feel a deeper stretch. This classic stretch can help relieve stiffness in your spine, shoulders and neck and improve your mobility. Editor's pick Exclusive

Victoria residential property Real estate agent sacked over allegations he secretly sold properties to his partner When you’re in an all-fours position, you can limber up other body parts, too, Ferriere says. Try reaching forward with each arm or stretching each leg out behind you and doing a few hip circles. Ultimately, these exercises are “giving you a little extra buffer to live your life”, Nordengren says, so your body is strong, steady and prepared for the unexpected. World.title: Ange Postecoglou has moved to Saudi Arabia. How should we feel about that?
World.content:
Analysis SportSoccerSaudi Arabia Ange Postecoglou has moved to Saudi Arabia. How should we feel about that? Vince Rugari August 18, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ange Postecoglou has made a career out of taking the road less travelled; of eschewing the easy, obvious thing in favour of the biggest available challenge. Not for the first time, he’s outdone himself. Ange Postecoglou on the job during Al-Nassr’s Saudi Pro League game against Al Fateh. Getty Images It’s been just over a year since he was unceremoniously dumped by Tottenham Hotspur after delivering the club’s first trophy in 17 years, and just under a year since his brutal sacking by Nottingham Forest after 39 disastrous days in charge. Popular wisdom was that, to overcome the perception that he was damaged managerial goods, Postecoglou, now 60, would have to leave the Premier League and rebuild his reputation elsewhere: perhaps a big club in Germany or the Netherlands, where he could re-establish his credibility and set up a swift return to England. But nobody thought he would go this far off Broadway.



Postecoglou’s next chapter began over the weekend, without any of the fanfare that came with the last couple. You may not have even known it happened: in the early hours of Sunday morning (AEST), Al-Nassr opened the new Saudi Professional League (SPL) season with a 3-0 win over Al-Fateh. Loading Cristiano Ronaldo, 41, who increasingly resembles a wax likeness of Cristiano Ronaldo, sported a notable new haircut as he watched on from the stands, not yet ready to play after his recent wedding, having told Vogue (as you do) that this would “probably” be his final season. It will revolve around his pursuit of the 24 more goals he needs to become the first player in history to score 1000 career goals in official competitions. Postecoglou could be the coach who gets him there. He welcomed Ronaldo to his first team meeting of the season by calling him “Cris” and congratulating him on his nuptials. He is now attached to the perpetual CR7 content machine. This is his new world. Postecoglou’s two-year contract with the reigning Saudi champions reportedly gives him a salary of almost $20 million per year. Pretty good work, if you can get it; the road less travelled, in this instance, is also paved with riyals. View post on X



Is this really where we envisaged him taking his managerial talents? And where are we, exactly: does this mark the beginning of the end of the great Angeball odyssey, or is this just a brief interlude before his triumphant resurgence at the highest level? At this point, we should take a deep breath. Australians, in particular, should be very careful about turning their noses up at Postecoglou’s decision to work in Saudi Arabia, lest we engage in exactly the same sort of Eurocentric snobbery that Ange has always railed against. View post on X You can’t, on one hand, accuse English pundits of underestimating Postecoglou’s previous achievements in Australia, Japan and Scotland because of where they took place, and then on the other hand dismiss Saudi Arabia as some sort of barren footballing wasteland. It’s not: Saudi Arabia was a legitimate football country before the Public Investment Fund decided to start spending big a few years ago, and it still is.



The cynical view is he’s only gone there for the cash, which doesn’t quite square with the relentlessly ambitious Postecoglou we know. The generous view is that he has taken arguably the most high-profile job in club football outside of Europe, and is now in charge of a squad with more quality than many top clubs in Europe: beyond Ronaldo, there’s Samu Costa, Sadio Mane, Joao Felix, Inigo Martinez and Kingsley Coman, plus a host of tidy Saudi internationals. This is entirely consistent with Postecoglou’s general worldview: that worthy football exists beyond the borders of Europe, and that coaches should go wherever they feel they can make the biggest impact. Ange Postecoglou is pictured during an Al-Nassr training session. Instagram Cristiano Ronaldo won his first Saudi title with Al-Nassr last season. Getty Images It is, though, possible to be respectful of Saudi football and also acknowledge the undeniable truth that, for Postecoglou enthusiasts, watching the Riyadh derby just isn’t going to hit the same as a North London derby, or an Old Firm clash. Nothing against the Saudi Pro League; that’s just how it is.



But it’s his career, not ours; he has more than earned the right to do whatever he wants, and owes an explanation to nobody. In pure football terms, this is a cracking challenge. Al-Nassr are the reigning champions of Saudi Arabia; this is the first time Postecoglou, who normally specialises in fixer-uppers, has taken charge of a team defending a league title. That’s new. They’ve never won the AFC Champions League, so there’s his big target to aim for, along with winning the league again. He’s also got to adapt his brand of football to new conditions, in a place where it’s never not hot. He has to somehow manage the gigantic ego of a player who is within sight of an unprecedented individual milestone, and who famously doesn’t press – which would be a lot easier to deal with if this player didn’t run the entire show at Al-Nassr. And he’ll do all this in the knowledge that whatever success he has will be downplayed in Europe, because it’s only Saudi Arabia, and his failures will be magnified, because it’s Saudi Arabia. This is not a pragmatic career choice. Ange Postecoglou. Getty Images There are, of course, some uncomfortable ethical considerations. Any player or coach who goes to Saudi Arabia is participating in that country’s efforts to build its public image in a certain way. Does that make this sportswashing? Is every coaching appointment in Saudi really an elaborate act of propaganda? Does sportswashing even actually work if human rights issues are brought up every time someone signs for a Saudi club? Should Postecoglou not get the Tim Cahill treatment, then? Is Socceroo Aziz Behich also guilty, having spent six months on loan at Al-Nassr in 2024? Do we consider Kevin Muscat as doing the bidding of the Chinese government because the club he coaches is owned by a state-owned company?



Or is there another way to view this: that the Saudi football “project” is also a case of a football-mad country which happens to have the means to invest at a staggering scale into the thing that it loves? Are they not engaging in exactly the kind of “nationalistic approach” Postecoglou once said was required to climb the ladder in world football, having given up hope it would ever happen in Australia? Or is any investment from the Saudi government inherently tainted? Where is the line? You can wrestle with these questions at your leisure, but there are no especially satisfying answers. Related Article Premier League Socceroos teenager’s $33m deal sets stage for dream Premier League debut Success there may not win over Postecoglou’s biggest critics, but it can be a road back to the top. We have proof: Matthias Jassle, who has replaced Eddie Howe as Newcastle United manager, went straight to the Premier League from Al-Ahli. After also being sacked by Spurs, Nuno Espirito Santo spent a year at Al-Ittihad before returning to England with Nottingham Forest – so it can be done. And if he can get Ronaldo swooning in public about how good a coach he is, all sorts of doors could open for Postecoglou one day. Who knows? For him, the road less travelled is often bumpy, but it rarely leads to a dead end. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport are sent every Monday.

World.title: Transport Minister Chris Bishop defends commissioning another Auckland harbour crossing report
World.content:
Government looks into second harbour bridge Morning Report Download MP3 6m

The Transport Minister is defending commissioning another report on a second harbour crossing in Auckland.

More than $106 million has been spent on consultants and contractors to date, but there is still no plan for what should be built and how.

On Monday, Chris Bishop announced plans for a detailed business case due next year.

He told Morning Report on Tuesday that previous reports have answered the 'why,' and now it needs to answer the 'how.'

"This will be multiple billions of dollars, one of the biggest projects we've ever built in New Zealand, and it's really important we get it right. I think everyone would agree on that," Bishop said.

"So, all the expert advice on this from when you do a mega project from the Infrastructure Commission and from others is that you need to follow a proper, thorough process, and that's what we're doing.

"We're going to do a detailed business case. That will take a bit of time, but that will give Cabinet, whoever is in the Cabinet, whether it's us or another set of parties, that will give the Cabinet good decisions on how to make an informed decision, and that's what we're all about."

Bishop said the NTZA had done two investment cases into a bridge next to the existing one and also into a tunnel.

He said it looked at what's preferable to be built from engineering, network connectivity, and transport point of views.

Bishop said if he had announced then they were building a tunnel, he'd be asked to explain how.

"You would say, 'well, how are you going to pay for it?' And then you'd say, 'how much is it going to cost?' And then you'd say, 'when's it going to start?' And then you'd say, 'how's it going to be delivered?'

"We need to answer all of those questions because they're completely legitimate questions that the government has, and we need to do that work, and that's what we're going to do," he said.

"I think we're taking a very thorough, evidence-led approach to this."

He said another report did "absolutely" not mean they were back at square one.

"People who are framing it like that are, frankly, being a bit misleading and a bit mischievous," he said.

"There's been a huge amount of work done over the last two years or so, and, frankly, over the last four years, this whole process actually started with an indicative business case kicked off by the previous government."

Bishop said in 2027, Cabinet would be in a position to decide on what to build and how to pay for it.

"Once we have that information in a package, there'll be a range of options we look at, we'll be able to make an informed decision," he said.

"My hope would be that whoever is in government does it on a cross-party basis, because this will span multiple parliaments and multiple governments, and we need to get it right.

World.title: Disputes Tribunal orders Kmart to pay Christchurch couple over contaminated sand
World.content:
RNZ national

Kmart has been ordered to pay thousands to a Christchurch couple whose toddlers played with asbestos-contaminated sand.

Last year, the retail giant was part of a nationwide recall of coloured play sand products, after they tested positive for tremolite - a form of asbestos associated with higher cancer risks at low exposure levels.

Elle Chrisp and David Dingwall took Kmart to the Disputes Tribunal, seeking re-imbursement for costs associated with asbestos contamination and future medical monitoring.

The Christchurch pair claimed $60,000 in total.

In a recent decision, the tribunal ordered Kmart to pay the family $15,185.42 to cover costs associated with asbestos testing and remediation.

It found the play sand purchased was unsafe, not fit for purpose and not of acceptable quality under the Consumer Guarantees Act.

Elle Chrisp says the family is very happy with the outcome of the tribunal's case. Supplied / Screenshot

Kmart to pay Christchurch couple $15k to cover asbestos costs Morning Report Download MP3 5m

Elle Chrisp said the family had bought 4kg of the sand and it was in their backyard where their three-year-old twins played with it.

But she said from time to time the sand would end up inside the house as well as it came in on their shoes and clothes.

"We had our sand independently tested, it came back with tremolite asbestos, we were phoned and the advice we were given was to evacuate our home immediately taking just the clothes on our back, nothing else, leaving everything behind."

That was because further environmental testing was needed to find out exactly where the asbestos contamination was, she said.

Fortunately the testing showed the contamination was limited to backyard area, she said.

The family incurred a number of costs in this process, she said, including lab testing, having to dispose of a lot of items such as toys that were stored outside and remediation to make the outdoor area safe.

The family was also not able to use the outdoor area for 67 days until it was remediated, she said.

Chrisp said they took the case to the tribunal because the product was unsafe and that was what they wanted to establish.

"We weren't seeing that communicated anywhere, parents were told that they were overreacting, it was low risk, it was never low risk, it was never safe and that was what the decision came to."

She said she was pleased that Kmart had to attend the tribunal hearing.

"Because we did not have any engagement from them at all prior to going to the tribunal and that's why we were so thankful the disputes tribunal process existed because it put us on an even footing with a huge company who otherwise could have ignored us."

The tribunal process which doesn't use lawyers was great because it was built for ordinary people to be able to get a fair outcome, she said.

Chrisp said they were very happy with the outcome of their tribunal case.

"Ultimately for us it was wanting a public ruling that this is enforceable."

Referee Cynthia Hawes said the sand should not have been offered for sale.

"I do not think that any reasonable parent, acquainted with the fact that the moulding sand contained asbestos, and regardless of the quantity or proportion in the sand, would purchase it for his or her child to play with."

The claim for medical expenses was not allowed.

A Kmart spokesperson said the product recall was part of a broader industry issue.

"When the matter became known to us, we acted quickly by removing affected products from sale, issuing recall notices, and supporting customers with refunds and guidance on safely disposing of the products based on regulatory advice."

They said the company was reviewing the tribunal's decision.

"We remain focused on supporting our customers on this matter while being guided by evidence, expert advice and the relevant regulators."

Consumer NZ head of research and advocacy Gemma Rasmussen said Chrisp and Dingwall spent months gathering evidence, and forked out thousands of dollars to take Kmart to the Disputes Tribunal.

She said the ruling found "firmly in the family's favour".

"It is completely reasonable for them to undertake everything that they did from testing to vacating their home, and Kmart should have to pay for that."

Rasmussen said the ruling did not set a precedent, but it sent a clear message and she hoped other families were encouraged to make claims.

However, she said the order ultimately showed the difficulty in getting redress following a product safety failure.

She said current laws were too reactive and regulatory reform was needed.

"Our market place has dramatically changed from major retailers like Kmart selling thousands of goods to people shopping on platforms like Temu and Ali Express, and we really need the government to take this a little more seriously."

World.title: Emergency crews tackle house fires, crashes overnight
World.content:
Emergency services had a busy night and early morning responding to several fires and crashes.

In Māngere, emergency crews responded to a single vehicle crash at 3.22am on Tuesday where one person suffered moderate injuries and was taken to Middlemore Hospital.

Fire and Emergency tackled a house fire in Maketu in the Western Bay of Plenty after a mattress caught fire, about 4am.

In the South Island, a fire in a back yard close to houses caused two sheds to burn in South New Brighton in Christchurch.

Fire investigators will check the cause later on Tuesday. FENZ said the fire was put out with no damage to nearby houses.

In Woolston, a house fire was extinguished about 3am.

World.title: Port union says it was left in the dark over $800 million Lyttelton upgrade
World.content:
Lyttelton reveals ambitious port project Morning Report Download MP3 3m

The company behind the South Island's biggest port is being accused of keeping workers "out of the loop" on its $800 million upgrade plans by one of its unions.

This is despite an assertion by its chief executive that it briefed its entire workforce several months ago on a proposal, described as "the most ambitious port project in a generation".

Lyttelton Port Company (LPC) will spend $821m expanding its container terminal and building a new 388-metre deepwater wharf at Te Awaparahi Bay.

The expansion plans include a five-hectare container terminal, four new ship-to-shore cranes and semi-automated gantry yard cranes, with the work expected due to be completed by 2031.

The company said in an announcement on Monday the project would help meet growing demand from South Island exporters and accommodate bigger ships.

LPC chief executive Graeme Sumner said 92 percent ships being built today could not fit into Lyttelton Harbour.

"The reality is that if we didn't do this, those larger container ships would be unable to arrive here," he said.

"We are running out of land as well in order to be able to handle the number of containers that are coming through."

Mark Wilson of the Rail and Maritime Transport Union says they had called for better engagement over the project to no avail. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

The announcement also follows a recent decision by Christchurch City Council's investment arm and LPC owners Christchurch City Holdings' Limited (CCHL) to reject an unsolicited proposal by global port operator DP World and three Canterbury rūnanga to lease the port's operations.

Sumner told reporters at Monday's announcement it would need to employ an additional 50-100 people during development, although long-term, automation would ensure greater output at the port with similar staffing levels seen at present.

When asked if the unions had been briefed on the plans beforehand, Sumner said the company made a presentation to all staff about eight or nine months ago.

"The joke I suppose amongst the staff is maybe you could talk about it a little bit less. It is something that we see as being strategically absolutely vital," he said.

"So we've taken our staff along with us the whole way."

The Rail and Maritime Transport Union's (RMTU) Lyttelton branch secretary Mark Wilson rebuffed this suggestion, arguing they had called for better engagement over the project to no avail.

"We certainly haven't been brought along the whole way," he said.

"We have concerns around the expansion of the port will mean for our members. There's certainly a component of automation that could be implemented in his new wharf."

An artist impression of the Lyttelton Port expansion at Te Awaparahi Bay. Supplied / Lyttelton Port Company

The union would have liked to be more involved with the business case to understand the reasons for needing to do the upgrade, he said.

A lack of transparency had extended to the community and the mana whenua who had also "really been left out of the loop," he said.

"We need a management structure that actually treats the workers, mana whenua and the community as strategic partners in the operation of the port.

"We have no relationship at the present time and it's quite unfortunate and quite disconcerting."

The project would be funded mostly through additional borrowing alongside an equity contribution from CCHL.

LPC recorded a net debt of about $202m at the close of the 2025 financial year, which would mean higher costs for port users.

"We will be talking about that later in the year and releasing a price pathway going forward so people can see how it's going to be funded," Sumner said.

"They will be reasonable. But at the end of the day, it's a substantial lick of infrastructure that needs to be funded and it will have to be supported."

World.title: Aged-care report calls for major systemic reform - but at what cost?
World.content:
Report calls for urgent action over aged care system Morning Report Download MP3 4m

Representatives from the aged-care sector are welcoming a mammoth report calling for major systemic reform, with one saying everyone agrees that doing nothing but pumping more money into it wasn't going to work.

Minister for Seniors Casey Costello says "there's no denying there's a significant price tag attached" to the report's recommendations.

Aged Care Association head Tracey Martin says she's pleased to see a shift from conversations about the problem to having some about solutions.

"The system itself is fragmented and disconnected, and it's not just money that is sometimes falling through those cracks, it's human beings."

Recommended overhaul of aged care would see people paying more Checkpoint Download MP3 9m

Aged Care Commissioner Erin James also welcomed the report, but said her key focus was ensuring the reforms were grounded in improving quality of care and upholding the rights of older people.

The Ministerial Advisory Group on Aged Care in New Zealand, chaired by former Labour health minister David Cunliffe, has made 40 recommendations, including the government committing to "significant price uplifts" and lowering the threshold at which people with assets must pay more towards their care.

The report stated current settings could not meet future demand "safely, equitably or sustainably, without major deliberate system change", and the cheapest option would be to reform the system.

Martin told RNZ the group was right to suggest a more integrated system.

"Aged care is healthcare," she said. "We're part of a continuum of care, so we need to be working more closely together."

Urgent reform needed for our ailing aged care system Morning Report Download MP3 7m

She said there were a lot of "moving parts" in their recommendations, but where people were willing, "anything's achievable".

Some of the suggestions - including differentiated room prices - were new to her and she'd need to make her way through them.

"A higher amount being paid on a daily basis for a brand new room compared to a new room compared to an old room," she explained.

"I really need to get my head around that, because on first blush, I'm worried that it will negatively impact small owner operators, charities, and not-for-profits, because they have the oldest stock."

Martin wasn't surprised at the overall costs and said the reality was this group of New Zealanders who had recently been "the bulk of the taxpaying public" were getting older.

"This was always going to cost more money", but she suggested ensuring every dollar spent was done so efficiently and effectively.

There would also need to be a conversation about intergenerational wealth, and "those who have money paying for their living expenses and their accommodation expenses", Martin said.

She encouraged the government to take time to digest the report - "let's not do anything rash".

In the next few months, she hoped to meet with sector representatives to look at where they agreed, and also the "niggly bits" that needed to be discussed and "make sure there's no unintended consequences".

Aged Care Association head Tracey Martin is pleased to see the conversations shift to solutions. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Aged Care Commissioner Erin James told RNZ the current aged-care system was under significant strain and wanted quality of care to remain the focus of any future system.

She acknowledged urgency was needed to consider how care was delivered to a "rapidly ageing population", but the critical question was whether it would make care for older people better and safer.

James supported increasing access to home-based care, which was "highly desirable" for many older people. She said it also introduced increased risk of harm.

Previously, concerns had been raised about the lack of regulatory levers in respect of home care, James said, which was provided by a "largely unregulated workforce in a person's home".

She said accessibility of care, wherever it was provided, was a critical component of "safe, rights-based, person-centered care".

"My role as the aged-care commissioner is to ensure that older people's rights remain embedded in in the design of any future system."

James was also pleased the advisory group engaged with the issue of workforce.

"A comprehensive strategy about future workforce is a critical part of of any discussion about changes" and it wasn't just capacity, but capability too.

Costello was asked about the report on Checkpoint on Monday, acknowledging the "significant price tag" that came with it.

Asked about the cost to provide the funding uplifts recommended by the group, she was reluctant to be drawn on any specifics, until the Ministry of Health considered the report and reported back with its advice.

"There is significant investment needed, but if we don't invest in the system, everyone ends up in hospital or we end up with really poor health outcomes, further burdening the health system."

She said improving the health of older New Zealanders and keeping them well as long as possible would "produce a return on investment".

Asked about increasing the amount paid by individuals for their care, Costello said the burden of this system to future generations had been discussed repeatedly.

She said there needed to be a "really honest conversation" about the future of aged care. Costello said it was important to put some perspective around whether that was paid for by taxing more New Zealanders or a discussion of "where does that cost recovery come from".

She agreed that healthcare should be delivered by the state, but suggested other components could be considered to make the system more sustainable.

World.title: OFC supports withdrawal of FIFA Forward Enterprise proposal
World.content:
Members of the Oceania Football Confederation (OFC) have stated their support for the withdrawal of the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal initiated by FIFA president Gianni Infantino.

Infantino's proposal, which created a firestorm regarding good governance and transparency within football's world governing body, sought to sell 21 percent of FIFA's commercial rights for its flagship competitions like the World Cup to private investors, to raise about US$4.2 billion (NZ$7.b).

It was strongly opposed by the European (UEFA), South American (CONMEBOL), and North and Central American (CONCACAF) confederations.

The OFC stated its position on the proposal following the conclusion of an OFC Executive Committee meeting in Auckland on 12 August.

"OFC recognises the progress achieved over the last decade in advancing football development in Oceania under FIFA's leadership and encourages FIFA to use the review as an opportunity to identify and implement any changes that may be necessary," the OFC said in a statement.

"Good governance, transparency and respect for established institutional processes are fundamental to the effective administration and sustainable development of football. These principles are essential at every level of the game and should be upheld consistently by all football stakeholders."

The OFC said development of football remained its priority.

"The Confederation will continue to support initiatives that strengthen the game and create meaningful, sustainable opportunities for football development across Oceania and globally."

Meanwhile, OFC member New Zealand has indicated it has withdrawn their support for Infantino, who is seeking re-election for the top FIFA job in 2027.

New Zealand Football (NZF) said in a statement it was also seeking an independent review of the steps undertaken to develop the FFE scheme.

"After careful consideration, NZF has formed the view that decisions and actions within FIFA have contributed to a breakdown in trust and increased division within international football, and that an independent review is required to restore confidence and trust."

World.title: Why this future star has 'goosebumps' over triathlon's future
World.content:
The future of triathlon in Australia is looking very bright — particularly on the Gold Coast.

And 19-year-old rising star Aspen Anderson is hoping to play a big part in that future.

Last week, AusTriathlon formally opened its new high performance hub at the Miami Aquatic Centre, a home for the sport's best athletes and coaches, as well as the future, developing talent through the Ascent Academy.

It's a move that positions the Gold Coast right at the heart of the multi-sport universe leading into the 2032 Olympics.

The proposed location of the triathlon events at those Brisbane Games is the Gold Coast, and that is something that has Australia's top athletes very excited.

Aspen Anderson says knowing that a friendly, smiling face will be there at the new high performance hub was motivating. (Getty Images: Commonwealth Sport/Kevin C. Cox)

"I think having a home, for a home Olympics is really special," Anderson told ABC Sport on the Gold Coast.

"Sometimes it [training] is a bit of a slog when you have to put the headphones in and you're just trying to get it done.

"But knowing that there's always someone that can go for a ride with you, yeah, it definitely helps.

"It's like a strength in numbers kind of thing. Some days when you're not feeling great, they're always there to lift you up and someone's always got a smile on their face, and on your hard days, they might be having a great day, and vice versa, when you're having a good day, you can help a friend out too.

"This hub is definitely a great step forward, it's been hard in previous years where you're kind of just floating between venues. Now, having this locked in is really exciting."

Aspen Anderson has an athletics background and competed in the Women's U20s race during the 2023 World Cross Country Championships. (Getty Images: World Athletics/Cameron Spencer)

Reigning World Champion Matt Hauser agreed, saying the hub was a huge step forward for the athletes.

"For sure I wouldn't be able to do this sport if I was just training solo, seven days a week across the three sports," Hauser told ABC Sport.

"I think it's a really important dynamic that you also get that racing exposure in training and you're able to push each other and go to another level than you would have previously without someone there pushing you.

"Having that culture piece, having everyone on the same path and knowing that when you're putting the hard yards in, when your heart rate's maxing out, when you've got a sore body at the end of the week, everyone's in the same position and they're motivated to get to the same place as you are is, I think, really important, especially when we move towards Brisbane 2032.

"Everyone wants success for the country … so to be on that journey together and have that centralised program here in Miami now is, I think, really powerful."

Anderson noted that Hauser has "led the way" in bringing Australia back to the top step of world triathlon.

The 28-year-old claimed the world title on home soil in Wollongong last year, becoming the first Australian since Emma Moffatt in 2010.

It put Australia back on top of the triathlon world after a lengthy absence, and with the global hiring of new high performance coaches like British former European champion Non Stanford-Royle and Germany's former world champion Daniel Unger, hopes are that Hauser's success will be just the latest in a long line of triumphs.

Anderson herself is clearly on the right pathway to emulating some of the greats of the past.

Aspen Anderson won two gold medals at the 2023 Youth Commonwealth Games in Trinidad and Tobago. (Getty Images: Commonwealth Sport/Kevin C. Cox)

A double gold medallist from the Youth Commonwealth Games in Trinidad and Tobago in 2023, the Victoria-born teenager made her World Triathlon Championship Series debut earlier this season.

At the event in Quiberon, France, in June, Anderson led off Australia's mixed team relay to a sensational fourth place finish.

"I was really fortunate to get to experience the mixed team relay," Anderson said.

"I loved it. It was so fun, it's short enough that you're still with all the best of the best, like I'm lining up next to [Luxemburg's European champion] Jeanne Lehair and [French mixed team relay world championship gold medallist] Emma Lombardi, and I'm like 'wow, these are people that are performing on the biggest stages and here I am, just hey guys'.

"I had a bit of a fangirl moment but it was a great experience."

Aspen Anderson first took up triathlons in high school. (Getty Images: Commonwealth Sport/Kevin C. Cox)

Fresh from that fourth place, a couple of weeks later Anderson made her full individual World Championship Series debut in Hamburg, finishing 38th as the second-youngest of all the competitors in the race.

"I wasn't even planning to do World Series races this year, that was not even really on the cards, and then I think I just had a little bit too much momentum and they were like, 'oh, let's just go for it,'" Anderson said.

"Hamburg was another extreme … the crowds and everything, it was insane.

"It was definitely a big step up but it wasn't as big as everyone made it seem, I think maybe I over-hyped it a little bit in my head.

"But now I know what it's like and I know what to expect for next time. Every race is different though, so you never know what to expect."

Anderson will race in Weihai, China, at the end of the month, and has also been named to the Australian under 23 squad for the 2026 World Triathlon Championship Finals in Pontevedra, Spain, later this year.

This too came somewhat as a surprise for a teenager well and truly on the fast-track to the top.

It's made the prospect of a home Olympics all the more tantalising.

Anderson cites Cassandre Beaugrand's victory in Paris as being a huge inspiration. (Getty Images: Lars Baron)

"It's always something in the back of your mind," Anderson said.

"I'm someone that's really realistic, so I don't want to get ahead of myself, I'm kind of taking it race by race or day by day and really enjoying the process of doing that.

"But yeah, there's some days where you just get goosebumps thinking about it, just, wow there's an Olympics literally out the front door; there's talks of it being in Tallebudgera or Currumbin, and if it's in Currumbin that's literally where I live, so that would be something you could write in a fairytale ending.

"Cassie [Beaugrand, Paris 2024 Olympic champion] and what she did at her home Olympics, I think it's … yeah it literally is giving me goosebumps now thinking about it.

"Having the support of a home base going for something like 2032 is insane — and LA would be a lovely stepping stone for that, it would be lovely just to dip the toes in the water and still be competitive and then I think, yeah, it would be lovely to have a fairytale ending in Brisbane."

World.title: Options slim for new Australia Test cricket batters
World.content:
Australia's nine wicket defeat at the hands of Bangladesh have thrown up yet more questions about the state of Australian batting.

Twin failures by opener Jake Weatherald and number three Marnus Labuschagne have only increased the pressure on both batters.

Moreover, the repeated failures of the battling line-up, with the exception of Steve Smith and Cam Green in Darwin, have continued a pattern which was partially masked by last season's Ashes success.

Shock loss to Bangladesh reveals Aussie cracks On paper, Australia's full-strength team should have wiped the floor with Bangladesh. But a lack of application to their Test match craft has left Australia vulnerable to teams that are driven to succeed in the longest format.

Labuschagne hasn't scored a century since July 2023 — 22 Tests ago — during which time he's averaged just 25.23.

Jake Weatherald is averaging 20.36 in his six Tests since the beginning of the Ashes last summer, with just one score above 50.

The question is, does Australia make changes now ahead of the second Test starting in Mackay on Saturday?

Skipper, Pat Cummins, openly mused on the subject in his post-Test press conference on Sunday.

"I think that's the question over the next couple days," Cummins said.

"We'll sit down and have a think; the selectors will have a think.

"Is there something there that's going to take us forward, or is it something starting to become a trend that we think needs to be changed?

"So, it's trying to work out, do you need to intervene now, or do you let it play out and think [the current group] is the way forward?"

Pat Cummins is searching for answers after the disaster in Darwin. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Australia's head coach, Andrew McDonald, said the disastrous display in Darwin was clearly not good enough.

"Call it a trend, call it what you will, we believe our players are better than what they're putting out there at the moment," he said.

"And that falls on us as coaches as well; our job is to get the best out of playing group.

"I think if you go back to the original squad [of 13] that was picked, it was quite skinny.

"I think Bailes, George [head selector, George Bailey] left it very open as to you know, we could add depending on what we saw going through."

The obvious problem is that we are in the middle of winter season and most batsmen last played first-class cricket around five months ago.

It means the selectors don't have recent form to go off and so any decision about bringing in a player from outside the squad of 13 is going to rely on hunch as much as hard facts.

If it's the current group, the only other batter available in the squad is Josh Inglis, who scored 100 on debut against Sri Lanka in January 2025, but was dropped after his fifth Test during last summer's Ashes series.

Josh Inglis has had some time in the Test team, with varied success. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Inglis last represented Australia in the white ball format playing One-Day Internationals and T20 matches on the tour to Bangladesh in June.

The 31-year-old wicketkeeper-batter played five matches in this year's IPL for the Lucknow Super Giants, scoring 266 runs at an average of 53.2 and a strike rate of 186.

Inglis opens for Australia in the short forms of the game but hasn't batted higher than four in Test cricket and bats in the middle order for Western Australia in the Sheffield Shield.

Is he the long sought-after answer to open for Australia? His record and usual batting position suggests not.

If not Inglis, then the selectors will have to look outside the current squad where pundits are putting forth names including Matthew Renshaw, Sam Harper, Nathan McSweeney, Cooper Connolly, Campbell Kellaway, Sam Konstas and Kurtis Patterson.

Queenslander Renshaw was part of the wider squad that trained in Brisbane before the Sri Lanka series and is a possibility to replace Weatherald as opener.

Matthew Renshaw has played successfully as an opener for Australia. (Getty: Robert Cianflone)

He scored 499 runs in six matches at 49.9 in last year's Sheffield Shield, with three centuries and a 50.

While those numbers don't scream "pick me", they are actually a stand out in what was a disappointing summer for Australia's first-class batters: his average was second only to Jack Edwards's 51.75 for batters who scored more than 300 runs.

Former Test opener and Queenslander, Matthew Hayden is a fan of the 31-year-old.

"I want to see Matt Renshaw and I've been saying this for at least 12 months. I think he is match fit," he told Channel 7.

"I think the selectors knew what he was, now I want to see what he actually is."

Renshaw was also a member of the Australian side that played limited overs matches against Bangladesh in June.

He played the last of his 14 Tests against India in Delhi more than three years ago when he came in as a concussion sub for David Warmer and scored just 2.

Victoria's keeper/batter Sam Harper scored the second most Shield runs last year behind his teammate and former Test player, Peter Handscomb.

Sam Harper has batted well for Victoria, but can he step up to Test cricket? (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Harper scored 677 runs at an average 35.63 in his 11 matches which included Victoria's loss to South Australia in the Sheffield Shield final played at the end of March.

Of late, 29-year-old Harper has been part of the Galle Gallants title winning side in Sri Lanka's T20 competition, the Lanka Premier League.

He was the second highest scoring batter in the competition with 425 runs at an average of 38.63 and a strike rate of 163.46.

The question around Harper, who has proven himself a successful T20 batter over the years, is whether he could translate last year's Shield runs to the Test arena, and possibly even step up a level?

One player who has been playing regular first-class cricket is the former Test opener, Nathan McSweeney.

Nathan McSweeney was tried, briefly, at the top of the order. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

McSweeney was drafted into the Test side two years ago to replace the retired David Warner partnering Usman Khawaja at the top of the order.

He lasted just three Tests, where he made 72 runs at an average of 14.4.

More recently he's been playing for Northamptonshire in England's One-Day Cup and County Championship Division Two.

His record in eight first-class matches for Northants has been solid, scoring 589 runs — placing him fifth on the run-scoring charts — at an average of 49.08.

Batting at number three, he captained South Australia to last season's Sheffield Shield title and, at 27, he has added leadership qualities, more experience and maturity since he last played for Australia.

Cooper Connolly is the other former Test player who's been mentioned in dispatches.

Cooper Connolly is an option for the future. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Connolly played his one and only Test in Sri Lanka, where he batted at eight scoring four runs.

He hasn't played a first-class match since last March — one of four he played for Western Australia — scoring 216 runs in total with a top score of 70 and an average of 30.85.

He was part of the Australian team on the limited overs tour of Bangladesh highlighted by his man of the match performance in the third ODI where he scored 149 as an opener alongside Inglis.

Earlier in the year he scored 107 off just 59 balls for Punjab Kings in the Indian Premier League to become the youngest ever overseas centurion in that competition.

The Western Australian will turn 23 this year and so has youth on his side and is sure to play a part in Australia's Test side in the future.

The question is: Is he ready now?

Another youngster whose name keeps coming up is Victoria's Campbell Kellaway, who scored 509 runs in the last Shield season with one century and two 50s at an average of 26.78.

Campbell Kellaway gives another potential option as a prolific run-scorer at Shield level. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Kellaway was a member of the Cricket Australia XI which beat Bangladesh by an innings in a warm-up match in Darwin before the first Test.

Unfortunately, he was bowled for a duck off five balls.

Another young gun, Sam Konstas, has failed to grab his chances at the highest level.

The New South Welshman is unbelievably still only 20 but seems to have packed more into his brief career than many more senior players.

The five Tests he played following his dynamic Boxing Day debut against India two years ago have netted Konstas 163 runs at an average of 16.3.

Like Kellaway, he failed in the recent tour match against Bangladesh scoring 1.

Sam Konstas has already had a couple of memorable moments in his career. (AAP: Bianca De Marchi)

Konstas is a constant in the selectors sights with a credible 660 runs in last season's Sheffield Shield at an average of 33.

The issue seems to be taming the impetuosity and proving he has the temperament to grind out a Test innings.

The forgotten man in Australian cricket is 33-year-old Kurtis Patterson.

Patterson scored 619 runs for NSW in the last Shield season at an average of 36.41.

His two Tests against Sri Lanka in 2019 included a not-out century but he was a victim of timing, squeezed out of the side as David Warner and Steve Smith returned from bans following the sandpaper scandal.

Patterson was a member of the CA XI, scoring 53 batting at number three which shows he's still in the thinking of selectors.

World.title: Golf course in court as parklands protesters take on SA government
World.content:
In what's been described as a David and Goliath battle, a trial has begun in the Federal Court, with two South Australians challenging the state government's redevelopment of the North Adelaide golf course.

Public servant Edwin Kemp Attrill and Kaurna Arabana woman Janette Milera are challenging the redevelopment, arguing it is in breach of federal conservation laws.

In front of other protesters opposed to the parklands project outside court, Mr Kemp Attrill said the unfolding legal process was "very nerve-wracking".

"It's a big uphill battle for us but we're really proud to be standing here," he said.

Ms Milera said she was taking action because she thought it was the right thing to do.

"This case is about respecting cultural tradition and truth telling," she said.

For [SA Premier] Peter [Malinauskas], it's a new golf course. For me, it's a bloodline.

"This case we're doing is because the parklands belong to the people and they need to be protected."

Protesters opposed to the state government's actions in the Adelaide parklands gathered outside the Federal Court. (ABC News: Leah MacLennan)

The state government announced its plan to redevelop and expand the golf course, as part of its bid to move the LIV Golf tournament into the city.

It said 585 trees would be cut down in the process, to be replaced with new plantings.

The state government passed laws earlier this year, taking control of that part of the parklands away from the Adelaide City Council, to allow it to go ahead with the redevelopment.

But the removal of trees sparked protests and the legal action taken by Mr Kemp Attrill and Ms Milera.

The redevelopment of the North Adelaide course has involved the felling of hundreds of trees. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

In his opening address, the lawyer for the pair, Arturo Dal Cin, told the court the Adelaide parklands were given national heritage listing in 2008.

He said more than 400 trees had already cut down at the golf course — a number he said accounted for 15 per cent of all the trees in the area marked for the first stage of the development.

"Recognition of parklands necessarily includes recognition of established trees, because a necessary element of parklands is established, mature trees," Mr Dal Cin said.

He said the works have impacted the national heritage values of the parklands.

"A fundamental issue in this case, one of the fundamental issues, is the extent to which your Honour finds the removal of trees to this scale to be a significant impact on what the appellants will be contending is a national heritage value — namely the parklands and their protection," he said.

Trees were removed from the area in May. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Mr Dal Cin said evidence would also be presented during the trial about the impact on Aboriginal cultural heritage and on local flying fox populations.

'Assault on democracy'

Before going to court, government lawyers wrote to Mr Kemp Attrill, warning him he could be liable for $4 million in costs if he lost.

Outside court, Mr Kemp Attrill said the government had not backed down.

"It's really concerning to us that in a public interest case the government has continued to say that they will essentially crush us if they win," he said.

"We think that's incredibly unfair and it's an assault on democracy in South Australia."

Mr Kemp Attrill had submitted an affidavit to the court saying he was "shocked" when he saw the loss of trees.

On cross-examination, he was shown aerial pictures of the course before and after the tree removal.

Crown lawyer Alison Doecke KC asked if a significant number of trees remained in the parklands following the works.

"I put to you that when one has regard to the aerial view, it is very hard to identify where the trees have been removed," she said.

"From the two photographs, yes," Mr Kemp Attrill said.

He said he often walks his dog around the golf course at night, and he has noticed the loss of trees.

"Walking around the perimeter, you can notice there's more sky," he said.

The redevelopment of the course was announced as part of plans for LIV Golf. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Ms Doecke suggested to Mr Kemp Attrill that "the significant change in the appearance of the site is because of the removal of the grass, not the removal of the trees. Do you accept that?" she said.

"No, as I said, it was noticeable as soon as the trees were removed; the view was different," Mr Kemp Attrill said.

"Standing outside the fence, if you're not right up against the fence you actually don't see the grass, you can only see the trees, and that was a noticeable difference."

But when asked by Ms Doecke if he would concede "there's still an awful lot of trees on the site", Mr Kemp Attrill said "yes".

Speaking at a media conference, Premier Peter Malinauskas said his government has acted lawfully.

"All the advice that I've received from the relevant agencies is they've sought to comply with all requirements as they've gone through it," he said.

" I've said all along that any individual is welcome to take up their rights to challenge things in court, as is being done in this particular instance. "

The trial is expected to take five days, with government lawyers to present their response on Wednesday.

World.title: Sydney Swans CEO confirms police investigating alleged incident 'involving several players'
World.content:
The Sydney Swans have confirmed several of their footballers were involved in an "alleged incident" in Melbourne last night.

The Swans issued a statement just after midday today.

"The Swans have notified the AFL and relevant authorities and cannot provide further comment at this stage," the club said.

Victoria Police separately issued a statement saying detectives were investigating a report of a sexual assault in East Melbourne.

The Sydney Swans stayed at the Pullman in East Melbourne last night. (ABC News)

"The incident occurred at a hotel on Wellington Parade in the early hours of the morning," a spokesperson said.

"The exact circumstances are yet to be established, and the investigation into the incident remains ongoing."

Sydney Swans chief executive Matthew Pavlich called a press conference this afternoon that lasted less than one minute.

"We're still piecing together exactly what's transpired here and have our own set of internal inquiries ongoing," he said.

"Safe to say, we're extremely shocked and disappointed that this has taken place and that the players have found themselves in this situation.

"We understand the level of interest in the matter, and there's going to be lots of speculation, but given it's a police matter right now, that's all that we can say."

Matthew Pavlich addressed the media this afternoon. (ABC News)

The AFL released a brief statement.

"The club made the AFL aware of the matter which is currently under Victoria Police investigation," the statement read.

NSW Police Minister Yasmin Catley said she was unaware of the details of the allegations, but she was confident Victorian authorities would take them "very seriously."

"We have to be mindful of the fact that the alleged offences occurred in a different jurisdiction. So, they [Victoria Police] will be leading that investigation," she said.

Asked if she would be seeking a briefing from police herself given it was a high-profile case allegedly involving Sydney-based AFL players, she said: "The police will definitely lead on that" and "brief me accordingly".

"The investigation is underway, I think we should let the police do their work in Victoria, and the NSW police will let me know if I need to know anything."

The Swans were staying in Melbourne overnight after their 36-point win over Essendon at the MCG yesterday.

Sydney is sitting in second spot on the AFL ladder heading into the final round of the 2026 season, with the finals due to start within weeks.

The team has had 17 wins this season and is due to play its next game at home at the SCG against North Melbourne.

World.title: No smiles as Chris O'Connell advances, while Aussie women's campaign ends
World.content:
Chris O'Connell and Adam Walton have made it four Australian men in the third round of the Cincinnati Master, while Talia Gibson's loss to Aryna Sabalenka left the women's draw without green and gold representation.

Gibson was beaten 6-2, 7-6(7/2) by the world number one in an hour and 52 minutes, while O'Connell and Walton joined Alex de Minaur and Rinky Hijikata in the round of 32.

But O'Connell was in no mood to celebrate after progressing thanks to an injury retirement by 11th-seeded opponent Casper Ruud.

The Australian qualifier picked up his fourth win in five days at the Masters 1000 tournament in what is proving his most profitable week of the season, but there were no smiles as he sympathised with Norway's three-time grand slam finalist on his concerning retirement after 64 minutes play.

Ruud had started well, moving into a 5-2 lead in the opening set, but the Sydneysider powered back to take the first set, sealing it 7-5 with an ace, as Ruud began to look in increasing discomfort with a back problem.

With Ruud leading the second set 2-1 on serve, the Norwegian world number 17 stretched for a wide serve and immediately decided enough was enough, going to the net to offer his hand to the Aussie.

Clearly with one eye on the US Open, where the main draw starts a week on Sunday, 2022 Flushing Meadows runner-up Ruud was not keen to take any risks.

For world number 129 O'Connell, it was the continuation of an excellent spell following his first-round victory over Poland's world number 68 Kamil Majchrzak.

He will next meet Brazilian teenage superstar Joao Fonseca, who defeated Botic van de Zandschulp 6-4, 7-6(7/2), and victory in that match would push O'Connell back to the verge of the world's top 100.

Talia Gibson's loss to Aryna Sabalenka leaves no Australian women in the Cincinnati singles draw. (Getty Images: Robert Prange)

Walton made it four Australians through to the third round along with Hijikata, who faces Jakub Mensik, and national number one Alex de Minaur, who meets British Wimbledon hero Arthur Fery.

Walton, the 27-year-old Queenslander currently ranked 98 in the world, overcame the 29th-seeded Peruvian Ignacio Buse 6-4, 6-3 in 72 minutes to set up a showdown with either American Ben Shelton, the eighth seed, or Jaime Faria of Portugal.

World.title: After constant chopping and changing, Green goes 'back to what worked'
World.content:
Cameron Green has delivered for a shell-shocked Australian side to give himself breathing space at number five, leading captain Pat Cummins to predict a long stint in one position in the batting line-up.

Green's 104 in the second innings of the nine-wicket loss to Bangladesh in Darwin was his first in Australia and also broke an 11-innings run without passing the half-century mark.

The 27-year-old all-rounder has been heavily criticised in Australian cricket for not turning his undoubted potential into results.

But his knock in the loss means he leaves the Northern Territory as one of the only Aussie batters who can hold their heads high, with Cummins "not too sure" on the best course of action to turn things around before the second Test starts in Mackay on Saturday.

Shock loss to Bangladesh reveals Aussie cracks On paper, Australia's full-strength team should have wiped the floor with Bangladesh. But a lack of application to their Test match craft has left Australia vulnerable to teams that are driven to succeed in the longest format.

"We're always quite individual, everyone goes about it slightly differently, so coaches will work with each player individually," he said.

"I don't think there was a huge trend, everyone got out a little bit differently, but I think it's pretty clear it's not quite functioning as well as we'd like as a group.

"If we need to make some changes to our style, we've got a week or so, we better do it pretty quickly."

Cummins said before the Test that Green had been encouraged to "intimidate" and he did it the way he knows best, driving with commanding power and poise while accumulating runs at a steady rate without taking risks.

It is a method that has worked in Sheffield Shield cricket and he showcased why Test selectors have persevered with him despite the outside noise calling for his head.

Green's third Test century did not lead to a win but that was largely due to the failure of the rest of the order to stay with him in good batting conditions on the third and fourth days.

Australia will consider making changes to the underperforming top order for the second Test in Mackay that starts on Saturday, but Green will be one of the first picked.

"I'm sure he will get an extended run somewhere," Cummins said when asked if Green had tied down the number five position.

"I thought he was really impressive and controlled his innings. He looked in total command of his skills out there. He just needed one or two of us to bat alongside him."

Green and Steve Smith were the only Australian batters who could be happy with their output. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Green struggled in the last Ashes series, as many batters did, making just 171 runs at an average of 24.42 after being moved around from fifth to eighth in the order.

He earlier did a solid job on the West Indies tour, averaging 30.66 at first drop as the only member of the top three to average more than 20 across the three Tests.

"We obviously think very highly of Cam," Cummins said.

"The last Ashes series probably didn't go as well as he would have liked but before that on the West Indian tour he was probably our best batter in really tough circumstances when he was batting a little higher.

"It was great for him to go out there and show the rest of the world how good he is."

Quick hits as Bangladesh wraps up famous win Litton Das was wrong-footed behind the stumps, and Mehidy Hasan Miraz suffered a worse fate in front of them. Here are the quick hits from day four of the first Test between Australia and Bangladesh.

Green was fortunate in the final session on the third day when an inside edge off Taskin Ahmed grazed his leg stump on the way to the boundary.

The bails were not dislodged and the all-rounder dug in and made the most of his reprieve.

Green told Fox Cricket after his knock that he had approached his innings against Bangladesh like he used to do "back in the day".

"I think I've just been chopping and changing a little bit recently, so it's nice just to go back to what worked," Green said.

"It has been a long couple of months so it is nice to get a few rewards for it."

As for the critics, Green said it just came with the territory.

"I feel like there are always wolves when you are playing Test cricket. When you play for Australia, you always have to perform," he said.
